News.title: Brand & Co are ‘Sons of Savile’ protected by TV bosses – but unlike sicko Jimmy these predators will not die unpunished
News.content:
Next

IT was always significant that rock stars have loathed Russell Brand with a vengeance.

Twenty years ago, Bob Geldof took to the stage at the NME Awards to collect an honour. The ceremony was compered by Brand, then at the height of his sleazy fame.



“Russell Brand,” said Sir Bob, his voice dripping with contempt: “What a c***.”

Later that year, Brand suffered an even greater humiliation at the GQ Men of the Year Awards when Sir Rod Stewart publicly called him out for boasting that he’d “had a go at” Rod’s daughter Kimberly.

Rod stepped on stage to accept a lifetime achievement award and told Brand, sitting in the audience, to stand up. “You went with my daughter, did you?” seethed Sir Rod.



“Russell, stand up.” Brand sheepishly got to his feet.

“I took her out for an evening,” Brand simpered, an inveterate bully who caved as soon as he was ­confronted. “Did you behave ­yourself?” asked Rod.

“I never touched that girl,” Brand grovelled. “F***ing right you didn’t,” said Rod.

“You can’t just come up here and boast. I speak here as a father.”

Yes, both Geldof and Sir Rod were speaking as fathers. Brand’s name had been linked to Geldof’s daughter Peaches, then 16.



And Brand had boasted he’d had sex with Rod’s daughter Kimberly, then 27. It was a lie.

“He was humbled, absolutely humbled,” Rod later told Michael Parkinson.

“Because you don’t do that. Even in my heyday, I wouldn’t have done that.”

Bob Geldof and Rod Stewart ­recognised something in Brand that is equally true of his friend, the comedian and author David ­Walliams.

The latter were never simply womanisers. They were never merely promiscuous.



There was always something ­nastier, bleaker and darker in the way they used and disposed of — I nearly said “women”, but that doesn’t quite cover it, does it?

Brand and ­Walliams were never rock stars. They were nothing like rock stars — who, in my observation, tend to follow their own moral code.

Brand and Walliams are something else. They are the sons of Jimmy Savile.



Before he was exposed, Brand interviewed Savile on his radio show.

While Walliams put his letter to Jim’ll Fix It on the back page of his autobiography.

For a debauched lifetime, Savile raped and assaulted his victims in hospitals, schools, children’s homes and television studios.

How did he get away with it?

Because, like convicted rapist Brand, and alleged sexual predator Walliams, he was allowed to.



Savile was protected, empowered and enabled. His employers at the BBC looked the other way.

As children were raped under their noses, they just did not want to know.

“It is now clear that Savile was hiding in plain sight,” said a report into Savile’s crimes two years after his death in 2011.



“And using his celebrity status and fund-raising to gain uncontrolled access to vulnerable people across six decades.”

Brand hardly kept his depravity a secret. In a bitterly ironic prophecy, he even made a joke on a TV panel show about doing a ten-year stretch for rape. How the audience roared with laughter!

And for all of Walliams’ charity work, his interest in teenage girls could hardly be called a state secret.

No, it is not the rock stars of this world who are without any moral code.

It is the funnymen, the light entertainers, the happy hosts like Rolf Harris, Stuart Hall, Huw Edwards, David Walliams and Jimmy Savile, and the much- lauded late-night wide boys like Russell Brand, who demanded to be celebrated, even when his conquests were without consent, even when he could not remember the names and faces of his victims.



In 2004, Jonathan Ross, a close friend to the sons of Savile, made a joke at the 15th annual British Comedy Awards that will now hound him for a lifetime.

“And like all 15-year-olds, it’s drunk, it’s unpredictable and it’s probably going home with David Walliams,” smirked Jonathan, before the cameras panned across to his chortling pal.

Ross now claims he knew nothing about the appetite the Little Britain star had for ­dangerously young girls and he was merely repeating a joke that a team of writers had given him.

And that would be a lot easier to believe if Ross, like the craven best pal of the playground bully, had not gleefully joined in Brand’s ­hideous harassment of Andrew Sachs, then 78, as they relentlessly crowed about Brand sleeping with the elderly Fawlty Towers actor’s granddaughter in 2008.

All these years later, the sheer nastiness of the act still beggars belief.



And it was done from the hallowed halls of Radio Two in Broadcasting House.

Brand told us what he was — a vicious sexual predator, cackling at the humiliation of his victims.

Walliams was rumoured to be a hunter of under-age girls.



From the BBC to Britain’s Got Talent, our broadcasters did not simply look the other way when Brand, Walliams and yes, Jimmy Savile, were demonstrating to the world how vile they were. Those great broadcasting ­institutions held their coats.

I spent my early 20s on the road with rock stars. I have seen the wild side of the street.

But I never saw anything as brazenly nasty as Brand. And I never saw any ­musician, even the wildest of the wild boys, flaunt their dubious ­sexual preferences like Walliams.

Rock stars tend to have their own standards of basic humanity, their own common decency. The sons of Jimmy Savile are different.

In all my years on the road with bands, some of the baddest boys in the land, I never witnessed ­anything as blatantly vicious as the phone calls Brand and Jonathan Ross made to Andrew Sachs in 2008.



Is it any wonder Brand turned out to be a rapist? The sheer pleasure he took in the tormenting of him should have been a wake-up call to the nation. To the BBC.

All the left-wing luvvies like Andy Burnham and Ed Miliband and Lucy Powell were licking Brand’s cowboy boots for years after he gleefully tortured an elderly man because he’d had sex with his beloved granddaughter.

Brand showed the world he was a woman-hating abuser. He crowed about it.

Just as Walliams hardly made an effort to disguise his ­preference for girls of tender years.

When Brand was having sex in the disabled toilets of the BBC with the winners of 6 Music competitions, when Walliams was said to be entertaining young girls in his bathrobe in his BGT dressing room, they were part of the tawdry Savile tradition of hiding in plain sight.



As with Savile, too many were bullied into silence by the activities of Brand, Walliams and the next pervert who gets pulled kicking and screaming from the rotten woodwork.

But that is changing. Why is Russell Brand in prison doing a ten-year stretch for rape and sexual assaults?

Why are Walliams’s books being withdrawn by his publisher?

Why is he unlikely to be stepping out of the shower in a BGT ­changing room any time soon?

Why have their friends deserted them? Why does nobody want to touch them with a rancid barge pole? Why are they getting exactly what they deserve?



Because a few brave women would not keep silent — no matter how they were threatened.

Because a handful of brave women have come forward to tell their truth, uncowed by legal threats and online abuse and a criminal justice system that is geared to protect the wealthy and the powerful.

The women who relayed their experiences in court about Brand, and on camera about Walliams, have made it easier for more ­victims’ voices to be heard.

And they will be heard.

Jimmy Savile died in his bed in 2011 without ever facing criminal charges, convictions or punishment.



It is unlikely that the sons of Savile will go unpunished.

News.title: Putin orders UK to stop defending Europe with nukes as tyrant reveals peace demands & Ukraine ‘offered Nato lifeline’
News.content:
Next

VLADIMIR Putin has demanded that the UK stop defending Europe with nuclear weapons if Britain wants to end the tyrant’s invasion of Ukraine.

The ultimatum is on a new list of brazen demands made by the Russian dictator which lay out his terms for ending the nearly five-year-old war.



It has also been revealed that the US offered Russia the rest of the Donbas region in exchange for Ukrainian Nato membership as part of peace talks, according to Volodymyr Zelensky.

Washington has not confirmed the Ukrainian president’s comments – which come shortly after a week of unsuccessful negotiations between Kyiv and Moscow.



On Saturday it was reported that Russian officials had drawn up a maximalist checklist of terms for ending Putin’s invasion.

The shameless document demands that Nato remove all troops from Eastern Europe and the Baltic states.



It also says Finland must leave the defence pact – having joined in the wake of the war.

The policy paper goes on to say Nato must rule out sending troops to Ukraine – and only then will Putin allegedly weigh up a ceasefire.



The document also seeks to put an end to “the supply of any type of Western weapons and military equipment and products to Ukraine”.

Russia would keep any occupied territory it still controls after the fighting stops, the paper adds.

In exchange, Moscow could approve Kyiv joining the EU – a minor concession for such megalomaniac demands.



The document, dated to November 10, was first reported by Bild.

It is strikingly similar to the far-reaching demands made by Putin in late 2021 – when he asked Nato to back down across the continent.

He went on to invade Ukraine just months later.

Putin is desperate to have Western troops pulled back to the alliance’s borders as they were last century.

More and more countries in Eastern Europe have asked to join Nato over recent decades out of fear of Russian aggression.



The threat was most starkly highlighted when Moscow invaded Georgia in 2008.

Putin’s latest document serves as the foundation for any future talks between Ukraine and Russia.

The discussions are currently being mediated by Donald Trump‘s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.

His ridiculous proposals are likely to be thrown out by Nato and Ukraine.

The UK is the only European country to commit its submarine-based nuclear deterrent to the wider defence of Nato.



On Thursday, after meeting European leaders in Dublin, UK prime minister Andy Burnham said continental security was not to be compromised for Russia.

He said: “There was a very strong feeling that Russian demands to put the question of European security architecture or European security arrangements into this negotiation.

“Well, no, that’s not up for negotiation. It’s for Europe to decide its own arrangements, Europe and Europe alone.”

Finland has also ruled out leaving the defence alliance.

It comes as Zelensky said on Saturday the US floated the idea of Kyiv ceding the remaining Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership.



Ukraine has long sought to join the Western pact – but the move has historically been ruled out by the US and others like Germany.

Moscow controls much of the Donbas region.

Kyiv has said it is unwilling to give up sovereign territory.

Zelensky said of the proposal: “The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?’

“This was the first time this had been raised.”



The Ukrainian leader also said if he received a draft peace deal with security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine’s military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.

Trump, Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping are expected to meet on the side-lines of a Shenzhen summit next week.

On Thursday, they are set to discuss AI, the Iran war, but not Russia’s war in Ukraine, according to senior US officials.

News.title: Newly surfaced pics show ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang holding smiling ‘Chinese spy’ lover’s waist after affair exposed
News.content:
Next

NEWLY surfaced photos show ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang getting hands on with his alleged Chinese spy mistress – years before the affair was revealed.

The shamed tech titan, 63, was spotted with his hand on the waist of smiling businesswoman Alice Huang as the pair locked eyes at an event in Taiwan in June 2024.



The billionaire stepped down from his role at the chipmaker this week following reports he had secret extramarital flings with three women.

Alice, 49, who shares the same surname but is not related to the ex-CEO, is believed to be a Chinese spy, according to US intelligence.



In the risqué snaps, the pair exchange friendly smiles as they embrace each other following a speech delivered by Huang at the COMPUTEX event.

She appears to congratulate the then Nvidia boss enthusiastically – with Huang even placing his left hand on her lower waist.

Alice was introduced to Huang by her own husband, with the pair first meeting in December 2023.

Their affair is believed to have begun in 2024.



Huang, who is married to his college sweetheart wife Lori, has also been accused of having two additional affairs.

Earlier this week reports emerged he allegedly loved- up with Nvidia‘s healthcare vice president Kimberly Powell.

And hours later a report claimed he had a secret fling with yet another employee at the chipmaking giant.



Huang’s dramatic fall from grace has wiped $200billion off the company’s value this week.

The leather jacket-loving casanova, who founded Nvidia more than three decades ago, resigned on Thursday amid the spiralling scandal.

He is set to appear before Congress to answer questions related to national security and his relationship with Huang.



The FBI has also launched an investigation into him.

Meanwhile, the White House has come under fire for not properly assessing claims Huang was romantically involved with a suspected Chinese spy, despite being briefed on the situation months before it emerged.

The former Nvidia CEO was a pivotal figure in balancing China-US relations amid the deepening AI race.

He pushed for Washington to greenlight critical AI chip sales to Beijing.

Elon Musk has also weighed in on the saga, warning Nvidia could lose out on critical supply chain deals without Huang in place to broker them.



The Tesla and SpaceX boss said Huang was an instrumental figure.

He said on X: “Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost.

“If Jensen gave me his word about computer delivery or I asked for components to be accelerated, he always came through.”

Nvidia, the world’s second most valuable company, makes graphics processing units (GPUs) used in AI data centres.

News.title: David Walliams whistleblower Lucy Beaumont’s bravery should be applauded but call to change law of consent is ridiculous
News.content:
Next

COMEDIAN Lucy Beaumont should be applauded for her bravery this week.

There is nothing funny about becoming a whistleblower, but she has exposed what is really going on in the land of TV when the cameras aren’t rolling.



I respect her for speaking out. But I cannot get my head around her call for “staggered consent” to be put in place on the back of the Russell Brand and David Walliams scandals, as if it could be some sort of magic solution for the future. It isn’t.

Not just because it’s ridiculous to think it’s the government’s job to legislate who is in your bedroom. But because even if they brought this law change in, it wouldn’t work.

It isn’t enough. It would be pointless in the fight against all the perils which children today face.



There is only one thing that could potentially stop older men like Brand preying on schoolgirls — and that is the law of Mum and Dad.

Lucy has backed the Close The Consent Gap campaign, which ­proposes making it a criminal offence for adults aged 20 or older to have sex with 16 and 17-year-olds unless the age gap is restricted to three years or less.

Of course, on the surface, that makes sense. No OAP should want to date a teenager.

And a law change could stop those creepy, middle-aged blokes who want to date a pretty young girl from ­pursuing a teenager for fear of prosecution.

It could also clamp down on women who seem to think it’s OK to date a toyboy, even though they are old enough to be the lad’s mother. Bringing it in may help in those cases.



But what about the real, nasty and evil ­predators? They won’t stop to think about this law or the potential ­consequences — and merely carry on as they were.

Maybe that’s something Brand will be chewing over now he’s been transferred to his new jail.

It was one of his accusers who first raised the concept of staggered consent several years ago because she had a sexual ­relationship with him when she was 16 and he was in his 30s.

It didn’t bother him. Because the real criminals don’t care about laws, just like he didn’t care about his victims.

There are many women who now accuse Britain’s Got Talent judge Walliams of “grooming” them when they were teenagers. One says he began contacting her when she was 15 and another described a “sexual assault” at the same age.



I feel utter sympathy for each and every one of those victims. And their families. They were children who were young, impressionable and preyed on. It must be devastating for all of them.

But, tragically, these cases must now serve as a warning to every family out there.

Because we shouldn’t simply be legislating on who can date who. We must go back to stronger parenting.

This law wouldn’t be able to assess the emotional maturity of a teenager or work out the power dynamics in a relationship.

It wouldn’t be able to tell if they are vulnerable, desperate for love and have a longing for fame.



Only a loving parent who is doing their job properly can truly see that. If they care about the children, they must now realise it is essential to talk about the perils out there, and give them the sort of education you can’t get at school.

Parents need to monitor what is seen online, because the money-grabbing social media companies won’t protect kids from evil.

These businesses don’t care in the way a parent must. When I was a teen and dated boys that my father wasn’t keen on, he made it known.

If they’d been double my age, he would have acted. Maybe in this modern world there needs to be more old- fashioned parenting where mums and dads lay down the law and prevent kids from dating someone they really shouldn’t.

They won’t like it. But it could be what saves them.



FREIDA A CUT ABOVE

THE stories of celebrity hairdresser John Frieda poured in after his death.

But the most staggering part of his life is how he started out.

He was the salon dogsbody who, as he once put it, was “the best towel-folder and floor-sweeper in the business”.

His attention to detail and hard graft helped him get noticed, sell a lot of Frizz Ease and amass a £260million fortune.

That is the kind of success story of starting at the bottom of the ladder and working to the top that we all want.



But can our school leavers and graduates do that now? Not a chance.

Those entry-level jobs aren’t there because bosses don’t want to employ NEETs – they just can’t afford to.

Which is why former minister Alan Milburn’s youth welfare review and resulting plans to get the next generation into work – which could cost £6BILLION a year – seem so unrealistic.

They will see young people moved off the main sickness and disability benefits and on to “youth allowance” or “additional cost allowance”. Fewer will be entitled. But this is just swapping one benefit for another.

What they need are actual jobs. And crippled businesses can’t afford to take them on.



First, the Government must reverse the employer National Insurance contributions increase and freeze any rises in the minimum wage, instead of landing us all with another benefit bill.

Only then can businesses take on the young people they say they want to help.

D’OHS & CONS

RIDICULOUS conman Lee Andrews has had “Katie P” inked on his penis and he’s so proud that he’s been flashing his new tattoo to pals in Dubai.

Lucky them!

But perhaps not the best idea… as the world now knows he didn’t have room for her full name.



CHARLES’S ROLE IN CREATING ROCK ROYALTY

THERE hasn’t been much to laugh about this week, but the thought of King Charles being a fan of rock superstars Muse brought a smile to my face.

Then again, perhaps it would be odd if he wasn’t a fan.

The Devon band received an early career grant from what was then The Prince’s Trust to help buy essential musical equipment.



So, he can claim to have played a small part in getting them off the ground.

SHAME FAGIN MUM

SHOPKEEPER Shamly Sud has been slammed for sharing a video of a child aged about three, wearing Lilo & Stitch pyjamas, blatantly nicking food from her garage shop.

In the scenes, with the girl’s face blurred, you can see her expertly packing five items down her PJs – and Shamly rightly says that the blame is purely on her mother.



She’s shocking, and if someone spots that child and intervenes, it will be no bad thing.

Taking your child out in pyjamas is lazy, but acting like a modern- day Fagin means she deserves every bit of public shaming she gets.

DELIVEROO really can bring out the worst in us.

I am totally guilty of using it for that late-night bottle of wine, craving for special fried rice or emergency groceries.



But this year, the company says its biggest seller to ­customers was ice cubes.

I wasn’t one of them. When you’re heading into a heatwave, you know the score.

And I draw the line at ­paying for ­frozen water.

WAKEY BAKEY

AFTER suffering with a major hangover this week, the thought of waking up in the new Greggs hotel filled me with absolute joy.



The blue and gold-coloured rooms in the Newcastle hotel could be tricky to deal with the morning after.

But there’s a special phone next to the bed so you can order any Greggs goods in your hour of need.

And what I really needed was pastry. Lots of it.

News.title: Chinese AI firm linked to Iran’s regime shares sensitive satellite images of RAF base in new spying scandal
News.content:
Next

A CHINESE AI satellite firm linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps shared high-res images of an RAF base over several months.

MizarVision tracked the positions of US bombers at the Fairford site from the start of the Iran War, leaving them vulnerable to drone strikes.



Military experts said the company’s brazen actions would have “spooked” the Americans, who decided to move their nine Rockwell B-1B Lancers from the Gloucestershire RAF base last month.

Some of the MizarVision images — which rely on an AI tool to identify and tag military assets from satellite photos — are posted on Chinese social media platform Weibo.



The company, which produces precise data by fusing information from commercial and radar imaging satellites, also published images of the Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia on February 27, the day before the Iran War began.

US officials said it was likely the posts were linked to Iran’s attacks there less than two days later, which cost a US serviceman his life.

Former British Army Colonel Simon Diggins, now a security analyst, said terrorists could use MizarVision imagery for targeting.

He said it was plausible to link information from them to a threat against RAF Fairford which saw counter-terror police arrest seven men in September.



He said: “I think it was that which probably spooked the Americans, who were probably thinking, ‘They know where our bombers are’.”

Dr Mark Hilborne, of King’s College London’s Defence Studies Department, added last night: “It is highly likely this company could pass that information on to Iran.”

He said MizarVision could be analysing sensitive sites over the UK all the time, adding that the Russian military Wagner Group used similar imagery to target Ukraine’s battlefield positions.



It comes as RAF Lakenheath — another UK base used by the US Air Force — was put on lockdown on Friday night after “suspected unauthorised drone activity” near the site in Suffolk.

That followed an Iran-linked security threat at nearby RAF Mildenhall on November 9 which led the USAF to remove at least 12 aircraft.

A Ministry of Defence spokesman said: “We keep the security of our personnel, sites and capabilities under constant review and take appropriate measures to protect them. We actively track commercial satellite imagery which is publicly available and monitor threats.”

He said Lakenheath had “returned to normal security” yesterday.

News.title: Woman, 80, fighting for life after being ‘doused with liquid & set on fire’ in flat as distraught family demand answers
News.content:
VILE ATTACK Woman, 80, fighting for life after being ‘doused with liquid & set on fire’ in flat as distraught family demand answers







Next

A PENSIONER has been left fighting for her life after allegedly being doused with liquid and set on fire in her home.

Brenda Raymond, 80, was discovered alight in the first-floor communal area of a block of flats in Watford, Hertfordshire, at 12.47pm on November 9.



The 80-year-old sustained catastrophic injuries and was rushed to hospital where she remains in critical condition as her distraught family demand answers.

A 33-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit arson with intent to endanger life and has since been bailed with strict conditions.



In a statement, her family said: “Words cannot describe how distressing the past few days have been for us as a family.

“Our beautiful, chatty, fun-loving and much-loved Brenda, who loves to keep fit and dancing, has suffered catastrophic injuries in the most devastating of circumstances; circumstances which have left us all in complete shock.

“We simply cannot understand why anyone would have wanted to hurt her in this way. Someone out there knows something. They know what happened to Brenda.

“We are desperate for answers and are pleading for anyone with information to please come forward. If you know anything at all, no matter how insignificant it may seem, please speak to police or contact Crimestoppers anonymously.



“We would ask that our privacy is respected as we continue to navigate our way through this unimaginably difficult time.”

Police believe Brenda was attacked as she returned home and sprayed with an accelerant before she was set alight in her flat.

Evidence recovered at the scene also suggested that a flammable liquid was poured through the letterbox of another property in the area.

Detectives are urging any witnesses to come forward, especially if anyone saw a person wearing a face covering, balaclava or mask, acting suspiciously or fleeing the scene.

Officers are also keen to hear from anyone who heard screams before emergency services were called, or is aware of anyone who purchased flammable liquid around the time of the harrowing attack.



Detective Inspector Adam Bridges, from the Major Crime Unit, said: “This was an appalling and deeply distressing attack on an elderly woman who suffered horrific injuries after being set alight outside her own home.

“Our thoughts very much remain with Brenda and her family as we continue to do everything we can to find out what happened and who is responsible.

“Her family are understandably distraught and have taken the step of releasing her name and photograph to help jog people’s memories around this distressing and highly unusual incident.

“Someone out there knows something. You may have witnessed suspicious activity, heard a conversation, noticed unusual behaviour, or captured something on CCTV or dash cam footage without realising its significance.

“Please do not assume that what you know is too small or unimportant to tell us about. It could be a seemingly insignificant piece of information that provides investigators with the breakthrough they need.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“If you know anything about what happened to Brenda or think you may have information that could assist our enquiries, please come forward. Your information could be crucial in helping us find answers and bring those responsible to justice.”

Anyone with information is encouraged to contact the force’s dedicated online portal, call 101 quoting Operation Tibbin or Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

News.title: Body of man, 26, found in canal after Coronation Street star issued urgent missing person plea during two-week search
News.content:
TRAGIC FIND Body of man, 26, found in canal after Coronation Street star issued urgent missing person plea during two-week search







Next

COPS have discovered the body of a 26-year-old man in a canal after a Coronation Star issued an urgent missing person plea.

The man’s body was sadly found in the Birmingham and Fazeley Canal, shortly before 9am today.



West Midlands Police believe it is the body of 26-year-old Dylan Mandaracas, who went missing last month.

Dylan vanished after he was last seen on CCTV on Walmley Close, Sutton Coldfield, on October 28 at around 6pm.



Officers said the body was discovered in the water just off Kingsbury Road.

The force doesn’t believe there to be any suspicious circumstances surrounding the man’s death.

His family have been informed, with cops now working to help the coroner.

Dylan was last seen wearing a checked shirt with black work trousers and was close to the Fox Stonehouse Pub.

Actor Tony Maudsley, a friend of Dylan’s mum, previously issued an appeal.

The Benidorm star said: “Posting this for a close friend whose son has gone missing.



“Hoping the power of social media can help this desperate family. Please share far & wide.”

A spokesperson for West Midlands Police today said: “Shortly before 9am today (Saturday) we were called to reports that a man’s body had been discovered in a canal off the Kingsbury Road, Tyburn.

“Sadly, we believe the man to be 26-year-old Dylan Mandaracas, who had been reported missing on 2 November.

“We have carried out enquiries and don’t believe there are any suspicious circumstances surrounding his death.

“His family has been informed, and our thoughts are with them at this sad time.



“We will now be working to support the coroner.”

News.title: Young people should have legal guarantee of job or training, Milburn tells BBC
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has described Milburn's forthcoming report as a "watershed moment," but stopped short of committing to implementing its recommendations in full.

Burnham also insisted paying for the reforms would not mean "more money" but "spending differently" in government when pressed on the large upfront investment they are expected to require.

Asked whether he would accept the politically sensitive report in full, Burnham declined to provide that "blanket assurance".

Speaking at the Welsh Labour conference on Saturday, Burnham said that the report addressed the "youth detachment" that has been on the rise since the pandemic.

"It can't be right that we've stripped away support from young people as a society, as life is getting harder for them and growing up is getting more difficult," he said.

The prime minister added that the government was also looking at a new vision for schooling that is "not focused solely on the university route" and which offers technical education alongside traditional academic learning.

Lord Blunkett, a former Labour home secretary, told the BBC that money from cutting benefits spending should be reassigned to supporting employment "at least in the immediate future".

Speaking on Radio 4's Today programme, he said reforms should focus on "transferring resource that currently goes into paying for failure, keeping youngsters at home, isolated, lonely, into actually putting the money in and the resource and the commitment in to making those jobs available".

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has previously said the government should not be spending "lots of time" on employment schemes, which she said would ultimately fail.

Her party and Reform UK have argued for significant cuts to welfare, including to fund a boost to defence.

Reform economy spokesman Robert Jenrick said: "This review is pointless unless we get action from Burnham straight away.

"It cannot be right that this continues for another 10 years before the youth benefits bill comes down."

Green Party leader Zack Polanski said it was "disappointing" the Milburn review had "come up with the same tired conclusions" on youth unemployment.

Polanski added: "Using benefit sanctions to force young people into low-paid, insecure work doesn't solve the structural inequalities they face, and it deepens poverty."

The Liberal Democrats want the government to introduce a 100-hour work experience guarantee and a careers coach for every young person.

They believe this would equip youngsters with the best possible skills before they leave school.

The TUC - the umbrella group for unions in the UK - welcomed Milburn's proposal of a legal guarantee as a "game changer", describing the country's number of Neets as a "national emergency".

But it stressed that funding for additional support for young people should not come from public service budgets. "In further education, funding needs to be targeted at the workforce, as well as provision, to tackle the recruitment and retention crisis and massive pay disparities in the sector," it said.

"A zero sum approach would be wrong and counter-productive."

News.title: Neets review won't be for the faint-hearted - and will test Burnham's appetite for a welfare fight
News.content:
It's an ugly acronym. And it's an even uglier situation.

The reality of so-called "Neets" in the UK - young people who haven't got jobs, aren't studying or being trained up - has seen hundreds upon hundreds of thousands in their late teens or early-20s struggle to find a decent future for well over a decade.

It costs the taxpayer billions. And the human cost is variously described as a disaster, a national shame, even a moral crisis.

When the phrase Neet was first coined by Tony Blair's Downing Street in 1999, the focus was on 170,000 or so teenagers who were not in education, employment or training. After many attempts at solving the problem, add in a pandemic and years of a sluggish economy, it's acute - with nearly a million under-25s in that situation.

A tome full of proposals to try and fix it once and for all will be published on Tuesday, after a year in the making.

How the government reacts will test its appetite and capacity for radical change, and the prime minister's real, not rhetorical, hunger for tricky political arguments.

The canny smooth talker behind the huge review, former Labour MP Alan Milburn, wants you to know that Andy Burnham knows exactly what's coming.

Speaking to me in Liverpool, where in Merseyside 14.5% of 16 to 24-year-olds are unemployed,, external he tells me: "All the way through, the prime minister, the chancellor, all the ministers, they know what's going on. It won't be a surprise to them when this is launched and that gives it a fighting chance of actually being implemented."

But his collection of proposals is not for the faint-hearted.

On top of a plan to stop under-25s claiming the main sickness and disability benefits, Milburn will argue for a dramatic shift in the balance of what the taxpayer spends on benefits for young people compared with what is spent on support to help them get into work.

He says the amount spent on young people's benefits is 25 times as much as that on employment support - and he wants to shift it to a drastically different two to one.

He won't put specific numbers on it yet, but accepts openly that means a significant number of young people losing their benefits or facing cuts.

But that would come with a chunky expansion of the amount of further education, training, health support and likely jobs subsidised by the taxpayer too. A big cut to state support on one side of the ledger, but a big increase on the other.

And to make sure that government gets really serious about improving the mess, Milburn is asking for a new law that would give young people a guarantee of help and support - a job, an apprenticeship, a training place, or perhaps health treatment so they are able to work - an "opportunity guarantee".

He told me he won't fall into the "elephant's trap", where a feisty teenager could sue the prime minister if they didn't get the job they fancied. But the idea is to put a legal duty on the authorities in a similar vein to councils' obligation to look after children in care, or to provide accommodation or advice to homeless people.

News.title: Noel Fielding 'appalled' by jokes he made with Russell Brand
News.content:
Noel Fielding has said he is "appalled" by jokes he made alongside Russell Brand when the pair appeared together on TV and at live shows.

The Great British Bake Off presenter said in a statement to the Sun he was "horrified and deeply disturbed" to learn of Brand's crimes, after the disgraced comedian was jailed for rape and sexual assault.

Footage of Fielding and Brand joking about rape with TV presenter Jonathan Ross on an episode of Channel 4's Big Fat Quiz of the Year in 2007 has resurfaced in the aftermath of Brand's conviction.

Fielding described "some of the jokes" he made as "horrible and inappropriate", and said he had not been in contact with Brand "for many years".

"I was horrified and deeply disturbed to learn of Russell Brand's crimes, which I was completely unaware of until they became public knowledge. My thoughts are with the women whose courage brought him to justice," Fielding said.

"I appeared on TV, radio and live charity shows with him, and whilst we played it up for the cameras and in the media, I considered it a professional relationship, rather than a personal one. I have had no contact with him for many years.

"Looking back at some of the jokes I made alongside him I was appalled. They were horrible and inappropriate, and I very much regret them."

Ross has also released a statement distancing himself from the remarks, saying that his "thoughts are with the many, many women who have bravely come forward."

Among the resurfaced footage is a clip of Brand and Fielding laughing on an episode of The Russell Brand Show, which aired on BBC Radio 2 in 2007. In it, Brand joked about kissing and holding an underage grasshopper.

"How do you even know if it's a child or an adult? You don't even care, do you," Fielding responded.

Brand can be heard replying: "It's a mistake I've made. I've had a lot of problems in the past, because I thought a grasshopper was above age. Before I know it, I'm in it, right, I'm kissing it, I'm holding it. Then it turns around and looks at me with onyx eyes and says: 'I'm 12.'"

Brand and Fielding also performed charity gigs together as The Goth Detectives.

News.title: 'Can you believe it?': SpaceX catches part of its Starship rocket on return to Earth
News.content:
SpaceX has successfully caught the top part of its huge Starship rocket on its return to Earth for the first time.

"Can you believe it?," a commentator said as large crowds cheered at the launch site in Texas.

The company had hoped to catch both the bottom and upper stages of the rocket using mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on its launch tower.

But the first catch of the rocket's booster was aborted a few minutes after the launch on Friday. The booster was diverted to the ocean, bursting into flames just above the sea.

The top part, known as the Ship, returned to Earth a few minutes behind schedule at around 15:27 local time (21:27 GMT) on Saturday and was successfuly caught.

News.title: Philippines takes the crown in first Eurovision Song Contest Asia
News.content:
The Philippines has won Asia's first ever Eurovision Song Contest with 19-year-old singer Carmelle and her women's empowerment anthem, Sobra-Sobra.

She received 211 points in total to win what was a nail biter to the end.

Despite its success with fans, the future of Asia's Eurovision depends on a huge commitment from broadcasters and sponsors.

The BBC's South East Asia correspondent Jonathan Head reports from Bangkok.

News.title: Even Grand Theft Auto's original creators haven't been able to play GTA 6
News.content:
After a 13-year wait, two delays, and several high-profile leaks, the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 is fast approaching.

The next chapter in the nearly 30-year-old series, where players explore open worlds and break the law, has created an extraordinary level of anticipation.

And with developer Rockstar Games keeping their biggest release yet, tightly under wraps, even the people who helped bring the original to life aren't getting special treatment.

"We're all waiting to see what they've done," Dave Jones, GTA's co-creator, tells me, sitting alongside the original game's writer and publicist, Brian Baglow.

Have either of them been able to play the new game ahead of launch?

Baglow shakes his head. He's not complaining, though. "I've got the pre-order," he says.

News.title: The search to find a friend for Jojo the gorilla after a lifetime of being alone
News.content:
In 2015, a young male gorilla named Jojo took his first tentative steps onto grass.

Until that moment, the 11-year-old ape had spent almost his entire life in a tiny cage at a private zoo in Gabon, after being taken from the wild as an infant. His family had been killed by the poachers who took him.

More than a decade later, Jojo is settled into a sanctuary â but he still lives alone. He hasn't had a family since he was taken, or indeed any gorilla friends.

Jojo's carers at the Lekedi Foundation in Gabon want to find a companion - possibly another rescued or zoo-bred gorilla â that Jojo could live and bond with. But finding him a friend - and bringing them into his life - is not straightforward.

"He's probably the most extreme case of isolation I've ever seen in a great ape," says Prof Gillian Forrester from the University of Sussex, who is studying Jojo as part of research into great ape psychology and how to help rescued animals recover from trauma.

News.title: Brand, Walliams and Married at First Sight: Is this a reckoning for the entertainment industry?
News.content:
This week, the dark side of television has come crashing into the open.

On Monday, disgraced entertainer Russell Brand was jailed for rape and sexual assault.

Twenty-four hours later, author and comedian David Walliams was unmasked and accused of preying on young women.

By Friday the Metropolitan Police had launched an investigation into further allegations about him.

Also in the last week, Married at First Sight UK has been cancelled following allegations of rape on the hit TV show.

These are all very different stories, but each can be seen as a major reckoning with abuse of power and culture in the industry.

So why is this all happening now?

In reality, the glut of recent days is something of a coincidence.

All these revelations began with journalistic investigations that started years ago.

From my own experience - including in my Panorama on Married at First Sight UK - I know investigations typically take a very long time to reach a conclusion, from initial tip-off, to evidence-gathering, corroboration, getting responses, and eventually reporting.

"The truth is, these stories have a long build up. It can be incredibly difficult to get [them] in the papers," Sunday Times columnist Hadley Freeman told me.

In the case of Brand, there was then a police investigation too, before an outcome was reached in court.

Together these stories represent the consequences of changes that began years ago, rather than a sudden cultural shift in the entertainment industry.

It should also be said that Walliams denies the allegations against him. The men accused of rape and sexual misconduct on MAFS UK have also denied all the allegations.

What has changed is that women (because it almost always is women) have seen others speaking up - which, according to broadcaster Kirsty Wark, has given them "courage to do the same". She describes those who have come forward as "beyond brave".

News.title: Man dies after being stabbed by gang of masked men
News.content:
A murder investigation has been launched after a 27-year-old man was stabbed in Manchester.

Officers were called to Moss Bank in the Crumpsall area of the city shortly after 01:30 GMT following reports that a man had suffered several stab wounds. He later died from his injuries in an ambulance.

Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said initial inquiries suggested the victim had been attacked by "a number of males" all believed to have been wearing dark clothing and balaclavas.

The suspects are believed to have fled the scene in the direction of Ash Tree Road, said a force spokesperson who added that no arrests had been made and inquiries were continuing.

News.title: UK ethics watchdog chief steps back from role over sexual misconduct claims
News.content:
The head of the government's main ethics watchdog has stepped back after it emerged he was investigated in a previous job over alleged sexual misconduct involving female colleagues, and had, in one case, been sanctioned.

Stuart Sterling was appointed as the first chief executive of the newly formed Ethics and Integrity Commission in October 2025.

The existence of the allegations against Sterling, and the investigations into them, were first reported by the Sunday Times.

Following the report, a government spokesperson said: "These are serious allegations. Stuart Sterling has stepped back from his role while we swiftly establish the facts."

The Labour Party promised in its 2024 manifesto to create the commission to "ensure probity in government" in response to scandals during the Covid pandemic.

As its head, Sterling's role included advising the prime minister on tackling misconduct in public life.

The Sunday Times reported that, in 2003, Sterling had been subject to a "full misconduct hearing" when he was a junior officer with Northamptonshire Police in what was treated as a case "of sexual harassment".

The paper said he had been accused of inappropriately touching the breasts of a female colleague in a police station, and a male colleague who allegedly witnessed the event had reported him to his superiors. It reported that he had been suspended on full pay.

A representative for Mr Sterling said: "Stuart states that a full disciplinary process was held regarding the complaint in 2002. He complied with this fully. It resulted in a sanction."

The Sunday Times reported that he was given a financial penalty of two weeks' pay. It said that, at the time, that was the maximum sanction possible short of forced resignation. He then received two police commendations and was promoted to be a detective sergeant.

The Sunday Times said that by 2008 Mr Sterling had been reported to the force again after another allegation of sexual misconduct against a female colleague, this time at a social gathering outside work.

Mr Sterling's representative said: "He denies that the alleged incident in 2008 ever took place. He was never subject to any criminal investigation, but the allegation was examined by professional standards".

The representative added: "He was not required to resign from the force. He left voluntarily".

Northamptonshire Police has confirmed that it holds a digital record of a misconduct process from 2002.

It did not comment on the later allegation.

In 2009, Sterling joined the Cabinet Office. It is not clear what vetting process he underwent. He has since served in a variety of senior roles and in 2019 was seconded to the National Police Chiefs' Council. In 2023 he received an OBE for helping to plan the funeral of Queen Elizabeth.

It is understood the Cabinet Office will now examine whether appropriate and correct disclosures of information were made.

News.title: King jokes with Elton John as he marks 78th birthday with radio show
News.content:
King Charles and Sir Elton John joked about the problems of ageing as the pair joined for a special radio show to coincide with the monarch's 78th birthday.

Sir Elton, 79, was joined on his regular Rocket Hour radio show for a special episode during which the King shared his musical memories as the pair chose 14 songs together.

The programme also marked the 50th anniversary of the King's Trust and highlighted how musicians have supported the charity's efforts.

"We and the Trust are definitely still standing," the King said, as he highlighted Sir Elton's track I'm Still Standing as one of his favourites because of the song's "message of resilience".

The music legend joked in reply: "I'm still sitting now, though" giving a large laugh, with the King chuckling: "With occasional bits dropping off here and there. I know this is a terrible problem as we get older."

The special was recorded last month at Apple Music Studios in south London and premiered on Saturday morning.

The King recalled Sir Elton's 1986 performance at Wembley Arena, which marked the charity's 10th anniversary.

"I suspect that no-one who was present on that night in 1986 could possibly forget your performance of I'm Still Standing," King Charles said.

"I know people in all kinds of circumstances find this song inspiring, not only for its marvellous spirit, but also its message of resilience. And certainly, 40 years on from that remarkable concert, we and the Trust are definitely still standing."

News.title: Burnham suggests Welsh Labour lost sight of devolution as review criticises ex-first minister's strategy
News.content:
The prime minister has told members of his party that Welsh Labour may have lost sight of some of the principles of devolution before it was thrown out of power in a historic election defeat.

On Saturday morning Andy Burnham addressed the first Welsh Labour conference since May's Senedd election.

He suggested the previous Labour government did not do enough to pass powers down to communities, and said it was "hard" to accept the party was no longer in power after 27 years of running the Welsh government.

He spoke before a review into what went wrong concluded that former First Minister Eluned Morgan's political strategy of calling out Westminster played a role in the party losing power.

The report by Prof Anand Menon, of PF Global, said Morgan's calls for constitutional change like the devolution of policing and the Crown Estate did not get through to voters.

A source close to the former first minister said it was "ludicrous" to suggest that Morgan was focused on constitutional issues.

Meanwhile, Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates has criticised his party for focusing too much on powers for the Senedd.

In a subdued speech, Burnham said he wanted to see "one Labour team" where "everyone" was "signed up and on the same page."

He spoke ahead of the publication of a review of what went wrong at the election.

Since he became prime minister he has been lobbying the Welsh government to devolve more powers to local councils.

"Somewhere along the way perhaps we lost sight of some of the principles that drove devolution in the first place.

"We probably stopped listening as much as we should have, and actually stopped driving power down into every Welsh postcode which is what the vision to me really should always have been about - about people and places."

He said the party would accept its defeat and "come back stronger" with a "vision for a stronger Wales in a fairer United Kingdom."

Burnham said he wanted to achieve the sense of a "one Labour team for Wales" where the party is "pulling in the same direction".

"Where I'm pulling with you and not creating problems for you or going against what Ken or colleagues want to achieve.

"We will put forward a vision for communities up and down Wales, as well as giving Wales a stronger national voice."

News.title: Magnificent Wales end 73-year New Zealand hoodoo
News.content:
Nations Championship

Wales (21) 35

Tries: T Williams, Lake, Griffin, James, Rees-Zammit Cons: Costelow 5

New Zealand (21) 28

Tries: Ratima, Sititi, Fineanganofo, Lakai Cons: Mo'unga 4.

Wales celebrated a first victory against New Zealand in 73 years with a brilliant performance to spark astonishing scenes in Cardiff.

Steve Tandy's unfancied side lifted a nation as they broke a 34-match losing sequence against the All Blacks that stretched back to 1953.

In a nine-try Nations Championship thriller at the Principality Stadium, Wales led 14-0, 21-7 and 35-21 before they held off New Zealand with a wonderful defensive display in the final quarter, led by flankers James Botham and Jac Morgan and lock Dafydd Jenkins.

The home side produced a stunning start with tries from inspirational scrum-half Tomos Williams and captain Dewi Lake inside the first six minutes.

Prop Archie Griffin also added a first-half try, but New Zealand responded with scores from scrum-half Cortez Ratima, number eight Wallace Sititi and wing Fehi Fineanganofo to level the score 21-21 at half-time.

Wales centre Eddie James and wing Louis Rees-Zammit scored early second-half tries before New Zealand flanker Peter Lakai pulled one back.

The remarkable Wales defence followed as they held up the All Blacks three times over the line to stop New Zealand scoring, to evoke wild celebrations.

News.title: Family's two-year fight to bring killer driver back from Latvia
News.content:
Days after her 12-year-old son was killed by a BMW driver travelling at 70mph, Louise Slater sat outside the suspect's home, gathering the courage to plead with his family to hand him in.

She had been given the name and address of Aleksanders Dolars after her son Keaton was killed in a hit-and-run in Coventry.

Distraught, she was preparing to knock on the door when a neighbour approached and asked what she was doing.

When she explained, he told her the family, from Latvia, had packed up and left a day or two earlier.

Keaton's suspected killer had fled just hours after leaving him dying in the road.

What followed was a relentless two-year fight by his parents to track him down and bring him back to England to face justice.

He was finally jailed on Friday, for nine years and four months.

This article contains upsetting details

Dolars' name had been already circulating locally before police identified him as their main suspect on 18 June 2024, four days after Keaton was killed.

A family waiting at nearby traffic lights said their seven-seater "shook violently" as a BMW driver sped past at what appeared to be far more than the 30mph limit. Moments later, they saw something fly into the air behind them.

The car did not stop.

As it disappeared from view, the family noticed a black rucksack and a single shoe lying in Radford Road and realised a child may have been hit.

News.title: Thousands turn out in Edinburgh to protest against AI data centres
News.content:
Thousands of people have joined a protest in Edinburgh against the building of large-scale AI data centres.

Demonstrators with placards - and some dressed in costume - assembled at the top of the Royal Mile before marching towards the Scottish Parliament.

The event comes at a time of widespread debate about the environmental impact of data centres and is part of a wave of protests across Europe.

The Scottish government will soon publish new planning guidance on data centres and said it was developing a strategy to maximise the "public benefit".

News.title: Milder weather coming before more cold health alerts take effect
News.content:
Another round of cold health alerts is set to come into force on Sunday following a brief break from the weekend's subzero temperatures.

After readings dipped as low as minus 7C early on Saturday, most places on Sunday morning will be milder and free of frost.

Widespread rainfall is likely with hail and thunderstorms possible for parts of Wales and southern England.

Into the new week, the wintry chill is set to return with UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) cold-health alerts beginning for the north-east and north-west of England and Yorkshire and the Humber from 21:00 GMT on Sunday.

News.title: Deputy working security at South Carolina gun show fatally shoots customer who shot him
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A deputy working security at a gun show in South Carolina fatally shot someone who fired on him Saturday, authorities said.

The Lexington County deputy was taken into surgery and was in stable condition, the sheriff’s office said in a statement.

The sheriff’s office did not release any additional information about the shooting at the Jamil Temple, where the South Carolina Arms Collector Association was holding the gun and knife show. The group did not immediately respond to an email and phone call seeking comment.

According to the rules for the gun show, posted on its website, loaded weapons are banned except for on-duty police officers, and all weapons must have their actions secured.

The Jamil Temple is owned by the Shriners and is frequently rented out for gun shows, jewelry expos, roller derbies and other events.

News.title: Affluent LA residents living by the iconic Hollywood sign are fed up with tourists. Now they’re suing
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

It’s lights, camera, frustration for Los Angeles residents living near the iconic Hollywood sign who say selfie-taking tourists have taken over their neighborhood.

About 100 homeowners are suing the city, claiming officials have failed to stop tourists from clogging narrow roads, trespassing and leaving trash, including cigarette butts that could spark wildfires.

Filed October 26, the lawsuit does not seek monetary damages. Instead, residents want a court order forcing the city to address crowds that block driveways, create safety hazards and disrupt their neighborhood. The suit also names LA Mayor Karen Bass and Councilmember Nithya Rama as defendants.

Traffic camera data showed more than 48,200 vehicles passed through the area over 13 days this summer, up 15 percent from the same period in 2025, according to CBS News.

Emergency vehicles have also struggled to navigate the narrow roads, CBS News reported, with residents citing delays for police, ambulances and fire engines.

open image in gallery About 100 Los Angeles homeowners are suing the city over growing tourist crowds near the Hollywood sign, citing traffic, trespassing, litter and wildfire risks ( Getty Images )

“It's like there's a festival every day, especially in the summer,” Rose Ware, a 74-year-old estate agent who has lived in her home for 32 years, told The Times Friday. “Bumper-to-bumper traffic. Emergency vehicles can't get through. Lots of tourists smoke cigarettes and they get very belligerent when you ask them to stop.”

Residents blame a viewing platform built about 15 years ago, along with social media and mapping apps, for drawing more tourists to the area.

Visitors now crowd the winding roads day and night, leaving behind trash, discarded cigarettes and even bottles of urine and soiled diapers, residents said.

Ware said she understands the sign's appeal but believes the city has failed to accommodate the crowds.

“But it's not the tourists' fault. They come here expecting a world-class site to experience the sign, but it's not here. The parking's terrible,” she told the newspaper.

The Independent has contacted an attorney representing the homeowners and representatives for the City of Los Angeles for comment.

The sign was originally built in 1923 to promote a real estate development called Hollywoodland. The final four letters were later removed, turning it into one of the world's most recognizable symbols of the entertainment industry.

Millions of visitors flock to the landmark each year for photos. Fences, security cameras and motion sensors surround it to prevent trespassing and vandalism, but residents say tourists still wander onto their lawns and try to park in their driveways.

“It's like a pilgrimage for them,” Ware said. “They take a million pictures, trampling on people's lawns and yards for the best shot.”

open image in gallery The suit seeks a court order requiring the city to address the tourist crowds rather than monetary damages ( AFP/Getty )

David Smalley, a 46-year-old comedian and restaurant owner, told The Times that his doorbell camera caught a woman letting her child urinate in his yard. But his biggest concern is wildfire risk, with tourists continuing to ignore no-smoking signs.

Residents have collected hundreds of cigarette butts as evidence for their lawsuit, the outlet reports.

The City Attorney’s Office said it has worked to ease congestion by increasing LA Police Department and Department of Transportation staffing, stepping up traffic and parking enforcement, and towing vehicles during busy periods.

“The Hollywood sign draws visitors from around the world, and the neighbors who live beneath it shouldn’t have to absorb the gridlock and safety risks that come with that on narrow hillside streets. Councilmember Raman has been working to address this since she took office,” the attorney’s office said in a statement to The Independent.

The office added that this summer’s Friday-through-Sunday deployments from July Fourth through Labor Day marked its largest investment in the effort to date.

“Building on those deployments, we have also identified funding for a pilot Hollywood Sign Traffic Management Plan that will test a new approach to staffing and traffic control on peak visitor days and holidays, along with a study of longer-term solutions for access and congestion in the area. We’re moving forward with that work now, so a plan is in place ahead of the 2028 Olympics,” the statement concluded.

In a statement to CBS News, Bass' office said the LAPD has dedicated additional units to traffic and parking enforcement and worked with transportation officials on a neighborhood traffic plan.

“The Mayor's office will continue working to address this issue with our public safety partners,” the statement read.

Ilan Wurman, the attorney representing the homeowners, said the city should adopt crowd controls similar to those around the Eiffel Tower in Paris, including ticketing, access restrictions and alternative viewing spots.

“We're not telling the city how to do it, but we're telling them that they're legally obligated to do something,” Wurman told The Times.

The lawsuit has received little sympathy from some tourists, who argue that homeowners should have expected crowds when moving next to one of LA’s most famous landmarks.

News.title: Government ethics chief accused of groping former police colleague’s breasts
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The chief of the government’s ethics watchdog left a previous role in the police after being investigated over sexual misconduct accusations including allegedly grabbing a colleague’s breasts, according to a report.

The Sunday Times reported that Stuart Sterling has stepped back from his role as chief executive of the Ethics and Integrity Commission (EIC), a body that “promotes the highest standards in public life”, and deals with the prime minister and public authorities on matters concerning ethical standards.

The 48-year-old will now face pending a civil service inquiry. A Cabinet Office spokesman said: “These are serious allegations. Stuart Sterling has stepped back from his role whilst we swiftly establish the facts.”

Mr Sterling was suspended from his detective constable role in Northamptonshire Police in 2003 after the groping incident, the outlet reported. He was reportedly permitted to return to his duties after he admitted wrongdoing and considerations regarding whether to initiate criminal proceedings were dropped.

Years later, he left the force after being investigated over another allegation of sexual misconduct, which he denies. Sterling says he “left voluntarily” - but did not confirm whether he was under investigation at the time.

The Independent understands that the investigation into Sterling’s role at the EIC will assess whether the correct and appropriate information was given before his appointment.

open image in gallery Wootton Hall, the Northamptonshire Police headquarters ( Instagram/@northamptonshirepolice )

In 2002, sources told the newspaper that a 24-year-old Sterling had walked up to a female colleague in her mid-thirties from behind after she took off her stabproof vest, and placed two hands on her breasts.

A male colleague reported the matter to superiors later that day, with Mr Sterling suspended on full pay. But in March 2003, and after having dropped the possibility of criminal proceedings, he was instead fined two weeks’ pay, a move described as a “wholly exceptional outcome, appropriate to the circumstances”.

After his return to work Sterling was moved to a different police stations, going on to be promoted to detective sergeant and receiving two commendations.

In 2006, another incident allegedly took place in a social setting following a police shift, but Mr Sterling has denied it ever occurred.

He was investigated again as the Northamptonshire Police’s anti-corruption unit began probing the previous investigation that allowed him to stay in the force half a decade earlier, the outlet reported.

Sterling left the police before becoming a civil servant under the Cabinet Office in December 2009.

He has since served in multiple Cabinet Office, Home Office and Foreign Office roles, was seconded to the National Police Chiefs’ Council, and received an OBE in 2023 for his role in Queen Elizabeth II’s funeral in 2022.

A representative of Sterling told The Times: “Stuart states that a full disciplinary process was held regarding the complaint in 2002, he complied with this fully. It resulted in a sanction.

“He denies that the alleged incident in 2008 ever took place. He was never subject to any criminal investigation, but the allegation was examined by professional standards.

“He was not required to resign from the force. He left voluntarily. He is not aware of any anti-corruption investigation ever taking place.”

A Northamptonshire police spokesman told The Independent: “We have a brief digital record confirming a misconduct process in 2002” but that much of the added information would have been “paper-based”.

The Independent has contacted the EIC for further comment.

News.title: SpaceX’s Starship returns from orbit and is captured by launch pad arms in a dramatic first
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

SpaceX’s Starship made a triumphant return to Earth on Saturday, caught in midair by giant mechanical arms where its journey began 22 hours earlier.

It was the grand finale that Elon Musk and his team hoped for — the first-ever capture of a Starship flying back from space. But with the first-stage booster exploding shortly after Friday’s liftoff from Texas, the company fell short of its desired double catch.

Wreckage remained in the Gulf of Mexico, cordoned off by buoys, as the stainless steel, bullet-shaped spacecraft lowered itself upright at the launch pad.

The dramatic, sci-fi-like capture helped blot out the booster’s messy miss.

“Can you believe it?” shouted SpaceX commentator Dan Huot.

SpaceX officials said Saturday’s catch demonstrates the full reusability of Starship, intended for moon and Mars travel. Although Friday’s booster recovery failed, the company had already made three previous booster catches, validating the technique.

NASA welcomed Saturday’s news. The space agency is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon later this decade and help build a permanent lunar base. Musk’s ambitions are even grander: He wants to launch a fleet of Starships to build a city on Mars.

The world’s largest and most powerful rocket — a 407-foot (124-meter) behemoth — blasted off late Friday afternoon from SpaceX’s Starship base near the U.S.-Mexican border. Separating neatly from its booster before things went awry, the upper-stage spacecraft soared into orbit and released 26 advanced Starlink satellites.

Starship continued circling the world 165 miles (265 kilometers) up, with live views of itself and Earth streaming down via Starlink. The spacecraft completed 14 laps around Earth, outshining the previous mission’s one to two laps.

It was SpaceX’s 15th flight of a full-scale Starship since 2023 and its only second trip to orbit.

SpaceX reported that everything on the spacecraft, including its vital heat shield, appeared to work well.

As for the booster, SpaceX’s Kate Tice said its engines stopped firing too soon on the way back down. The booster’s guidance system sensed it wasn’t in the right position and automatically initiated the watery detour and self-destruction. Engineers are still investigating the cause.

SpaceX expects to begin launching Starships from Florida’s Kennedy Space Center within the next few months. That is the starting point for NASA’s next Artemis mission, which will skip the moon and remain in orbit around Earth for lunar lander practice.

Artemis III’s four astronauts will attempt to dock their capsule with not only Starship but Blue Origin’s Blue Moon. The two companies will take turns delivering crews to the lunar surface. NASA is targeting as soon as 2028 for Artemis IV, humanity’s first moon landing since the Apollo era more than half a century ago.
