World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: US envoy Kushner says he aims to broker Europe-Russia talks on Ukraine
World.content:
Europe’s direct engagement with Moscow as part of Ukraine-Russia peace talks is edging closer to becoming a reality.

Share US envoy Kushner says he aims to broker Europe-Russia talks on Ukraine on social media

US envoy Jared Kushner has said he is working with Russia, Ukraine and Europe to move peace talks to the next stage, including facilitating direct engagement between Europe and Moscow.

Kushner told reporters Saturday that “both sides” know that compromises will be necessary to end the war, and that he and fellow envoy Steve Witkoff were now working on next steps.

Trump son-in-law’s comments follow peace talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday that failed to reach a breakthrough on ending the war, but resulted in a prisoner exchange.

The prospect of Europe’s involvement in the talks has grown in recent weeks, with leaders agreeing on Friday to send five representatives of European countries to represent the bloc at future peace talks.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Wednesday he did not think it was possible to think about European security “without Europe”.

The Kremlin has signalled an openness to negotiations with Europe, but it has criticised a lack of proposals from the bloc.

The five countries attending are the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, and Poland – the five countries that have signalled readiness to send troops as part of a “coalition of the willing” to secure Ukraine in the event of a ceasefire.

In a lengthy post on X on Saturday, French President Emmanuel Macron said that the bloc must “state clearly” what it wants for the post-war period, “including to the Russians”.

Macron also stated his belief that Ukraine, which has Europe’s largest conventional army, has a key role to play in Europe’s post-war context alongside NATO, which he added is a “place where it fully belongs”.



Zelenskyy said Friday that US negotiators had asked during the Abu Dhabi talks whether Ukraine would withdraw its troops from its eastern region of Donbas in exchange for joining NATO.

The war has raged while negotiations continue. November leaks from Russia’s official statistics agency showed that Russia’s war effort has so far cost the lives of at least 450,000 soldiers.

World.title: India’s Assam state demolishes homes of 132 Muslim families
World.content:
NewsFeed India’s Assam state demolishes homes of 132 Muslim families

Authorities in India’s Assam have demolished the homes of 132 Muslim families, citing illegal encroachment on government land. Residents say they were settled there after fleeing the 1983 anti-Muslim riots. Researchers say the evictions have disproportionately targeted Bengali-origin Muslims.

World.title: Can being ‘non-Western’ cost you your home in Denmark?
World.content:
Can being ‘non-Western’ cost you your home in Denmark?

NewsFeed Can being ‘non-Western’ cost you your home in Denmark?

Denmark’s Supreme Court is set to rule on whether families can be forced from their homes under a law that divides residents into ‘Western’ and ‘non-Western’. Al Jazeera’s Nils Adler reports from Copenhagen, where evictees of majority ‘non-Western’ estates are fighting back.

World.title: Deadly car bomb blast kills two near Syria’s capital
World.content:
NewsFeed Deadly car bomb blast kills two near Syria’s capital

At least two people, a man and a girl, have been killed in a car bomb explosion in Jaramana, near Syria’s capital Damascus. Security forces cordoned off the area and say they are launching an investigation into the blast.

World.title: More than 100,000 rally across France in new Yellow Vest protests
World.content:
Share More than 100,000 rally across France in new Yellow Vest protests on social media

More than 100,000 people have taken to the streets in France in another round of cost-of-living rallies organised by the “Yellow Vests” and various youth movements.

Saturday’s protests saw a decline in turnout compared with previous weekends and stayed largely calm, authorities said.

The Ministry of the Interior reported that 106,000 people took part in protests nationwide, including 24,000 in Paris – down from 146,000 people nationwide and 46,000 in Paris last week. Student unions place Saturday’s protest numbers higher, at 200,000 people, including almost 100,000 in the capital.

The country has been gripped by high-school blockades, mass demonstrations, and strikes for more than a month, with protesters rallying against falling educational standards, cost-of-living increases, low wages, and police violence.

A number of demonstrators also carried signs targeting President Emmanuel Macron, who has faced significant criticism from protesters.

Some rallies in recent weeks have seen violence at the fringes, and the first major protest on October 17 saw looting in cities across France. Since then, police presence at rallies and controls on transport and permits to protest have been expanded.

Marseille, France’s second-largest city, banned protests over the weekend, but the prefecture announced that some 3,500 people still took to the streets. Local media reported that tear gas and a water cannon were used against protesters and shared images of fires burning in a popular local square.

In Lyon, local media reported that roughly 8,000 people took to the streets. They shared images of masked protesters chanting in front of fires lit in the street and police charging and using tear gas.



Tear gas use was also reported in Nantes, Bordeaux and Paris.

More protests planned

Unions have called for a new day of strikes on Tuesday after rejecting a government promise to increase the minimum wage by 0.6 percent as “crumbs”.

If the demonstrations go ahead, they will take place on the eighth anniversary of the Gilet Jaune – which translates to “Yellow Vest” in French – movement, which rocked the beginning of the Macron government in 2018 with two years of protests triggered by rising fuel prices.

On Tuesday, the Yellow Vests will “celebrate their eight years where it all started: on roundabouts and toll booths all over France”, Yellow Vest protest tracking website 17octobregiletjaune.net writes.

World.title: Tens of thousands march in latest Portugal housing protests
World.content:
These were the biggest protests against rising housing costs in Portugal since the social movement began weeks ago.

Tens of thousands of people have taken to the streets of more than 30 towns and cities in Portugal to protest against surging rental prices, demanding urgent government action to address the country’s worsening housing crisis.

Organised by the Casa Para Viver (A Home to Live In) platform, demonstrations on Saturday took place under the slogan “They will not steal our right to a home,” with protests in Lisbon, Porto, Faro, Portimao, Coimbra, Braga and other locations. It was the biggest national demonstration since the social movement began weeks ago.

Participants, ranging from teenagers to retired people, walked behind large banners, with the Lisbon march punctuated by drums, music, and chanting. Protesters called for caps to be placed on rent increases, greater legal protection for tenants against eviction, and more affordable housing. They also demanded the reversal of proposed changes to rental legislation.

One woman on a protest march in Lisbon told Al Jazeera that she was a business owner, “and I can’t afford a house.”

“I can’t say much more than this. I’m forty-years-old, I can’t go to a bank and just buy a house with my money,” she added.

Another woman told Al Jazeera that she had joined the march to protest “for a better life, for all of us, not just the young people, all of us, because we deserve to have a home.”

One man told Al Jazeera “we have been suffering this for the last three or four years, and I have many friends and family in this situation, they had to move because they cannot afford the rent. If you earn, for example, a thousand euros, and you have to pay rent of six hundred, seven hundred, then you cannot live, it’s impossible.”



Casa Para Vivir brings together approximately 100 housing associations and grassroots organisations, is seeking tighter regulation on rental contracts, short-term tourist accommodation, and vacant properties.

The protests come after parliament approved the government’s proposed changes to provide greater flexibility in rental contracts and accelerate eviction procedures.

Housing campaigners warned the changes could weaken tenant protections amid rising rents and limited housing availability.

Portugal’s rising property prices

House prices in Portugal have risen much faster than incomes in recent years, statistics show. Between 2015 and 2025, Portugal posted the biggest jump in the European Union in the home price-to-income ratio, with an increase of 61 percent, followed by the Netherlands with 34 percent, the EU statistical office Eurostat said last week.

There is no indication that the rise in housing costs is slowing. Between the first quarter of last year and the first quarter of 2026, property prices rose by almost 20 percent, the National Statistics Institute, a government agency, said last month.

Rental prices, too, have climbed significantly, recording a 68 percent increase since 2020, according to the government. Much of this jump in real estate costs has been fuelled by foreign buyers and investment funds, as the country’s relaxed climate near the ocean has attracted many remote workers and retirees.

The government has responded to the protests by lowering taxes on new construction, restricting short-term rentals, and promising to build 145,000 new homes, but it acknowledged that the effects will not be immediate, as Prime Minister Luis Montenegro was urged by Casa Para Viver representatives to engage directly with them.

The protests in Portugal in recent weeks took their cue from demonstrations in neighbouring Spain last month over similar issues around housing and forced evictions. A wave of youth-led protests has swept Europe in the latter half of this year, with demonstrators across the continent denouncing rising prices and a lack of future prospects.

World.title: Pope Leo urges end to violence in Peru during visit to remote Andes town
World.content:
In Santa Cruz de Succhabamba, the pope urges people not to respond to injustice with brutality.

Share Pope Leo urges end to violence in Peru during visit to remote Andes town on social media

Pope Leo XIV has called for an end to the violence gripping Peru, urging people not to respond to injustice with brutality, as he visited communities he once served as bishop.

“We feel threatened by the uncertainty of widespread violence and by the unspeakable suffering that continues to afflict so many of our brothers and sisters, he said, speaking at his former cathedral in Chiclayo.

Peru’s homicide rate has nearly doubled over the past five years, from 5.8 to 10.7 per 100,000 people. Reported extortion cases rose from 2,421 in 2019 to 26,734 in 2025, according to official figures cited by The Associated Press.

Security was a top concern for Peruvians in the last election. Conservative President Keiko Jujimori took office in July after promising to tackle crime. She has since declared states of emergency, including in Lima in August, then in September in prisons holding inmates linked to criminal organisations.

She has also pursued closer ties with Washington, bringing Peru into the ‘Shield of the Americas,’ a US-led regional coalition formed to carry out joint military operations against drug cartels.

Later on Saturday, in the Andean town of Santa Cruz de Succhabamba with a population of about 6,000, about 20,000 people came to an outdoor Mass, where Leo also addressed violence in society.

“Selfishness, injustice and evil are not overcome by brutality, but by prayer, patience and perseverance in denouncing what is wrong, by making our pleas with determination and working diligently to bring about the necessary changes,” said the leader of the Roman Catholic church.



He also drew attention to the suffering of rural communities he used to serve, where migration and declining birth rates are emptying villages.

“Let us think, for example, of the suffering of those who are forced to leave their homeland in search of a better future for themselves and their families in the great coastal cities,” he said.

Originally from Chicago in the United States and formerly known as Robert Francis Prevost, Leo arrived in Santa Cruz de Succhabamba by helicopter and was welcomed by a local band singing “Pope Leo, welcome home.”

He’d made the journey to the remote area many times before during his time as bishop of Chiclayo from 2015 to 2023, driving himself along winding mountain roads in a pick-up truck.

The pope, who holds both US and Peruvian citizenship, spent about two decades working in Peru as a missionary priest and bishop.

World.title: US blames outdated technology for nationwide flight disruption
World.content:
US blames outdated technology for nationwide flight disruption

NewsFeed US blames outdated technology for nationwide flight disruption

US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy says a telecommunications failure during routine maintenance triggered widespread flight disruption and a nationwide ground stop. The fault affected communication with aircraft and radar feeds.

World.title: A ‘Generational Clash’ Is Fueling Europe’s Protests
World.content:
Sébastien Ducros, a French data analyst who supports the widespread student protests in his country, has identified an obvious culprit for the lack of government funds for dilapidated schools.

“A huge portion of the money is going toward retirees, while many other things are being neglected,” said Mr. Ducros, 36. “I honestly think — even if it feels strange to say — that people like my parents are in a position where they should and could” surrender some of their pension payments, he added, saying that they were about to retire.

But Laurent Grinwald, 72, who retired recently after decades as a postal worker, isn’t eager for his pension to be reduced, particularly to pay for other state-funded services. Especially, he said, as rents and the cost of living have shot up.

“We’ve been working all this time,” Mr. Grinwald said, “and now, suddenly, the stance is, ‘Well, no, we’re going to start taking a bit more?’”

World.title: ‘Get Focused on London’: How Iran’s Agents Attacked European Targets
World.content:
As the U.S.-Israel war in Iran raged earlier this year, a man linked to Iranian criminal networks perched in front of a computer, on a video call with a teenager in London. The man wanted to make sure the teen, who was moments away from setting fire to a synagogue, carried out his plans.

“Light it up like a Christmas tree,” the man, an Iraqi named Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, urged the 17-year-old, according to U.S. prosecutors. The teen climbed over a wall and tossed a bomb through a broken window. “J’s mic is muted,” read the text on Mr. al-Hassani’s computer screen.

The synagogue arson in April was a small, violent part of Iran’s efforts to force an end to the bombing campaign that was pummeling the country, according to American investigators.

The attack was described in a federal indictment filed in New York this week. It revealed extensive new details about a wave of violence against Jewish institutions in Europe and U.S. targets, including a British air base used by American bombers. Prosecutors hold Iran’s agents responsible for the assaults.

World.title: Ukraine’s Starshield Access Is Being Restricted Again, Zelensky Says
World.content:
Ukrainian military operations were disrupted again this week along the front lines because of restrictions on Starshield, the satellite internet system developed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX and controlled by the U.S. government, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Friday.

Mr. Zelensky told reporters that speed limits of about 100 miles per hour were being enforced for Ukrainian devices connected to the system. It would be the second time in recent weeks that Ukraine’s Starshield connectivity had been throttled. The previous restrictions caused Ukrainian drones to lose their connection to the system if they flew above certain speeds.

Mr. Zelensky said that the latest speed limits took effect on Monday and were being enforced over Russian-occupied territories, not over all of Ukraine. That hurts Ukraine’s ability to strike Russian troops with drones in those territories.

Imposing restrictions on occupied territories is “very dangerous, because it already has political implications,” Mr. Zelensky said. “If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognizing the temporarily occupied territories as not ours,” he added.

World.title: Trump’s Oil Grab in Venezuela Is Testing the Country’s National Identity
World.content:
Like generations before him, Leonardo Silva grew up steeped in beliefs about the extraordinarily abundant resource that made Venezuela special. All the oil under their feet was theirs, they felt. Virtually free gasoline was a birthright. To be born atop this bounty was like winning the lottery.

Mr. Silva, 38, said his generation viewed oil as a cornerstone of the country’s national identity, when a booming economy allowed Venezuela to occupy a privileged tier in the global order. His children, he said, have a far less rosy view.

“To them oil isn’t important, it’s secondary,” said Mr. Silva, who works at a foundation in Caracas helping people with disabilities. “They don’t have that culture of us being a rich country. They just know that if you don’t work, you don’t eat.”

Oil has shaped Venezuela to an extent that is rare outside the Middle East for more than a century, becoming a defining feature of the social fabric like baseball, beauty pageants or the veneration of the liberation hero Simón Bolívar.

World.title: South Sudan’s National Election, Its First, Will Be Delayed
World.content:
The upcoming election was supposed to underwrite that agreement. But the peace deal has unraveled since March 2025, when Mr. Machar was placed under house arrest in the capital, Juba, and charged with treason. In recent months, the government has replaced opposition lawmakers with its own supporters and dissolved the unity government.

With Mr. Machar effectively sidelined, there are no credible challengers to Mr. Kiir, who is widely expected to win the presidential election. He has a broad national following, and his party controls state institutions and the news media.

The election faces stark logistical challenges. Civil servants have not been paid in more than a year, and parts of the country are controlled by armed groups, including Mr. Machar’s forces. Thousands of people have died in fighting and attacks on civilians. In March, more than 200 people were killed in a massacre in Unity State near the border with Sudan, according to human rights groups.

World.title: Two Celebrity Cases Put a Spotlight on British Courts’ Gag Orders
World.content:
Two recent cases have brought new attention to the ways that British laws can allow the wealthy and powerful to silence their critics.

The first was the rape and sexual assault trial of the comedian Russell Brand. Before his conviction last week, Mr. Brand had obtained an injunction prohibiting another accuser from telling almost anyone — including the police, her family and most doctors — about her claims that he assaulted her. (Mr. Brand has denied her allegations.) That injunction, first revealed by Dan Neidle, a tax lawyer and free-expression activist, apparently remains in force.

In the second instance, two British news organizations were temporarily blocked from reporting allegations of sexual misconduct against David Walliams, a television personality and author of children’s books, before a judge declined to make the injunction permanent. The Guardian newspaper and ITV News, a British broadcaster, published investigations last week into the allegations, which Mr. Walliams denies.

Though both men now face public scrutiny, the revelations of how they used court injunctions — essentially gag orders — to protect their reputations have provoked no shortage of public and political outrage. Judges in other cases have issued “super injunctions,” which prohibit publishing any information even about the injunction itself.

World.title: Eisenkot Accuses Netanyahu of Fueling ‘Racist’ Hostility Against Arabs
World.content:
Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief who is trying to form the next Israeli government, accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday of fueling a “racist” campaign against the country’s Arab citizens, in some of the strongest public criticism of his rival’s attacks on the community.

The comments were made days after Mr. Netanyahu delivered a divisive speech to the opening session of Parliament, or the Knesset, in which he referred to Arab lawmakers as “terror supporters” and “haters of Israel.” Diplomats and analysts condemned the remarks as a brazen display of hatred and incitement against Arab citizens, who make up about 20 percent of the overall population, and voted in massive numbers in inconclusive elections last month.

“Since the beginning of the election campaign, they have been subjected to a racist and aggressive campaign of delegitimization, fueled by the outgoing prime minister and those around him for political purposes,” Mr. Eisenkot said in a statement on social media.

“Arab citizens of Israel are an integral part of the Israeli story,” he said, adding that it was wrong to malign an entire community.

World.title: Caught Between Killers: Ebola on One Side, Islamic State on the Other
World.content:
Six months on, Ebola continues to hack a deadly trail across eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

When the outbreak was first detected in May, it resembled a single, giant blaze, with infections concentrated in a handful of towns in one province.

It has since morphed into a far bigger, more elusive foe, creeping into eight provinces and splintering into numerous hot spots as it moves through one of the world’s great rainforests.

Instead of one big fire, there are many now, scattered across a vast area about the size of Britain.

Health workers have corralled the virus where it was first detected, but infections are soaring elsewhere. Biakato, a small town deep in the rainforest, suddenly accounted for as many as one-quarter of new cases nationally. Yet its beleaguered residents were left almost entirely on their own, with dangerously little to defend themselves against the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.

“We see the same mistakes as before,” said Dr. Jean-Jacques Muyembe, who helped discover Ebola in 1976 and now heads Congo’s National Institute for Biomedical Research. “It’s as if we were starting from zero. It’s very disappointing.”

And if that were not enough, the campaign to contain the epidemic has run into a terrifying new threat: the Islamic State.

World.title: Copper wire upgrade caused nationwide flight suspension, US transport secretary says
World.content:
A nationwide US ground stop that caused thousands of flight cancellations was caused by an issue following a copper wire upgrade, Transport Secretary Sean Duffy said.

Duffy told a news conference that the government was trying to find out whether the problem was caused by "incompetence" on the part of the company doing the upgrades, or faulty equipment.

The US government does not believe it was as a result of a cyber-attack, although an investigation is still under way, Duffy said.

Friday's suspension was the longest such incident since the 11 September 2001 attacks on the US and the disruption is expected to last for days.

Maintenance was being carried out to switch from copper wire to fibre by a contractor called L3Harris, a technology provider company, Duffy said.

The US has "an incredibly old telecommunications system", he added.

"It was such an old wire that it was being discontinued," he said.

The transport secretary explained that a router that was being worked on had started flooding other air traffic control systems and created communication issues with planes which led the government to shut down the airspace for safety reasons.

Bryan Bedford, who heads the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), told the same news conference: "We see zero evidence of anything nefarious, and zero evidence of anything AI related."

On Saturday L3Harris said it had completed over 70% of the work to modernise communications infrastructure before the shutdown.

"We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the 13 November ground stop of our nation's air travel," it said in a statement.

"L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travellers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously."

World.title: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
World.content:
US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.

The US has not confirmed Zelensky's comments, which come after US President Donald Trump's envoys met Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelensky as part of US efforts to end the war between Russia and Ukraine.

Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance, but this has previously been opposed by the US and others while Russia has said another Nato member on its border is unacceptable.

Russia controls most of the industrial region of Donbas and Zelensky has consistently said Ukraine is unwilling to give up sovereign territory.

Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky said in remarks released by his office on Saturday.

He went on to say that if he received a specific proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.

US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital, Dublin, on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Putin in Moscow.

Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted. It has previously proposed limits on the size of Ukraine's military, territorial concessions and Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality as conditions of a peace deal.

Ukraine has rejected these, arguing that such constraints would hamper its ability to stave off any future invasion.

World.title: Italy fines Meta €805m over accessing users' photos
World.content:
Italian regulators have fined social media giant Meta â¬805m (Â£670m; $887m) for accessing Android users' photos without their specific consent.

Italy's Data Protection Authority said Meta did not properly inform about 20 million smartphone users that it had access to their photos and videos via a feature of the Facebook app.

It has given Meta 60 days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent separately.

The fine is among the largest an Italian authority has ever imposed on a tech giant.

A Meta spokesperson told the BBC that it planned to appeal.

The charge is related to a feature which suggests photos and videos from a user's phone gallery as ideas for posts.

Facebook requested access to users' photo galleries through a single app-wide authorisation. According to the Italian regulator, a preceding notice did not make clear that this would also allow Facebook to generate suggestions based on photos in their gallery.

The regulator said it took into account "the high number of people affected" and the fact it is "still ongoing for those who have not updated the app and for those who have already given their consent to the system".

It also cited "Meta's lack of co-operation".

Meta told the BBC: "We strongly disagree with the [regulator's] assessment of the facts, its application of the law, and the disproportionate level of the fine.

"This is a straightforward feature which helps people post photos and videos to Facebook. People must give permission on their device before it can operate, and they can change this permission at any time via their settings."

Last month, Meta, which is also behind Instagram and WhatsApp, was hit with its largest fine ever for its business practices.

A US judge in New Mexico ordered the company to pay $25bn (Â£18.6bn) after it found that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.

World.title: Philippines wins first Eurovision Song Contest Asia
World.content:
The Philippines have won the very first Eurovision Song Contest Asia, hosted in Bangkok and with 11 countries vying for the title.

Nineteen-year-old singer Carmelle was always a front runner with her women's empowerment anthem Sobra-Sobra, complete with its catchy rap section.

She earned 211 points in total - 93 from the jury and 118 from the public vote - ahead of Thailand's MANG x DAOU in second place with 170 points.

There was a joyous atmosphere at the One Bangkok Arena as the crowd cheered the contestants and celebrated the popular winner.

World.title: Second catch attempt as SpaceX Starship rocket heads back to Earth
World.content:
SpaceX will decide later whether to try to catch the top part of its huge Starship rocket as it returns to Earth.

The company had hoped to catch both the bottom and upper stages of the rocket using mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on its launch tower.

But the first catch of the rocket's booster was aborted a few minutes after the launch, and instead the booster diverted to the ocean, bursting into flames just above the sea.

The top part, known as the Ship, is due to return to Earth at about 15:15 local time (21:15 GMT) on Saturday.

This is the 15th test of Starship and the first that hoped to fully recover both parts of the rocket. SpaceX wants to make the top and bottom sections of Starship fully reusable so it can fly repeatedly and reduce costs.

The 124m-tall (407ft) rocket successfully blasted off from the Starbase launchpad in Boca Chica, Texas at 16:47 local time on Friday.

The plan was to grab the bottom part of the rocket - the Super Heavy booster - six and a half minutes later when it returned.

A "go" was initially given by mission control for a catch attempt at the launch tower, but the booster activated an automated abort, diverting instead to the ocean where it hovered above the water before exploding.

World.title: Sotheby's auction of $180m Van Gogh challenged over claims it was 'sold under duress'
World.content:
Auction house Sotheby's says it is working to resolve a dispute over the intended sale of a painting by Vincent van Gogh.

ChÃ¢taigniers en Fleurs, which carries an estimate of $180m (Â£136m), is due to go under the hammer in New York on Wednesday.

But representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family - earlier German owners of the work - say it may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.

Sotheby's say its own "extensive research" has not established this, but say they will work with the family to try and reach a solution.

"Sotheby's takes provenance and restitution matters extremely seriously and has undertaken extensive research into the ownership history of ChÃ¢taigniers en fleurs," Sotheby's told the BBC in a statement.

"We are aware of the concerns recently raised by representatives of the Fischer heirs and have been in dialogue with them regarding the painting's history.

"While our research to date has not established that the painting was sold under duress, we recognize the importance of engaging thoughtfully and constructively with the family and are committed to working toward a mutually satisfactory resolution."

The painting - whose name translates as Blossoming Chestnut Trees - is being sold as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection.

Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890.

It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934.

The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotherby's says.

Four other owners have had it since before it was put up for auction this year.

Fischer family heirs have instructed a lawyer who, according to the New York Times, external, has written to Sotherby's.

He is said to have told the auction house the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis.

The BBC has contacted the lawyer for comment.

World.title: Trump, Putin and Xi plan historic joint meeting in China next week, White House says
World.content:
Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are planning to meet on the sidelines of a summit in China next week, the White House has said.

The historic meeting between the respective leaders of the US, Russia and China will take place as Trump attends the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (Apec) summit in the southern city of Shenzhen, spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.

"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," she said.

It is understood Iran may also be discussed during the meeting of the world's biggest nuclear powers, but not Ukraine. Russia has confirmed the meeting. China has yet to react.

No agreement was expected to follow the talks, an unnamed, senior US official said, according to news agencies AP and Reuters.

Trump will arrive in Shenzhen late on Wednesday for the two-day summit between the 21 member states. He will also take part in bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday - their fourth meeting since the US president returned to office in 2025.

"President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the president of the United States, the president of the People's Republic of China, and the president of the Russian Federation," Wales said.

She said Trump's trip, which will also include attending an Association of South-east Asian Nations (Asean) summit in the Philippines on Tuesday, would "secure historic wins to the American people and advance America's interests in the Indo Pacific".

A nuclear weapons control treaty between the US and Russia expired in February, leaving the world's biggest nuclear arsenals without major guardrails and effectively marking an end to the arms control co-operation that helped resolve the Cold War.

The UN has urged both sides to agree a new framework without delay. Trump however said he could replace the deal with a better agreement that included China, which has been building up its arsenal.

Former senior US officials and analysts told the BBC at the time that seeking Beijing and Moscow's co-operation could create major hurdles and take years.

World.title: Arrested generals and a threatened VP: President's son fuels Ugandan succession fever
World.content:
In Uganda's military, even senior generals are finding that their rank offers little protection from the wrath of the country's powerful army chief.

Over the past 15 months, at least a dozen generals and senior officers have been arrested under Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the son of President Yoweri Museveni, in a crackdown that has unsettled the military's top ranks.

The arrests come amid growing political tensions over who will succeed Museveni, who has ruled Uganda for four decades.

Gen Kainerugaba, 52, is widely seen as a potential successor, although his ambitions appear to be facing resistance within the ruling party.

This week, he threatened Vice-President Jessica Alupo with dismissal and possible arrest, while suggesting he should take her position.

The ruling National Resistance Movement (NRM) has, however, rejected reports that its senior leadership had rejected a proposal to back Gen Kainerugaba as the next president, describing the claims as "completely false".

This has all fuelled speculation that the arrests are part of an effort to sideline military officers opposed to the general's presidential ambitions.

Others see the arrests as evidence of an anti-corruption drive in which senior commanders are held to account.

At the centre of the tension are two powerful powerful institutions: the military, where Gen Kainerugaba wields considerable influence, and the NRM, where questions about his political ambitions appear to be dividing senior figures.

A recent meeting of NRM's top leadership ended without agreement on a proposal to position Gen Kainerugaba as Museveni's successor, according to the AFP news agency.

Five party sources who attended the closed-door meeting told AFP that a vote was abandoned after several members spoke against the proposal.

Uganda's news website ChimpReports, however, said that most members who spoke backed the general's potential presidency, although some questioned his readiness for civilian leadership.

In a statement on Thursday, NRM Secretary General Richard Todwong Awany confirmed that the party had met on 10 November to discuss "political, social and economic issues".

He dismissed reports that the meeting had rejected a proposal to position Gen Kainerugaba as Uganda's next president, saying the party would communicate any decisions "through the right channel, at the right time".

World.title: Reopening Africa’s wounds, waiting for gangrene to set in, By Owei Lakemfa
World.content:
A tragedy engineered by Morocco, watered by Western Europe and the United States (US) with the connivance of the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) is unfolding in Africa. War has become inevitable on the continent with the UNSC reversing the peace process in Western Sahara and abolishing the United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO).

Africa had experienced colonialism but all 55 countries had become independent. However, a sister country, Morocco had tried to recolonise the Sahara Arab Democratic Republic, SDAR better known as Western Sahara. Africa had put its foot down. On 22 February, 1982, the Organisation of African Unity, now, the African Union (AU) recognised the independence of Western Sahara and admitted it as its full Member. A gluttonous Moroccan monarchy would not accept the decision of the African people and on 12 November, 1984, worked away.

After 33 years of wandering about and being rejected by the European Union, it returned on 31 January, 2017 like a prodigal son. Unfortunately the AU did not sufficiently interrogate Morocco but simply accepted it as a lost son. Now, that Morocco has repudiated the peace agreement and wants to colonise Western Sahara by force of arms, it is clear that the Moroccan establishment, had ulterior motives.

Also, Africa had not been critical of the United Nations, believing that its offer of peace which led to the establishment of MINURSO was genuine. The UN which is now pretending to be working for peace, has repudiated one of its basic principles in order to pamper Morocco and its Western backers. The UN Resolution 1514 of 1960 had proclaimed that: “All peoples have the right to self-determination; by virtue of that right they freely determine their political status and freely pursue their economic, social and cultural development.”

In line with this, the UNSC on 9 April 1991, passed Resolution 690 directing that a referendum be held in Western Sahara. Today, 35 years later with Morocco refusing to allow the referendum, the UNSC has rather than uphold its resolution, cancelled the referendum and, decided that only Morocco’s dubious plan in which Western Sahara will be ruled by King Mohammed VI, would prevail. This leaves our Sahrawi brothers and sisters with little or no alternative but to return to armed struggle.

On the other hand, this has sent the Moroccan establishment into celebratory mood. The Moroccan Monarchy celebrated with what it called “Unity Day” It declared that: “A 35-year chapter has now come to a close. Rooted in an anachronistic and outdated context, this Mission (MINUSO) has long served as a tool for internationalising the regional dispute concerning the Kingdom of Morocco’s legitimate recovery of its Saharan provinces.”

On the other hand, Western Sahara warned that it is willing to completely abandon the peace negotiations. The Representative of the Polisario Front to the UN, Sidi Mohamed Omar warned that if the UN draft is: “approved without substantial and significant modifications, the Polisario Front will have no choice but to withdraw from the entire peace process.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Ambassador Mike Waltz, US Representative to the UN in endorsing the end of the UN peace mission asked: “each of the concerned parties to negotiate a lasting peace.” He added: “Under President Trump’s leadership, the United States has done more for peace in Western Sahara this year than in decades.”

China had warned the UNSC against what it considered a one-sided approach to the Western Sahara issue.

Algeria which has for decades given political, moral and material support to the Sahrawi including granting them shelter in its Tindouf region, pointed out that the: “tragedy being endured by the Sahrawi people has oddly been diluted to the concept of refugee populations” It pointed out the well known fact that the Polisario Front is the legitimate representative of the Sahrawi and decried the: “failure of this Security Council”.

The UN Secretary-General António Guterres in his usual double speak, said ending the peace mission: “does not abrogate” the Saharawi people’s “inalienable right to self-determination” He called on all parties: “to respect and promote the rights of the people of Western Sahara.” The question is why has this not been respected for the nine years he has been in office? With the planned departure of MINURSO, he asked all: “to respect and promote the rights of the people of Western Sahara.” So, why is it that even with MINURSO, those rights are not respected. How does he expect King Mohammed IV who rules by decree even over Moroccans, to respect the fundamental rights of the Saharawi?

Tragically, the African Union whose founding Member is about being recolonised, has kept mute. If war breaks out again between Morocco and the Saharawi people, it is Africa that will suffer. So, why are African leaders quiet?

The move against the Saharawi is just one more step being taken by Western Europe and the US who amongst them, still own over sixty colonies. They are working for a world that would accept colonialism as normal. As part of this plan, the US in October asked the UN to end the mandate of its Special Committee on De-colonisation. It claims the UN Hearings on decolonisation are a waste of resources.

The US which once proclaimed that all men are equal and advertises a statute of Liberty does not want to end colonialism. Neither does it want the colonized to have a voice, not even at a UN Committee level.

If colonialism were to become normal as the West wants, it would not be long before they begin to campaign for the recolonisation of free countries. So, in fighting for the people of Western Sahara against Moroccan colonialism, we in the underdeveloped countries like Nigeria and South Africa would actually be fighting for our freedom.

Owei Lakemfa, a former secretary general of African workers, is a human rights activist, journalist and author.

World.title: Re: Obasanjo: Why debt is an instrument of leverage for purposeful governance, By ‘Tope Fasua
World.content:
On the contrary though, I posit that debt can build generations. In fact debt has built generations. All the countries that matter borrowed by leveraging their cash flows to get where they are. My earlier argument in the article stands. The Western world has only played with peanuts in Africa and we are not monkeys. One could argue that the recent engagements with China have been more promising and beneficial to Africa, and Nigeria in particular because we see the tangibles – roads, rail lines, airports etc.

The tragedy of our times is that there is so much ignorance in the age of information; so much illiteracy in a time when people are educated. The challenge for all is to speak up and keep repeating facts in the hope that somehow facts begin to sink in where they now seem bereft. The times present new challenges. Economies are not what they used to be. And we cannot solve the problems of today by using the same thinking that created them. These are my initial thoughts as I attempt a necessary riposte to the vehement political statements of former President Obasanjo. I call it political even though it is meant to be an economic subject – Nigeria’s debt. But the reasoning and delivery are so well-timed to do damage that the field of economics has to reject what was stated as fact and dump them in the trashcan of chicanery.

First, it is apposite to look at today’s national economies. There is a race for development and no nation wants to be left behind; not even North Korea, perhaps the most isolated country on earth. Every government is working to improve the lives of their people, build infrastructure, or at least create a legacy. In this development superhighway, nobody is slowing down for anyone. What is even more likely to happen is for those who can, to slow down those who are not wary of geopolitics. I wrote an article some months back where I charged that indeed the world has underinvested in Africa and that Africa (especially Nigeria) is certainly not over-borrowed. That conviction still stands.

In today’s world, we cannot run an economy without proper treasury management – which means leveraging our resources and cash flows for the future in order to grow bigger, provide better for our people and obtain the assets we need today for a greater future, such as tangible infrastructure. I wagered in my article that the smart nations of the world – most of them western – have ensured that they collected real leverage and have become where we all troop to for everything under the sun – education, health, tourism, technology, knowledge, information, skills and everything in between. I urged African nations to wake up!

It’s therefore a wonder why Obasanjo will make such a statement. I can only put this down to his political support for Peter Obi (who he probably hopes to use like dough in his hands), and age-long opposition to President Bola Tinubu who has naturally proved to be a tough cookie for anyone to gobble up and who certainly possesses a strong mind of his own.

History of National Debts

This is a fine opportunity to trace the history of national debts. Why do countries borrow? Do countries have to borrow? What happens if they do, or if they don’t? When we are stumped for answers it is always inevitable to look back to determine how we got to where we are. Making statements in reaction to immediate events is a mindset we should leave for the unwise. I was recently addressing a gathering where secondary school students were and I realised that we are raising them to be angry because almost all of them are not rooted in Nigerianism.

The only way our children can be invested in Nigeria is if they understand the history of Nigeria. Who founded Nigeria. What is colonialism and slavery? Why were the northern and southern territories merged? Who got us our independence? What caused political breakdown during the parliamentary government? What caused the first coup? Who died? And the second coup? And subsequent ones? Who were/are the key players of Nigeria’s First, Second, Third and Fourth Republics? What were their legacies? How have we managed our diversity so far? These questions and the answers to them are what will enable us to build our nation. We shouldn’t shy away from them.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

And on the matter of debt, we need history too. Below is what I found in a simple Internet search:

Ancient and Medieval Eras: Rulers in ancient Mesopotamia and the Roman world borrowed money for wars and public works, occasionally enacting “debt jubilees” or forgiveness decrees when obligations became unsustainable. In medieval Europe, tally sticks (notched wooden pieces split between the crown and creditor) tracked royal debts.

Rulers in ancient Mesopotamia and the Roman world borrowed money for wars and public works, occasionally enacting “debt jubilees” or forgiveness decrees when obligations became unsustainable. In medieval Europe, tally sticks (notched wooden pieces split between the crown and creditor) tracked royal debts. The 17th-Century Shift: The Dutch Republic revolutionised state borrowing by issuing long-term public bonds to citizens to fund its war of independence.

The Dutch Republic revolutionised state borrowing by issuing long-term public bonds to citizens to fund its war of independence. The history of the British national debt can be traced back to the reign of William III (a Dutchman, otherwise called William of Orange, who became King of England, Scotland and Ireland from 1689 to 1702), who engaged a syndicate of City traders and merchants to offer for an issue of government debt, which evolved into the Bank of England.

The Bank of England (1694): Britain adopted and formalised this framework with the establishment of the Bank of England, turning national debt into a permanent, tradable financial instrument, rather than a sign of royal bankruptcy.

Britain adopted and formalised this framework with the establishment of the Bank of England, turning national debt into a permanent, tradable financial instrument, rather than a sign of royal bankruptcy. Wartime Spikes: Throughout the 18th and 19th centuries, major conflicts (such as the Napoleonic Wars and the American Revolutionary War) were the primary drivers of debt. British debt-to-GDP surpassed 200 per cent following the Napoleonic Wars.

Throughout the 18th and 19th centuries, major conflicts (such as the Napoleonic Wars and the American Revolutionary War) were the primary drivers of debt. British debt-to-GDP surpassed 200 per cent following the Napoleonic Wars. World Wars I and II: Global conflict pushed debt to historic heights. US and British debt-to-GDP ratios peaked around or above 240 per cent–250 per cent by the end of World War II in 1945.

So, from the get go, we can see that nations borrow for projects. And the most important projects in the beginning, as humans gathered and cooperated in large civilisations, were wars. The first national borrowing by rulers were therefore for war – whether it was in Dutchland, England or America. In China, the Emperors viewed borrowing from people to fight wars as beneath their imperial dignity, so they resorted to fines and taxes when such events presented themselves. There is a second critical reason behind national debts and government borrowings, and that is because it secured the commitment and loyalty of the monied class behind their societies or nations.

When you give money to the King for a war, you stay behind that money and ensure your society survives. It could be argued that post-colonial nations like Nigeria never had that organic opportunity to secure the loyalty and commitment of the monied class and their people in this same manner, as we were quickly introduced to borrowing through global structures and foreign banks. But in general, borrowing is essential in today’s economy because national economies must now be managed with the prowess of bank treasurers. And the first principle at that level is never to sit on cash or fail to leverage in order to achieve more – especially as populations explode.

The idea is not to borrow recklessly. But Nigeria’s debt-to-GDP ratio at a mere 35 per cent is one of the lowest in the world today. An astute financier will wonder whether we had no need for money – no infrastructure to build, no population to take care of, no children to send to school, no old people to help with healthcare. Therefore, saying debts are worse than leprosy or that they are bad for a national economy, is a very careless fallacy to utter.

The Andrew Jackson Experience: Paying Down National Debts

And the world has learnt lessons around national debts. In the medieval times referenced above, a king borrows to fight wars, and when he dies, the debts die with him. In time, through the establishment of national banks or central banks, debts to nations were tracked beyond the death of specific monarchs. And some leaders have also tried to pay down debts because they believed that debts were bad.

One of such presidents was US President Andrew Jackson – who hated debts of any kind – and decided to square off and repay the national debt of that country (about $75 million in 1835). Jackson was a Tennessee landowner and land speculator who had lost money and fallen into debt himself before becoming president. He therefore abhorred the idea of borrowing money for anything. But his decision proved the distinction between running a household, company or government, because it resulted in a disaster for the US economy. When he paid down the debts by selling of federal lands, this is what happened:

Distribution of the Surplus: With the debt eliminated and money still flowing in from federal land sales and tariffs, the government accumulated a large cash surplus. Congress passed the Deposit Act of 1836, which distributed these surplus federal funds to the states.

With the debt eliminated and money still flowing in from federal land sales and tariffs, the government accumulated a large cash surplus. Congress passed the Deposit Act of 1836, which distributed these surplus federal funds to the states. Wildcat Banking and Speculation: Jackson had dismantled the Second Bank of the United States, removing central banking controls. The surplus funds sent to state banks (“pet banks”) led to a massive expansion of paper money and uncontrolled lending, fueling a frantic western land-speculation bubble.

Jackson had dismantled the Second Bank of the United States, removing central banking controls. The surplus funds sent to state banks (“pet banks”) led to a massive expansion of paper money and uncontrolled lending, fueling a frantic western land-speculation bubble. The Specie Circular: To curb land speculation and paper money inflation, Jackson issued the Specie Circular in July 1836, an executive order requiring buyers to pay for federal public lands only in hard currency (gold or silver).

To curb land speculation and paper money inflation, Jackson issued the Specie Circular in July 1836, an executive order requiring buyers to pay for federal public lands only in hard currency (gold or silver). The Panic of 1837: The sudden demand for hard coin drained banks of their reserves, burst the speculative bubble, and triggered the Panic of 1837. This led to bank failures, widespread unemployment, and a deep depression that lasted nearly seven years.

The sudden demand for hard coin drained banks of their reserves, burst the speculative bubble, and triggered the Panic of 1837. This led to bank failures, widespread unemployment, and a deep depression that lasted nearly seven years. Return of the Debt: The debt-free status lasted only about a year; the economic crash dried up government revenues, forcing the US government to resume borrowing.

From the above, the US could only maintain the debt-free status for just one year but suffered a seven-year recession. Historians say that if the US had maintained a debt-free status it would have ended up as a mere agrarian state, because the ability to borrow for ventures has positive effect on creativity and expansion whether for government, businesses or individuals. He equivalent of the meltdown that happened post-1835 in the US economy, today is that if Nigeria wakes up and fully repays its loans, then we can only grow our economy in tandem with what the government is able to raise as taxes, duties, rates and fines. This means the government will put the people under immense pressure. The economy will shrink into a recession, meaning poverty rates, crime, and unemployment will spike.

The idea is not to borrow recklessly. But Nigeria’s debt-to-GDP ratio at a mere 35 per cent is one of the lowest in the world today. An astute financier will wonder whether we had no need for money – no infrastructure to build, no population to take care of, no children to send to school, no old people to help with healthcare. Therefore, saying debts are worse than leprosy or that they are bad for a national economy, is a very careless fallacy to utter.

With infrastructure buildup at the level of Dwight Eisenhower’s National System of Interstate and Defense Highways, an addition of $10 billion to total debt stock should certainly not attract statements from President Obasanjo to the effect that ‘debt is worse than leprosy’. One can only put such statement down to politics; President Obasanjo is rooting for Peter Obi, a man he believes he can control, and a man who has not put down any progressive initiative for Nigeria apart from rabble rousing.

The Obasanjo Debt Repayment

We learnt about the Debt Trap in every Economics class pre-2006. It was the story of how Africa, Asian and some South American mismanaged debt, or were sometimes coaxed or arm-twisted by much smarter lenders categorised into the London and Paris Club. Precisely, affected countries were categorised into Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPCs) and those that were deemed rather capable of paying at least some of their debts. Nigeria fell into the latter group and was made to pay the sum of $12 billion in exchange for the write-off of $18 billion. Some prominent Nigerians, notable ex-Governor Tunde Fashola, expressed their opinion that Nigeria oughtn’t have reached such an expensive deal. Of course, 33 African countries, benefitted from the 2006 arrangement named the G8’s Multilateral Debt Relief Initiative (MDRI), which cancelled 100 per cent of eligible multilateral debts for many of the world’s poorest nations.

Following the 1970s oil shocks and collapsing commodity prices in the 1980s, 39 to 42 low-income countries became trapped in unpayable external debt owed primarily to Western governments, the IMF, and the World Bank. To qualify for the World Bank’s HIPC Initiative, these nations had to prove their debt burdens were unsustainable even after traditional debt-relief mechanisms. In Sub-Saharan Africa these countries include: Benin, Burkina Faso, Burundi, Cameroon, Central African Republic, Chad, Comoros, Côte d’Ivoire, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Eritrea, Ethiopia, The Gambia, Ghana, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Liberia, Madagascar, Malawi, Mali, Mauritania, Mozambique, Niger, Republic of the Congo, Rwanda, São Tomé and Príncipe, Senegal, Sierra Leone, Somalia, Sudan, Tanzania, Togo, Uganda, and Zambia. In Latin America, and the Caribbeans, Bolivia, Guyana, Haiti, Honduras, and Nicaragua. While in Asia, Afghanistan benefited from 100 per cent write-off from IMF, World Bank and others. (Laos, Myanmar, and Vietnam had appeared on early pre-2006 HIPC assessments but were dropped, like Nigeria and Kenya).

It is however noteworthy that by the end of President Obasanjo’s government, Nigeria was back in debt. Domestic debt stood at ₦2.05 trillion, while Foreign Debts stayed at $3.35 billion. The naira converted at ₦124 to $1, taking Nigeria’s total national debt to $19.8 billion at the time that President Yar’Adua took over. Nigeria’s debt rose to $45 billion as at 29 May, 2011 and $63.8 billion as at 29 May 2015 when President Buhari took over. The Tinubu administration inherited $113.42 billion in total debt (including the CBN Ways and Means figure). Today, the number stands at $123 billion. This rundown is important to debunk the false claim and false alarm going round that President Tinubu has been overborrowing. He has only been responsible, borrowing only when absolutely necessary. But as an ambitious government, the total turnaround that Mr President has embarked upon certainly requires funding.

With infrastructure buildup at the level of Dwight Eisenhower’s National System of Interstate and Defense Highways, an addition of $10 billion to total debt stock should certainly not attract statements from President Obasanjo to the effect that ‘debt is worse than leprosy’. One can only put such statement down to politics; President Obasanjo is rooting for Peter Obi, a man he believes he can control, and a man who has not put down any progressive initiative for Nigeria apart from rabble rousing. The statement also reeks of hypocrisy, given that Obasanjo struck what some call a terrible deal with the World Bank – with the whooping $12 billion repayment plus commissions everywhere.

Indeed one should add that Obasanjo contradicted himself. He was chums with the Bretton Woods Institutions in his time. But now he disparages them, when he spoke about mere bachelors and spinsters coming here to dictate policy to African countries; policies that, he said, lead to our ruination. He said “These brilliant boys will package everything very well academically. They tell us, and we take it, lock, stock, and barrel, and we use it. For a country of 250 million people, it is boys and girls who are not even married, let alone manage a home, who will tell us what we will do to manage our people, our country, and we swallow it, and we destroy ourselves… World Bank and IMF were not designed for us. They were not built by us. They were built before we became independent, and that’s the people who will determine what we do… (British Prime Minister James Callaghan received four euros per year for every sheep on his farm while the World Bank and IMF barred African nations from subsidising their own farmers).., debt is worse than leprosy because leprosy destroys only one person. Debt destroys generations.”

On the contrary though, I posit that debt can build generations. In fact debt has built generations. All the countries that matter borrowed by leveraging their cash flows to get where they are. My earlier argument in the article stands. The Western world has only played with peanuts in Africa and we are not monkeys. One could argue that the recent engagements with China have been more promising and beneficial to Africa, and Nigeria in particular because we see the tangibles – roads, rail lines, airports etc. For more than three decades most African countries have not seen finances for tangibles but only for soft matters such as gender violence, job acceleration, business-enabling reforms, etc.

To cap it, there is a video circulating online where President Obasanjo spoke about a certain Mrs Kruger, a World Bank/IMF executive who demanded a presidential welcome during his presidency. He spoke about how he sent her report to his then Economic Adviser, Professor Soludo (who always rejected ALL their recommendations), and Mrs Okonjo-Iweala (who always supported ALL their recommendations, given that she made a career in those institutions). He said he would then blend both positions and strike a midpoint, and that he warned Soludo to never show that he was against those institutions else ‘they will rub his nose in the dirt’ (his exact words).

So, President Obasanjo is very aware of what is going on and he knows that we are much smarter today. He is only playing politics… and that is unfortunate given where this country is today. I would have thought he should put his age-long political differences aside and support progress for Nigeria – on the back of reforms that no president was able to pull through. Why is he trying to pull back the hand of the clock for Nigeria by trying to smuggle a puppet in by means fair or foul?

‘Tope Fasua is the special adviser to the President on Economic Matters.

World.title: UN secretary-general marks last climate summit with call to make polluters pay
World.content:
António Guterres, the United Nations secretary-general, has renewed his call to hold fossil fuel companies accountable by making them pay for the harm their actions have done to poorer countries through climate change, marking a defining moment of his last UN climate summit in office.

Mr Guterres gave his final press conference at the 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, as the head of the organisation.

The former prime minister of Portugal has led the UN since January 2017 and exits the role on 31 December, when his second five-year term ends.

Mr Guterres addressed representatives of civil society groups, who gathered Friday to bid him farewell and recognised him with an award for using the UN’s platform to confront the world’s most powerful industries.

“You have given a voice to this injustice like no other leader,” Louise Hutchins, convener of the Make Polluters Pay International Coalition, said.

The session was filled with chants of “make polluters pay”, and speakers asked him to return to a future climate summit wearing an NGO badge.

Mr Guterres told the gathering that the UN’s loss and damage fund now exists but was “funded at a ridiculous level”.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Those who pollute the least are those who are paying the highest price,” he said.

He urged civil society to apply the counter-pressure needed to help governments understand that things must change.

The UN chief’s final address to a COP leaders’ summit on Wednesday urged governments to levy a tax on oil companies’ windfall profits and use the money to help vulnerable countries recover.

He also proposed a climate justice compact to help countries shift away from fossil fuels, noting that the climate crisis is outrunning the world.

Mr Guterres told the leaders he will no longer be secretary-general from next year, but said, “I will not stop telling the truth.”

At Friday’s press conference, he demanded an immediate and drastic cut in emissions by big emitters.

“You cannot build peace on a burning planet,” he said.
