World.title: South Africa: Africa's Waste Pickers Demand Recognition in Climate Action
World.content:
As COP31 puts zero waste on the climate agenda, waste pickers across Africa say the continent's circular-economy transition cannot succeed without the people who already recover and recycle much of what it throws away.

Waste is the third-largest source of human-caused methane emissions, accounting for nearly 20% of the global total, yet the sector remains underfunded and inadequately monitored.

The UN Environment Programme estimated that municipal solid waste reached 2.1 billion tonnes in 2023 and will be at 3.8 billion tonnes by 2050. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), improved waste management, through a circular economy and better treatment technologies, has the potential to make a substantial contribution to reductions in national GHG emissions.



Under its Global Climate Action Agenda, COP31 is championing the Zero Waste initiative, which seeks to unlock the climate potential of waste management through scalable circular economy solutions. The initiative is focused on preventing food waste, moving towards circular economy solutions that turn waste into resources, and encouraging countries to include waste-related methane reductions in their updated Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs). The aim is to prevent emissions at source and make waste management an integral part of national climate strategies.

The need is greatest in low-income countries, where 97% of waste is openly dumped or burned. Uncontrolled dumpsites and open burning threaten communities, contaminate water and release climate pollutants, and without knowing where these sites are, how much waste they receive and what they emit, effective intervention is extremely difficult. As COP31 pushes countries to include waste methane in their climate plans, some African investors say the continent has a chance to turn waste into an economic resource.

Waste pickers say they must be part of that shift.

Across Africa, waste pickers and reclaimers collect, sort and recover recyclable materials that would otherwise end up in landfills, rivers or the environment. Many still work with limited formal recognition, social protection, and decent working conditions. Their inclusion is therefore emerging as a key question in discussions about Africa's zero-waste future. A transition to more sustainable waste management systems, advocates argue, must build on the knowledge and contribution of existing waste workers rather than exclude them.

For the International Alliance of Waste Pickers (IAWP), the success of such initiatives will depend in part on whether the people already driving recycling and resource recovery are recognised as essential partners in their implementation.

In an interview, Eva Mokoena of South Africa's African Reclaimers Organisation (ARO) discusses the role of waste pickers in climate action, the opportunities presented by the Zero Waste Districts initiative, and the changes needed to secure their place in Africa's transition to a circular economy.

Waste is often seen as an environmental and sanitation problem, but it is increasingly recognised as a major climate challenge. Why does tackling waste matter for the fight against climate change, and what role can zero waste play in reducing emissions?

Waste is a climate issue because what we throw away does not disappear. Organic waste buried in landfills and dumpsites rots without oxygen and releases methane, a gas that traps far more heat than carbon dioxide in the short term. Open burning of waste adds black carbon and toxic smoke to the air our communities breathe. Every item that is landfilled or burnt also means new materials must be extracted, manufactured, and transported to replace it.

Zero waste addresses all of these at once. When materials are separated at source, recovered, reused and recycled, and when organic waste is composted or turned into biogas, methane from landfills falls and the demand for virgin materials drops. This is one of the fastest and most affordable ways to reduce emissions.

The key to making it work is already on the ground. Waste pickers and reclaimers are the people removing waste from landfills, rivers, and streams every day. With proper recognition, equipment, and collaboration from governments, municipalities, and residents, they can multiply the climate impact they already deliver.

Waste is often overlooked in climate talks, yet food waste and landfills are major sources of greenhouse-gas emissions, especially methane. What practical policies and local actions would most effectively reduce food waste and keep organic waste out of landfills?

The most effective policies are the ones that recognise and include waste pickers and reclaimers. They are the frontline educators of their communities: they already teach residents to separate and recycle what they buy and eat. Governments and policymakers should write waste pickers into waste and climate legislation, so that this work is formally recognised, supported and paid for.

In practice, this means separation at source, in households, markets and businesses before it reaches the landfill, with waste pickers leading door-to-door awareness and collection.

In logistics, waste picker organisations need access to land, storage facilities and transport, so that organic material can be collected, stored and processed close to where it is generated. Local processing of food waste should be turned into compost, manure and biogas through community-run facilities, creating useful products and income instead of methane.

Investment in people is also important. Incubating reclaimer cooperatives, with full access to logistics and infrastructure, is what turns good policy into results.

If we continue to ignore the people on the ground, we will keep struggling. If we invest in them, organic waste can become a resource for our communities.

How can African governments make waste reduction and the circular economy a more central part of their national climate policies?

Governments can start by recognising who already runs Africa's circular economy. Waste pickers and reclaimers are unrecognised heroes: many spend their own time and resources recovering materials and cleaning public spaces without pay or protection. Bringing them into national climate policy means three things.

First, recognition in law. National climate plans, including Nationally Determined Contributions, and waste management legislation should name waste pickers as essential service providers and set out their rights, their role and how they will be paid.

Second, a seat at the table. Waste picker organisations should take part in designing, implementing and monitoring these policies. When waste pickers help shape the rules, the rules work on the ground, and waste pickers gain the recognition and confidence to expand their work.

Third, real support. Recognition has to come with resources: equipment, infrastructure, social protection and fair payment for the services waste pickers provide to cities and to the climate.

Looking at initiatives such as Zero Waste Districts and the 1x100 campaign, how can these programmes translate into tangible benefits for African communities, from cleaner cities and reduced landfill waste to decent jobs and better livelihoods for waste pickers?

These programmes deliver real benefits when everybody works together: governments, municipalities, residents, the private sector and waste picker organisations. Waste pickers are already on the ground, in every neighbourhood and in every landfill. What makes the difference is giving them space, resources and a central role.

Education is the most important key. With educational tools, training and empowerment, waste pickers can lead awareness campaigns, help households separate their waste, and recover a much wider range of materials at once. The result is cleaner streets, less waste reaching landfills and rivers, and recycling that actually works.

For waste pickers, the benefit must be decent work: formal contracts, fair payment for collection and recovery services, safe working conditions and social protection. When district programmes are built around existing waste picker cooperatives, the jobs and income they create stay in the community.

Two African nations that have joined the Zero Waste Districts programme are Ghana and Kenya. What are the biggest waste management challenges these countries are hoping to address, and what makes the district-level approach different from previous efforts?

What makes the district-level approach different is that it starts from the community and from the organisations that already exist, rather than from large, centralised projects designed far away from the people who manage waste every day. Our affiliates in both countries describe it in these terms.

In Ghana, the Green Waste Pickers Cooperative Society Limited and the Kpone Landfill Waste Pickers Association are supporting community-led circular initiatives that build on existing cooperatives. These cooperatives drive the process of diverting waste at source, adopt measures to pre-process materials, and lead environmental campaigns in their communities.

In Kenya, the Nakuru County Waste Pickers Association is advancing zero waste through waste reduction, reuse, recycling and waste picking, alongside community-led initiatives, progressive policies and the promotion of a circular economy.

In both cases, the district becomes the unit where waste pickers, residents and local authorities can work side by side, and where results can be seen and measured.

Many African cities are still grappling with poor waste collection, overflowing landfills, and very limited recycling. What kind of investment and what kind of partnerships are required to build effective waste management and recycling systems across the continent?

Close 

The investment that works is investment in the people already doing the job. Instead of expensive systems that bypass or displace waste pickers, African cities should incubate reclaimer and waste picker cooperatives and give them full access to what they need.

In infrastructure, sorting centres, storage space and land can help make the work safer. In logistics, vehicles and equipment to collect and move materials efficiently are needed. Processing capacity with facilities to recycle materials and to turn food waste into compost, manure and biogas is necessary. Fair contracts are also a key issue to provide payments from municipalities for the collection and recovery services waste pickers provide.

The partnerships that work are inclusive ones. Municipalities, national governments, producers, funders and residents should partner directly with waste picker organisations, as equals and from the design stage. If we keep ignoring the people on the ground, cities will keep struggling with the same problems. If we invest in them, Africa can build recycling systems that are effective, fair and locally owned.

Given that COP31 is placing such a strong emphasis on zero waste, what specific commitments should African countries be demanding in order to ensure that waste reduction actually becomes a measurable element of climate action rather than just another one of the international promises?

African countries should demand commitments that reach the ground, not only the negotiating rooms. In particular, direct funding for equipment and machinery that allows waste pickers and reclaimers to recover and recycle more materials, including food waste.

Educational tools must also be designed with waste pickers and be easy to use for both reclaimers and residents, so that separation at source becomes everyday practice in every household.

Formal recognition of waste pickers in national climate plans and waste policies, with a guaranteed role in their implementation and measurable targets for diverting organic and recyclable waste from landfills, monitored with the participation of waste picker organisations, are commitments that promote long-term climate solutions.

Waste pickers are good at what we do, and we make sure that everyone we work with understands our livelihoods on the streets and in the landfills, and the important role we play. Climate commitments on waste will only become real when they are built with us.

World.title: Nigeria: Index Ebola Case - Swiss Diplomat's Wife Recovers, Discharged From Hospital
World.content:
Nigeriaâs Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) issued a public health advisory following the countryâs confirmed Ebola case.

Abuja — Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) has said that the Nigeria's Ebola index case- Swiss diplomat's wife has recovered and discharged from hospital in Switzerland.

The disease intervention centre had confirmed the infection on October 20, 2026 after the patient's blood samples tested positive at the Abuja Reference Laboratory.

After receiving preliminary treatment at an undisclosed private hospital in Abuja, she and her husband were subsequently medically evacuated to Switzerland with an air ambulance on October 26, 2026.

Addressing journalists in his office in Abuja on Friday, NCDC Director General, Dr. Jide Idris, said the Swiss authorities had announced the recovery and discharge of the woman after testing negative.

He said index case tested negative after receiving treatment in an isolation facility in Switzerland.

More details later...

World.title: South Africa: Joburg Turns Up the Heat As Residents Wait for Relief
World.content:
Outdoor workers should take regular breaks and residents should avoid direct sunlight between 11am and 3pm.

Cooler weather and thunderstorms are expected over the weekend, offering some relief from the heat.

Johannesburg residents face another scorching day on Friday, with emergency services urging people to drink water, take breaks and stay out of the midday sun.

The City of Johannesburg's Emergency Management Services says extremely hot conditions are expected to continue across much of the city. Outdoor workers have been urged to take regular breaks and residents should avoid direct sunlight between 11am and 3pm.

The South African Weather Service's heatwave advisory issued earlier this week included southern Gauteng, with persistently high temperatures expected until Friday, 13 November.



But some relief could arrive over the weekend.

Weather service senior forecaster Tokelo Chiloane said cooler conditions, accompanied by thunderstorms and thundershowers, are expected over the weekend.

Until then, residents have been urged to protect themselves from the heat.

"Residents are urged to stay hydrated, drink lots of water, avoid direct sunlight especially between 11h00 and 15h00 in the afternoon," Johannesburg emergency services spokesperson Robert Mulaudzi said earlier this week.

For street traders, gardeners, construction workers and others spending hours outside, regular breaks in a cool or shaded place are especially important.

The World Health Organization says older people, babies, outdoor workers and people with existing medical conditions face greater risks during hot weather. Residents should also check on relatives and neighbours who live alone.

Keeping cool does not have to mean switching on an air conditioner. The organisation recommends loose, light clothing, cool showers and wetting the skin with a damp cloth. Drink water regularly and avoid alcohol.

Never leave children, dependent adults or pets alone in a parked vehicle, even while running a quick errand.

Parents have also been warned to watch children seeking somewhere to cool off.

Mulaudzi urged families to keep young children away from dams and river streams to prevent drownings.

Heat illness needs prompt attention. Dizziness, weakness, intense thirst and headaches are signs to move into a cool place and drink water.

Confusion, seizures or a loss of consciousness require urgent medical help. Move the person into shade or a cool room and use cold, wet cloths to help cool them while waiting for assistance.

Close 

For life-threatening emergencies in Johannesburg, call 011 375 5911. The city says this number connects residents to emergency assistance, including ambulance and fire services.

World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: DR Congo Ebola Outbreak - Armed Groups Unrest Hold Back Response
World.content:
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) continues to spread amid repeated and ongoing deadly attacks on civilians and frontline health workers by armed groups that are obstructing efforts to stop transmission, UN responders said on Friday.

In an update, the UN Senior Ebola Response Coordinator, Julien Harneis, stressed that more people are being killed by Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) fighters than by Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus in recent days.

And yet the attacks on "tens of villages all across the south of Ituri and North Kivu (provinces) goes unnoticed", Mr. Harneis maintained. "People are scared, people are furious at the lack of action on this."

Up to 500 infections per week



Echoing that message, the UN World Health Organization (WHO)'s Dr Chikwe Ihekweazu, Executive Director of WHO's Health Emergencies Programme, said that despite much progress in containing transmission within eastern DRC, about 400 to 500 cases of infection are still being identified every week.

This trend is linked to the emergence of cases in rural and hard-to-reach areas.

In more positive developments, the WHO official noted that prevention efforts have led to "a significant reduction" in transmission in previous hotspots, in particular Bunia, Mongbwalu, Rampara and Nizi, all in Ituri province in eastern DRC.

Nonetheless, the violent unrest across the vast area impacted by Ebola creates huge challenges for responders.

"We've seen so many attacks on healthcare, attacks on communities as well, attacks on people providing care, and people losing their lives, nurses in burials," Dr Ihekweazu explained. "So, we need to keep working with the community, and this is very important. And working with the specific groups instigating these attacks."

Disease threats in addition to attacks

Communities are already facing outbreaks of diseases, malnutrition and displacement driven by decades of violent unrest fuelled by dozens of armed

groups that remain active in the resource-rich region.

Earlier this week, WHO condemned attacks against frontline healthcare workers and community awareness officers, including in Cantine-Aloya in North Kivu that killed 66 civilians including three health workers. Three health facilities were also looted.

Two weeks ago, a nurse was also killed and another health worker badly injured when they were attacked while responding to an Ebola alert in Tshopo province.

Tedros appeal

Other attacks have included an arson attempt on a treatment centre and stones thrown at a vehicle used for conducting safe and dignified burials, an indication of the need to continue to build trust with extremely vulnerable communities.

"We cannot focus only on Ebola. Some people in the affected communities have said told me personally that Ebola is a lesser evil compared to some of the other threats they face," WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus stressed earlier this week.

A massive humanitarian emergency

The DRC Ebola outbreak was declared in May and has since become the largest yet as it continues to spread faster than any previous outbreak in the vast country's east and northeast provinces.

To date, more than 11,000 cases have been confirmed and more than 5,000 people have died.

In a related development, the UN World Food Programme (WFP) warned that nearly 29 million people in the DRC face acute food insecurity, with most in the conflict and Ebola-affected eastern and northeastern provinces. That number is likely to continue to increase, said Jean-Martin Bauer, WFP Director of Food Security and Nutrition Analysis.

Briefing journalists via video in Geneva, Mr. Bauer stressed that conflict is driving the hunger crisis, in addition to the Ebola outbreak.

Close 

"What we need right now is access, and we need resources to avoid the situation becoming more difficult in the DRC," he said.

Hunger emergency

Latest UN-backed food insecurity expert assessments indicate that between January and June 2027, 30.3 million people will be in crisis levels of acute food insecurity or worse, with 4.2 million of this number experiencing "emergency levels" of hunger and the most acute needs in North Kivu, South Kivu and Ituri provinces "driven by persistent conflict and large-scale displacement".

Mr. Bauer noted that Ebola is just one of many disease outbreaks in DRC, but that it is compounding the hunger crisis for communities already struggling to eat.

"Families are being displaced, they're being cut off from their farms, from their livelihoods," he explained. "Food prices are rising, making affording a meal quite complicated for too many households."

World.title: Africa: Africa Made It: Turning Africa's Cotton Wealth into Jobs, Industry and Economic Power
World.content:
Africa Made It campaign was launched in Lagos, Nigeria, aiming to drive Africa's industrial sovereignty under the theme, "Power, Protect and Purchase."

Africa produces cotton, inspires global fashion and boasts a vibrant creative industry. Yet much of the economic value generated from these resources is captured beyond the continent. Launched during CANEX WKND 2026 in Lagos, Nigeria, the Africa Made It campaign seeks to change that narrative by promoting local manufacturing, strengthening Africa’s textile value chain and encouraging consumers to support African-made products.

Africa’s fashion and textile industries hold considerable potential to drive industrialisation, create employment and strengthen the continent’s economic independence. However, despite its abundant natural resources and creative talent, Africa continues to capture only a limited share of the value generated by its cotton and fashion industries.

The Africa Made It campaign, launched during the Creative Africa Nexus (CANEX) WKND 2026 in Lagos, aims to address this imbalance by encouraging African countries to move beyond exporting raw cotton and invest in a fully integrated fibre-to-fashion value chain.

Built around three pillars “Power, Protect and Purchase” the campaign seeks to mobilise governments, investors, manufacturers, fashion brands and consumers to strengthen local production and retain more economic value within Africa.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The initiative highlights the potential of the sector to contribute an estimated US$34 billion annually to Africa’s GDP through increased domestic textile and garment production.

In an interview with AllAfrica’s Nontobeko Mlambo, Abimbola Ogundairo, Senior Consultant at Africa Practice, discusses the campaign’s ambitions, the challenges facing Africa’s textile industry and the lessons other African countries can draw from Benin’s emerging manufacturing sector.

What inspired the Africa Made It campaign, and why is it important for the continent?

Africa Made It is a movement designed to showcase the investment potential of African-made brands, starting with the fashion industry.

Its significance lies in a challenge we have faced for decades: Africa contributes enormous value to the global economy but captures very little of the wealth generated from its resources.

Take cotton, for example. Thirty-seven of Africa’s 54 countries produce cotton, yet the continent captures less than 2% of the global cotton economy. And cotton is only one example. The same challenge exists in other sectors, including cocoa and gold.

Africa Made It aims to bring these conversations together and address the missing links in our value chains, particularly the lack of local processing and manufacturing capacity. We want to engage policymakers, development institutions, investors, businesses and other stakeholders across the value chain to explore how we can connect these different elements.

The objective is to ensure that more of the value Africa produces remains on the continent rather than being exported for others to benefit from.

How does the campaign align with CANEX’s broader ambition to develop Africa’s cultural and creative industries?

Platforms such as CANEX are incredibly important because the creative industries have long been overlooked as sources of economic value and cultural identity. Across Africa, young people are achieving remarkable things in fashion, music, art and other creative sectors, often despite limited institutional support.

Africa already exports enormous cultural influence and creative talent. Our fashion, music and artistic expressions have a global presence. The question is whether we have the mechanisms in place to capture the economic value associated with that influence.

CANEX provides an opportunity to bring the right stakeholders together. It allows creatives to showcase their achievements while engaging directly with policymakers, investors and institutions capable of providing the infrastructure, financing and policies they need.

What makes these platforms particularly valuable is their ability to move the conversation beyond isolated initiatives towards coordinated, sustainable solutions. We need to institutionalise the support systems that allow creative businesses to grow and ensure that the economic benefits generated by African creativity remain within the continent.

What are the campaign’s main objectives, and what changes does it hope to bring to Africa’s fashion and textile industries?

The campaign aims to unlock the enormous economic potential of Africa’s cotton-to-fashion value chain.

Research estimates that an investment of approximately US$1.8 billion across the continent could help create up to two million permanent jobs and generate US$33 billion in annual household income. For African countries seeking to accelerate industrialisation, increase revenue and create employment, this represents a significant opportunity.

Benin provides an interesting example. Through the development of the Glo-Djigbé Industrial Zone, the country has begun transforming its cotton industry.

According to the figures we have seen, Benin has moved from exporting approximately 90% of its raw cotton towards processing around 30% locally. The country is also reportedly exporting about 10 million garments annually and aims to create 300,000 permanent jobs by 2030.

These developments demonstrate what can be achieved when investment, infrastructure and industrial policy are aligned. This is why our campaign is built around three pillars: Power, Protect and Purchase.

Power means providing African manufacturers and businesses with the energy, financing and infrastructure they need to operate and expand.

Protect focuses on creating fair trade policies and addressing illicit imports and other practices that undermine the competitiveness of local industries.

Purchase is about encouraging governments, businesses and consumers to buy African-made products.

We must move away from the assumption that foreign products are inherently better. Buying African is not only an expression of cultural identity and pride. It is also an economic decision that supports local businesses, creates employment and strengthens our economies. Ultimately, we want to build a movement that brings all stakeholders together to close the gaps in Africa’s manufacturing value chain.

Why is it important for African consumers to recognise, support and take pride in locally made fashion?

As a Nigerian, I grew up in a society where people take enormous pride in wearing traditional clothing and expressing their cultural identity. For many Nigerians, wearing local styles is already part of everyday life. However, there is an important economic dimension to this conversation.

We may proudly wear African prints and traditional fabrics without realising that some of these materials are manufactured outside the continent. Ankara, for example, is widely associated with African fashion and identity, yet much of the fabric is produced elsewhere.

This raises an important question: when we celebrate our cultural identity through fashion, are we also supporting the local industries and workers who should benefit from it?

Cultural pride should translate into economic empowerment. We need to ensure that the clothes we wear and the products we celebrate contribute to employment, manufacturing and wealth creation within our own countries.

Africa has contributed immense cultural and economic value to the world for generations. We should also be able to capture the financial benefits of that contribution. We do not want to become a continent that proudly wears its cultural identity without benefiting economically from it. We can do both: celebrate who we are and build industries that create prosperity for our people. That is the thinking behind Power, Protect and Purchase.

What specific activities, partnerships or initiatives are needed to turn the campaign’s ambitions into tangible results?

Everyone has a role to play in building a sustainable African fashion and textile industry. The value chain begins with cotton farmers, who need access to agricultural inputs, technical skills and resources to improve the quality and productivity of their crops. It extends to processing facilities, storage, transportation, manufacturing infrastructure and the policies required to attract investment.

Governments have a responsibility to create enabling environments, while investors must recognise the opportunities available across the industry. Fashion businesses also have an important role. They should consider whether they are sourcing materials locally, working with African manufacturers and supporting artisans within their communities. The media and other storytellers can help raise awareness of the industry's potential and highlight successful initiatives. Development institutions and international investors also have opportunities to contribute.

Regional integration is particularly important.

The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) provides a framework for strengthening trade and industrial cooperation across African countries. For example, cotton could be grown in Nigeria, processed in Benin and transformed into finished garments elsewhere in the region. Different countries could contribute at various stages of production, allowing more of the economic value to circulate within Africa.

We should also recognise that fashion extends beyond clothing. Technology is creating new opportunities, including the use of artificial intelligence to improve garment design, sizing and the consumer experience.

The industry encompasses accessories, innovation, logistics and many other activities. Our challenge is to connect these different elements and ensure that businesses have access to the resources they need to grow.

You have highlighted Benin as a success story. What lessons can other African countries learn from its experience?

Close 

One of the most important lessons from Benin is the value of creating an environment that encourages private investment. The Glo-Djigbé Industrial Zone demonstrates how cooperation between the public and private sectors can support industrial development. The government has played a role in facilitating investment and establishing conditions that encourage manufacturing. Such partnerships are important because building a textile industry requires substantial investment in infrastructure, energy, transport and production facilities.

Benin’s experience also shows the importance of moving beyond the export of raw materials towards local processing and the production of finished goods. The country is now reportedly exporting approximately 10 million garments annually. Other African countries can learn from this approach by developing policies that attract investors, encourage industrial partnerships and support local manufacturers. Ultimately, the lesson is that industrial transformation requires coordination, long-term commitment and a willingness to invest in domestic value creation.

How will you measure the success of the Africa Made It campaign?

The campaign is designed to raise awareness, encourage dialogue and connect stakeholders across Africa’s cotton-to-fashion value chain. In the short term, success will mean generating greater recognition of the opportunities available in the sector.

We want to see more conversations involving policymakers, investors, development institutions, manufacturers and fashion businesses. We also want these discussions to lead to practical collaboration. That means identifying where investment is needed, which policies require reform and how institutions can work together to support local businesses.

African entrepreneurs should not have to succeed despite structural obstacles. They should be able to thrive because the right infrastructure, policies and institutional support are in place. In the longer term, success will be measured by tangible economic outcomes. We want to see investment mobilised, manufacturing capacity expanded and sustainable employment created.

The estimated US$1.8 billion in investment and the potential US$33 billion in annual household income illustrate the scale of the opportunity.

If African countries, investors and businesses work together, we can build stronger industrial value chains and ensure that more of the wealth generated by Africa’s resources and creativity benefits African people. That is the transformation Africa Made It hopes to achieve.

World.title: Niger: UNHRC Calls For Millions in Emergency Aid to Fill Critical Gaps
World.content:
Geneva — The UN Refugee Agency, UNHCR, warned on Tuesday of a deepening crisis that has caused tens of thousands of people to flee from Nigeria to neighbouring Niger and Benin, where problems of malnutrition and disease are surfacing.

Dominique Hyde, UNHCR director of external relations, said at a UN press conference in Geneva that nearly 64,000 people have arrived in Niger fleeing violence in northern Nigeria since the beginning of the year.

“They are adding to the growing humanitarian needs in a country already hosting more than half a million refugees and asylum-seekers, including some 327,500 from Nigeria, alongside people displaced within Niger itself,” said Hyde.



In the past decade, attacks by Boko Haram, Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) fighters and criminal gangs have displaced millions of people fleeing the violence.

“The impact of the violence is also being felt further afield, with several hundred Nigerians seeking refuge in neighbouring Benin,” said Hyde.

“Although the numbers remain relatively small compared to arrivals in Niger, these movements highlight the widening geographical impact of insecurity in northern Nigeria and the increasing distances families are travelling in search of safety.”

UNHCR said that most arrivals have sought safety in Diffa, in south-eastern Niger, and Tahoua, in western Niger, both bordering Nigeria, which are already grappling with insecurity, climate shocks and overstretched services.

The refugee agency said in October alone, around 1,200 people crossed into Diffa and another 3,400 into Tahoua, as violence continued to force families from their homes.

THOUSANDS OF NEWLY-ARRIVED REFUGEES

“Thousands of newly arrived refugees, many of them children, are struggling to survive with limited access to food, clean water, shelter and essential services, as humanitarian resources fall critically short,” noted Hyde.

In Diffa, more than 23,000 people, over two-thirds of them children, have arrived since the beginning of the year.

Many are living in makeshift shelters that offer little protection from the elements, while access to clean water remains a major challenge.

“Refugee women describe having to walk several kilometres to collect water for their families. With no nearby health facilities or schools, families are struggling to meet even their most basic needs,” said Hyde.

The UN agency said that protection concerns are growing and only around 5 percent of Nigerian refugees who arrived this year have been registered, due to limited resources.

Close 

Without documentation, refugees face additional barriers to accessing assistance and essential services, leaving them exposed to heightened protection risks.

“Education is another major concern, particularly for children arriving from Nigeria’s English-language-based education system, with no schools or transitional classes at some locations,” explained Hyde.

UNHCR said an urgent increase in humanitarian assistance, stronger coordination and additional operational partners are needed to address critical gaps in water, food, shelter, health care, registration and protection.

Beyond emergency assistance, greater investment is needed in livelihoods and longer-term solutions.

The refugee agency said it urged the international community to urgently fill these critical gaps while investing in more stable, sustainable futures for refugees and host communities, as it calls for $11.4 million for emergency solutions in Niger, Nigeria and Benin.

World.title: Ethiopia: Mekelle Residents Call for Sustained Federal Govt Efforts to Advance Reforms in Tigray
World.content:
Addis Ababa — Residents of Mekelle have urged the Federal Government to sustain and accelerate reform, reconstruction and development efforts in Tigray region.

The inhabitants further emphasized the need for consolidating progress toward lasting peace, stability and prosperity in the region.

The call was made during a consultative forum of Mekelle residents, presided over by Chief of Staff of the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF), Field Marshal Birhanu Jula.



Speaking at the gathering, Field Marshal Birhanu said the defunct TPLF faction had aligned itself with the so-called "Tsimdo" group, an alliance orchestrated by Ethiopia's historical adversaries to wage war against the country.

He said his engagement with residents was aimed at fostering dialogue, strengthening cooperation and encouraging collective efforts to ensure lasting peace and stability in Tigray region.

During the discussions, residents underscored their strong desire to see an end to conflict, identifying peace, security and sustainable development as their foremost priorities.

They called for the reconstruction of damaged infrastructure, expanded employment opportunities for young people and the restoration of security to enable communities to resume normal life without fear.

"Our foremost priorities are the reconstruction of critical infrastructure, the creation of meaningful employment opportunities for our youth, and the restoration of security so that citizens can go about their daily lives in peace," participants said.

Residents also welcomed the resumption of salary payments for civil servants and ongoing infrastructure rehabilitation efforts, describing them as important steps toward restoring normalcy and accelerating the region's recovery.

Concluding the forum, participants called on the Federal Government to maintain its commitment to Tigray, sustain ongoing interventions and accelerate reform, reconstruction and development initiatives to secure lasting peace and improve the livelihoods of communities across the region.

World.title: Ohio State's Jeremiah Smith becomes Big Ten's all-time leading receiver in just his third college season
World.content:
Jeremiah Smith's (likely) final college season might not result in another national title, but he is now in the record books.

In just his third college season, the Ohio State wide receiver became the all-time leading receiver in Big Ten history during the Buckeyes' 28-19 win over Northwestern.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Smith had 11 receptions for 117 yards and a score for the Buckeyes, who have free-fallen out of the College Football Playoff bracket. But with the performance, he surpassed Purdue’s John Standeford's Big Ten mark in the second quarter while remaining front and center in the Heisman debate.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Standeford had 3,788 receiving yards in his four seasons with the Boilermakers, but Smith now has 3,875.

Smith is one of just 11 players inside the top-50, and three inside the top-15, to spend less than four seasons in the conference.

He also tied Purdue's David Bell and Michigan's Braylon Edwards with his 17th 100-yard game.

Smith made a statement the second he set foot in Columbus, as he led the Big Ten in receiving yards and touchdowns as a freshman — and he has only gotten better.

Last year, he was an All-American and finished sixth in the Heisman vote. This season, his 15 touchdowns are tops in all the FBS, and he figures to be in the conversation to be the first pick in next year's NFL Draft.

UPDATED START TIMES FOR COLLEGE FOOTBALL GAMES AFFECTED BY FAA GROUND STOP, BROKEN DOWN BY CONFERENCE

Smith also led the Big Ten in catches and yards last year.

Smith accounted for more than half of the passing yards backup quarterback Luke Frahey threw on Saturday (201 total), as Julian Sayin continues to deal with an injury.

He figures to be yet another receiving star out of Ohio State in recent years, joining Chris Olave, Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Garrett Wilson, Emeka Egbuka, Carnell Tate and Marvin Harrison Jr.



The Buckeyes face Nebraska and Michigan to end their regular season.

World.title: Maher challenges Sarah Huckabee Sanders on 'socialism' as Arkansas governor defends free school breakfasts
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders credited her education agenda with helping her defy a sweeping blue wave in the 2026 midterms, defending free school breakfasts after Bill Maher questioned why such programs are labeled socialism only when Democrats offer them.

"We focused on issues over the last four years of things that really impacted the day-to-day life of the people that we were elected to serve," Sanders said during Friday’s episode of "Real Time."

"I made no secret coming in that education was going to be a top priority, and we have legitimately transformed education in the state of Arkansas."

GOV SANDERS REVEALS 'MAJOR BREAKTHROUGH' ON EDUCATION AS RED STATE POSITIONS ITSELF AS 'BLUEPRINT' FOR NATION

Sanders highlighted several measures Arkansas has taken to improve student learning outcomes, including deploying literacy coaches, expanding school choice, raising teacher pay and providing free breakfasts for public school students.

She described the breakfast program as a bipartisan effort to ensure children aren’t trying to learn on an empty stomach.

"But how come it’s only socialism when they do it?" Maher pressed, referring to Democrats.

Sanders drew a distinction between providing meals to schoolchildren and broader government giveaways.

BROOKE ROLLINS, DR. BEN CARSON: WE ARE PUTTING REAL FOOD BACK ON SCHOOL LUNCH TRAYS

"There’s a big difference between giving everything away for free and helping kids start out on the right foot," she said.

"I don’t know that I would say those are the same thing."

Maher clarified that he supported Huckabee Sanders’ initiative.

Democratic strategist Kaivan Shroff told Fox News Digital, "Maher’s question exposes the game pretty cleanly. When Democrats use government to help people, Republicans call it socialism. When Sarah Huckabee Sanders uses government to give every public-school kid free breakfast, it becomes common sense."

He added, "What Sanders really proved is that voters are a lot less interested in abstract fights about ‘big government’ than politicians pretend. If government is doing something visible that makes their lives better, they may reward it."

The Arkansas Republican's broader discussion with Maher also focused on her longstanding support for President Donald Trump, with Maher questioning whether her loyalty to the president sometimes conflicts with her own principles.

"It seems like you are policy-wise you diverge from him, but you will never say a bad word or leave any daylight between you and what he does, which is very often different than what you do as governor," Maher said.

SARAH HUCKABEE SANDERS ACCUSES 'THE VIEW' HOST OF TWISTING HER WORDS IN IMMIGRATION EXCHANGE

Sanders rebuked any suggestion that she has a "blind loyalty" to the president, stating that many of her policies align with Trump's, but she also disagrees with him on some issues.

"I certainly support and appreciate a president who gave me an opportunity," Sanders said.

"Does that mean I agree with everything? No. Does that mean I think he does everything right? No. Neither do I."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Sanders, who has served as Arkansas' governor since 2023, won by 15 points over her Democratic opponent Fred Love earlier this month, overcoming the blue wave that largely swept the U.S. – even in traditionally red or toss-up areas like South Carolina, Mississippi, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Texas and Georgia.

World.title: At least 100 people pulled from Mississippi River after New Orleans ship crash as lengthy salvage effort looms
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Roughly 100 people were pulled from the Mississippi River after a tanker struck a docked cruise ship in New Orleans on Friday, officials revealed Saturday, as the U.S. Coast Guard prepares for a potentially weeks-long operation to remove the capsized vessel.

New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said 191 passengers and crew members were aboard the American Heritage when the Atlantic Asphalt tanker struck the vessel near the Port of New Orleans.

Everyone survived, though eight people remained hospitalized Saturday, including two in serious condition. The other six patients were stable, officials said.

Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said crews were preparing to remove 16,000 gallons of fuel from the American Heritage before salvage operations begin. Divers were expected to assess the vessel, while pollution response teams monitored the river for potential leaks.

NEW ORLEANS BOAT CRASH CALLED ‘MIRACLE ON THE MISSISSIPPI’ AS EVERYONE IS ACCOUNTED FOR, OFFICIALS SAY

Burnham said crews had not observed any product in the river requiring removal but warned that hazardous materials could potentially escape during the operation.

"As the mayor said, we're talking weeks, we're not talking days, we're talking weeks. So we're going to do this safely and we're going to make sure that it's done right," Burnham said.

Moreno also revealed that the American Heritage's captain was injured but remained aboard until passengers and crew were accounted for, becoming the last person to leave the vessel.

"Every moment of the critical time [Friday], he did not want to leave his ship," Moreno said.

TWO DEAD, INCLUDING INFANT, AFTER BOAT CAPSIZES IN NEW YORK HARBOR; 12 RESCUED

The captain initially refused medical treatment until he knew where everyone was, according to the mayor.

Port of New Orleans Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montro said responders evacuated more than 80 people before the vessel overturned, while roughly 100 people ended up in the river.

Montro said she estimated the American Heritage capsized within 30 to 45 minutes of the collision, though the exact timeline remains under investigation.

Officials credited life jackets and the rapid response of emergency crews and nearby vessels with preventing fatalities.

Investigators are examining a possible steering issue involving the tanker, though the exact cause of the collision remains unknown.

11-NIGHT CARIBBEAN CRUISE ABRUPTLY CANCELED AFTER COAST GUARD DETAINS SHIP

"I can say though I do not have any indication that this is terrorism related in any way, shape or form, but again, the investigators will continue to keep working through that," Burnham said.

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) began arriving Saturday after travel disruptions delayed its response.

The collision occurred around 12:30 p.m. local time Friday, when the tanker struck the American Heritage, which had been docked for approximately two hours. The vessel began taking on water before capsizing.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The Atlantic Asphalt has since been moved from the collision site, while the Coast Guard has partially reopened the river to two-way traffic. A 500-foot safety zone remains in place around the wreck.

American Cruise Lines, which operates the American Heritage, is coordinating with local officials to assist displaced passengers as the investigation and recovery efforts continue.

World.title: 5 restaurant chains serving some of the best BBQ brisket in America, from New York to Oklahoma
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Brisket is an integral part of the menu at many barbecue joints, with one Texas restaurant recently sparking controversy after removing the cut of meat due to skyrocketing beef prices.

Americans eat about 58.5 pounds of beef per year as of 2025, according to the USDA — and diners seem to crave the tender, juicy cut that is brisket, which comes from the breast or lower chest of a cow.

AMERICA'S BEST FOOD CITIES RANKED BY EXPERT, WITH CHOICES THAT COULD INFURIATE LOCALS

The Takeout recently compiled a list of the best barbecue places in America to get brisket, citing smoking techniques, meat tenderness, flavor and customer satisfaction.

Here are five of the best barbecue restaurant chains in the country to get brisket — from New York to Oklahoma.

1. Mission BBQ

Since opening its doors on the tenth anniversary of the Sept. 11th terrorist attacks, Mission BBQ has been "proudly serving those who serve."

Dining rooms are filled with patriotic tributes to those who have served and protected the United States, and guests who drop in for lunch might catch the restaurant’s "daily salute to the Stars and Stripes," the chain’s website states.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Oak-smoked, tender brisket is served sliced or chopped on a sandwich, alongside other meaty classics like pulled pork or pulled chicken sandwiches, baby back ribs, smoked chicken and sausage, of which there are both jalapeño cheese and classic varieties.

Kids or those with smaller appetites can enjoy mini brisket sliders.

At its many locations across 24 states, Mission BBQ aims to provide authentic barbecue made with fresh ingredients — the website even notes the restaurants do not have freezers or microwaves.

2. 4 Rivers Smokehouse

After developing a love for brisket while traveling through Texas, John Rivers founded 4 Rivers Smokehouse, with the first location opening in Winter Park, Florida, in 2009.

The chain wet-ages its brisket for 30 days, then massages it with a spice rub before it's smoked for 18 hours.

"Great brisket can't be rushed. It's a labor of love that takes patience, passion and a dedication to getting it right every single day," 4 Rivers Smokehouse told Fox News Digital in a statement.

"It's part of who we are."

"At 4 Rivers, brisket is more than a menu item. It's part of who we are, and we're incredibly proud to share that tradition with our guests," they added.

Aside from enjoying sliced brisket on its own or in a sandwich, diners can also order a brisket bowl or add the meat to the specialty Smoke Stack burger.

3. Dinosaur Bar-B-Que

Created in 1983 as a concession stand to serve bikers at the Harley Rendezvous motorcycle gathering in Albany, New York, Dinosaur Bar-B-Que was the brainchild of John Stage and two partners — one of them named Dino, the company’s website states. Today, Dinosaur Bar-B-Que has locations in five cities in New York.

For its brisket, the chain uses USDA Prime beef that is aged for 30 days, smoked fresh daily over regional oak and hickory woods, then hand-sliced.

CLICK HERE TO 

A menu disclaimer says that, due to the "low and slow" daily smoking process, restaurants may run out of fresh smoked meats.

Guests can enjoy the brisket on its own or in sandwiches, combo plates and more. Additional menu items include pork belly sliders, a shareable shrimp boil, fried green tomatoes and a barbecue chopped salad.

4. Billy Sims BBQ

Billy Sims, the 1978 Heisman Trophy winner and a former NFL running back for the Detroit Lions, worked with his business partner Jeff Jackson to open the first Billy Sims BBQ location in Tulsa, Oklahoma in 2004.

The chain now has over 30 restaurants across six states, with a menu featuring brisket that’s smoked slowly over pecan wood and served in a variety of ways, including chopped, sliced, in sandwiches and tacos, and more.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Guests can also opt for a brisket plate which comes loaded with two side dishes, Texas toast, pickles, onions and barbecue sauce.

If a plate’s not enough, brisket and other meats can be purchased by the pound.

5. Sonny’s BBQ

Since opening in 1968 in Gainesville, Florida, Sonny’s BBQ has expanded to operate across eight states, and the chain takes barbecue seriously.

Those hoping to work as a pit master at Sonny’s must successfully complete the restaurant’s "P.I.T. Academy" education and training program, according to the website.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Brisket is smoked in-house each day, and it can be eaten on sandwiches, added to salads, or used as a topping on tater tots.

"The smoked wings, brisket, and baby back ribs were all moist and tender—just perfect," said a customer in a review on Yelp.

World.title: 'Dallas’ star Patrick Duffy says mother was killed rushing to husband after gunmen opened fire at bar
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Patrick Duffy's mother was doing a crossword puzzle when two armed men returned to the bar she and her husband owned in Montana, and one of them shot her husband. Moments later, she rushed toward him and was shot and killed, too.

The "Dallas" star, 77, recalled the final moments of his parents' lives during an appearance on the "Still Here Hollywood" podcast, revealing how the double murder unfolded and how he found the strength to carry on.

The murders took place nearly 40 years ago, on Nov. 18, 1986.

'DALLAS' STAR PATRICK DUFFY AND LINDA PURL RECALL START OF SURPRISING LOVE STORY: 'BOTH NERVOUS AS TEENAGERS'

"My parents were murdered when two young men robbed the bar that my parents owned in Montana," the actor told host Steve Kmetko. "My dad had thrown these two boys out because they were drunk and obstreperous. He just threw them out of the bar, and they went somewhere, finished whatever they were drinking, and the anger boiled up and they went back in."

Sean A. Wentz and Kenneth A. Miller were both 19 at the time, People magazine reported. Duffy's parents, Marie and Terence, were the only ones in the bar when the gunmen returned.

"It was very late at night," Duffy said. "There was nobody in the bar except my father and my mother, and they walked in with their shotguns. As soon as my dad saw them, this is in the testimony that came out in the court, my dad turned to them and apparently took a step towards them, saying, 'I told you to ...'"

WATCH: PATRICK DUFFY AND LINDA PURL FELL IN LOVE ONLINE

Duffy's father never finished his sentence.

"... That's when they opened up on him and killed him," Duffy said. "And then my mother was on the other end of the bar doing a crossword puzzle and took a couple steps running towards dad. And they shot her too."

"And then, if that wasn't stupid enough, instead of just running, they jumped over the bar to the cash register, took the money and a couple of bottles of booze and then left."

The Los Angeles Times previously reported that Terence and Marie's bodies were found by a group of people who had stopped for a drink after finishing their shifts at the nearby Montana Developmental Center. One woman spotted Marie on the floor but initially thought she might have fainted. When she saw blood on Terence, she went outside and flagged down a friend for help.

Duffy learned of his parents' deaths the following morning.

"... My sister had called she was completely devastated," he recalled. "... She was a police woman, and she was on her way to Montana. By the time I hung up the phone, there were film crews at the gate."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Duffy said Lorimar Television, the production company behind "Dallas," arranged transportation and other support for him following the murders.

"Lorimar [Television] called, everybody called, [the] support team got in there and said, 'We have the jet ready. We'll fly you to Montana. We'll take care of everything. We'll send a PR person with you to take care of all that.'"

Duffy said his Buddhist faith helped him cope with the loss. It also gave him the strength to tell his sons, Padraic and Conor, that their grandparents had been killed.

"The Buddhist philosophy is one of the continuous life cycle of your entity," Duffy explained on the podcast.

"... The first thing I did was, it was just as the boys were getting up to go to school, very young, and I said, '... I'm going to chant with you,' because we always chanted before they went off to school. I said, 'We have to chant for grandma and grandpa because they've both been killed, and we have to chant for them because they're going to understand it and hear it.'"

Miller and Wentz were convicted in connection with the murders and sentenced to prison, according to People magazine. Nine.com.au reported that Miller was released on parole in 2007, and Wentz was granted parole in 2015.

Duffy previously told Closer Weekly that he still remembered his parents as "pretty ordinary, pleasant people" who were "very social" before the murders.

"When my parents were murdered, I went through all the emotions of the horrific event — shock and anger and everything — but I never felt disconnected from [my parents]," Duffy said. "I never felt that immediate loss. I did not know why then, but in retrospect, it was a result of being Buddhist."

"There was something about the eternity of life that had set deep inside me," he also told People magazine in 2020. "As horrific as that was, I didn't feel disconnected from them."

World.title: Democrats push back across the nation after voters approve girls' sports protections
World.content:
The battle over girls' sports is moving from ballot boxes to courtrooms as the years-long national debate has gotten a new wrinkle this month.

Democrats are turning Election Day victories for the "save women's sports" movement into fresh fights to reject the will of American voters.

Voters in four states approved measures restricting transgender participation in school sports this month, but Democratic leaders in Washington and Colorado are either backing court challenges or considering changes to what voters passed.

JACKSON THOMPSON: WASHINGTON STATE DEMOCRATIC PARTY CALLS GIRLS' SPORTS INITIATIVE UNCONSTITUTIONAL

The results highlight a divide between approval at the ballot box and acceptance among political leaders, even as some officials and athletic administrators commit to following the new laws.

Washington: Democrats back court challenges

Washington’s Initiative 638 passed with roughly 56% support. It prohibits biological males from competing in female school sports and requires students seeking to participate in girls’ athletics to provide healthcare documentation verifying their sex.

The Washington State Democratic Party quickly made clear that it supported continued resistance.

"The fight over I-638 is just beginning," the party said in a Nov. 6 statement.

The party argued the initiative violates the constitution and endorsed organizations planning court challenges.

The ACLU of Washington, Legal Voice and Pacifica Law Group subsequently sued on behalf of the state teachers union, a nonprofit and parents. The lawsuit argues that the measure discriminates against transgender girls and imposes unequal privacy burdens on girls seeking to play school sports.

The challengers seek to prevent the initiative from taking effect Dec. 3.

Seattle’s school board separately authorized legal action over the measure, citing concerns about privacy, equal treatment and conflicts with existing protections. That authorization allows the district to pursue legal action; it does not itself suspend the initiative.

Democratic Attorney General Nick Brown, meanwhile, appointed outside law firm Bryan Cave Leighton Paisner to defend the law on the state’s behalf.

"My personal views do not dictate what laws get defended or the strength of that defense," Brown said.

ADF SEEKS TO DEFEND WASHINGTON GIRLS' SPORTS MEASURE, ARGUES STATE CANNOT FULLY REPRESENT FEMALE ATHLETES

Brown said the arrangement would ensure the initiative receives a defense while allowing his office to continue its other work protecting transgender rights.

Alliance Defending Freedom filed a motion on behalf of Female Athletes United to defend Washington’s voter-approved girls sports initiative against an ACLU-backed lawsuit, arguing that the state cannot adequately represent the athletes’ interests, on Friday.

The Nov. 13 motion asks King County Superior Court to allow Female Athletes United to join the case as a defendant to defend Initiative 638. The request seeks the court’s permission to participate; it is not an order granting intervention.

Colorado: Democratic governor-elect signals changes

In Colorado, voters approved Proposition 134 with approximately 52% support, requiring school and college sports teams to be designated male, female or coeducational and generally tying participation to biological sex.

Democratic Gov.-elect Phil Weiser has already signaled an interest in changing the measure.

"We’re going to have to take a look at these anti-trans measures and what adjustments are necessary and appropriate," Weiser said after the election, according to reporting by The Colorado Sun published by Colorado Public Radio.

Weiser raised concerns about potentially invasive eligibility verification. The measure does not expressly require genital examinations or establish a uniform statewide verification process.

He had not outlined specific changes in the reporting reviewed. Because Proposition 134 changes state law rather than the constitution, lawmakers can amend it without another statewide vote.

Demonstrators in Denver have demanded repeal. Supporters, including Protect Kids Colorado, have accused Weiser of disregarding the electorate’s decision.

Colorado’s athletic administrators have taken a more direct position on compliance.

"Like every member school, CHSAA must comply with the new law," a Colorado High School Activities Association spokesperson told Colorado Public Radio.

Denver Public Schools also said it would support students while following state law. The measure is scheduled to take effect Jan. 1, 2027.

Arizona: Measure passes despite Democratic opposition

Arizona voters approved Proposition 318 with approximately 59% support, expanding an existing law restricting male participation in girls’ sports.

The legislature referred the measure to voters with Republican support and Democratic opposition. Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs had vetoed similar legislation in previous years.

The proposition also restricts access to bathrooms, locker rooms and other private spaces based on sex recorded on an original birth certificate. It removes an existing provision allowing girls to participate on boys’ teams.

A pre-election lawsuit challenged the proposal, but a judge rejected the argument that it violated the single-subject rule and allowed it to remain on the ballot.

Opposition continued after passage. The ACLU of Arizona condemned the result, arguing that the measure further excludes transgender students.

"Lawmakers showed they would rather villainize vulnerable groups than defend our rights when they sent bad policies to the ballot, and unfortunately, some of those measures passed." said Victoria López, executive director for the ACLU of Arizona. "Proposition 317 will do nothing to make border communities safer, and risks labeling U.S. citizens and people seeking asylum as ‘terrorist organizations,’ Proposition 318 broadens an existing ban targeting trans student athletes to further ostracize kids who simply want to participate alongside their peers."

That statement did not announce a new lawsuit against Proposition 318. The absence of an announced post-election Democratic effort to block it should not be confused with an endorsement by Democrats who opposed it.

Nebraska: Voters approve constitutional protections despite opposition

Nebraska’s Initiative 442 received roughly 68% support, placing restrictions on male participation in female school and college sports into the state constitution.

A voter guide published by the Nebraska Democratic Party recommended voting against it.

The proposal also survived a pre-election legal challenge. The Nebraska Supreme Court ruled Oct. 16 that the petition’s statement of purpose satisfied state requirements, rejecting an effort to keep the measure off the ballot.

The ACLU of Nebraska criticized the result after passage and said it would monitor potential harassment and discrimination against students. Its statement did not announce a new lawsuit.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Unlike Colorado’s statutory measure, Nebraska’s constitutional amendment cannot be undone through an ordinary legislative amendment. It reinforces a sports restriction already established in state law.

World.title: Thousands of flights canceled or delayed Saturday after FAA’s nationwide ground stop
World.content:
Thousands of flights were canceled or delayed Saturday morning as airlines struggled to recover from a nationwide ground stop that halted U.S. departures for more than four hours Friday.

By 9:30 a.m. ET Saturday, flight tracking service FlightAware had logged more than 3,700 cancellations and 1,990 delays. Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, Chicago O’Hare International Airport and New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport were among the hubs experiencing the most disruptions, according to FlightAware.

The Federal Aviation Administration lifted the ground stop at 8:15 p.m. ET Friday. More than 7,000 flights were canceled Friday, and airports across the country filled with stranded passengers. Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and American Airlines said Friday evening that they were resuming flights.

A senior government official told NBC News on Saturday that the system that caused the outage had been identified and taken offline. The FAA said a router sent too much data, overloading older air traffic control equipment.

What caused the ground stop

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Friday evening that controllers began seeing inconsistencies in radar data and communications with aircraft at 3:36 p.m. ET. The FAA issued the ground stop at 3:54 p.m. ET, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”

Duffy said the FAA retained some radar and communications capabilities and halted departures as a precaution. Medical flights, including those transporting organs for transplant, were allowed to continue.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday night that authorities had found no evidence of a cyberattack.

“FAA was able to handle it. We did it out of an abundance of caution,” he said in a news conference from the White House Friday night. Earlier on Friday, he described the issue as a telecommunications outage.

Why disruptions continued Saturday

Airlines had to get planes and crews back into position after the ground stop, and some crews may have reached limits on how long they could stay on duty. Duffy said he expected air traffic to recover before the Thanksgiving rush.

But by 6 p.m., Reagan Washington National Airport had run out of room to park aircraft and Chicago O’Hare International Airport was nearing capacity, a source with knowledge told NBC News.

Deveren Werne was on an American Airlines jet that was about to take off from Indianapolis to Chicago when suddenly the pilots announced that all flights were grounded.

“At first, the pilot announced that there was some kind of radio issue,” Werne, 55, of Greenville, South Carolina, told NBC News in a telephone interview. “Then a little while later, the pilot said something like, ‘There is something going on that’s more serious than that.’”

Werne said he began hearing from friends who were also stuck on planes, including one on a runway in Chicago. His plane headed back to the terminal so passengers could get off.

Friday’s ground stop is perhaps the most severe consequence of what Duffy described as a decades-old air traffic control system that uses analog equipment, which has led to several issues and outages over the past few years.

In May 2025, radar screens at Newark Liberty International Airport went black during a 90-second outage.

Duffy said the legacy equipment will continue to fail and pushed Congress to approve $50 billion to overhaul the system. Congress last year approved $12.5 billion over five years to upgrade air traffic control, Reuters reported.

Mullin said although authorities cannot rule out a cyberattack, there was no evidence to suggest there was one. “There’s nothing completely certain right now. It doesn’t appear that way,” he said.

Meanwhile, Air Space Intelligence, the AI tech startup that is a vendor for the FAA on its new SMART system for air traffic control, insisted its software was not responsible for the nationwide ground stop.

“The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said in a statement posted to X.

Duffy said the SMART system is “completely disconnected” from the equipment that suffered issues Friday.

Several hours after the ground stop was announced, a top aviation expert estimated that anywhere from 300,000 to 400,000 passengers were stranded — and it was anybody’s guess when they would get to their destinations.

Chicago O'Hare International Airport, filled with waiting passengers. Jacek Boczarski / Anadolu via Getty

“Daily, we have about 25,000 flights in U.S. domestic markets,” Vikrant Vaze, a Dartmouth professor who specializes in commercial aviation logistics, wrote in an email to NBC News. “I would say we should have around 3,000 to 4,000 flights held up at this time over the past 2 plus hours.”

With planes stranded on runways, the likelihood increased that some of these planes would have to be diverted to other airports, the source said.

Aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti called the outage “extraordinary.”

Guzzetti emphasized that pilots are trained to operate through communications outages and that there are redundancies in place for such instances. Pilots “could get information relayed through other means” to ensure planes are spaced properly for landing.

There are different layers of communications — high-altitude, midlevel and the towers on the ground. The high-altitude control centers are the ones affected by the outage.

Nationwide ground stops are extremely rare

Ground stops across the nation are a rarity in U.S. history.

After the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, the FAA ordered an unprecedented nationwide ground stop. All civilian air traffic across U.S. airspace was halted and airborne planes were ordered to land at the nearest available airports.

In January 2023, the FAA grounded all flights for a few hours, blaming a failure in the Notice to Air Missions system, which alerts pilots to a host of potential dangers.

Officials at the time blamed contract personnel for the outage, saying they accidentally deleted files while working to correct the synchronization between databases. The error prompted a computer outage that lasted approximately an hour and a half, Department of Transportation officials said at the time.

World.title: FAA ground stop throws college football into chaos, while the NFL is safe
World.content:
A Federal Aviation Administration ground stop that lasted more than four hours and canceled over 7,000 flights Friday affected the travel plans for several teams across multiple sports.

Follow along for live coverage.

Multiple games in college football had to be rescheduled to accommodate new travel plans, while a handful of NBA teams changed their flights as a result of the ground stop. Every NFL game, meanwhile, will be played as scheduled, as all road teams were scheduled to travel Saturday.

A few backup referees for the NFL

Every NFL game will stick to its original start time, a league spokesman confirmed to NBC News. Teams playing Sunday typically do not travel until Saturday, meaning the league was largely unaffected by the Friday ground stop.

The New England Patriots and the Detroit Lions, who are playing in Munich, Germany, both traveled overseas well ahead of the stop.

While the league’s teams and players will arrive as scheduled, the NFL did have to modify officiating crews for Sunday’s games.

NFL referee Duane Heydt in Seattle on Oct. 25. Alika Jenner / Getty

“Due to the ongoing nationwide impact to air travel this weekend, the NFL has adjusted its officiating assignments for Week 10 games, reassigning officials to games within driving distance of their hometowns,” a league spokesman said.

Three backup referees — Duane Heydt, Barry Anderson and Don Willard — will be used Sunday. Heydt was assigned to a game in New Orleans and Anderson to one in Tennessee, while Willard will be the side judge for games in both Indianapolis and Cincinnati. (The kickoffs in those two games are more than seven hours apart, and the stadiums are separated by less than 120 miles.)

“Each of the league’s 17 officiating crews have a backup referee identified, and that individual trains throughout the year to work at the referee position should the need arise,” the league spokesman said.

Many college football games have been pushed back

Travel plans for more than a dozen teams were affected by the stoppage, according to The Athletic.

Some schools opted to fly out on Saturday morning for games scheduled the same day, while others — including the Alabama Crimson Tide playing at Vanderbilt — took a bus to their destination.

Several kickoffs were pushed back to later Saturday to accommodate new travel plans, including the games between Baylor and BYU, Arizona State and UCF, and Utah and Arizona.

The game between Oklahoma and Ole Miss, however, was pushed back to Sunday after Ole Miss couldn’t figure out its travel in time — and it drew a strong response from the Sooners.

“We were told that Ole Miss explored every avenue to travel to Norman and play on Saturday as planned. But, unlike every other team traveling for competition tomorrow, they were unable to find a solution,” Oklahoma Athletic Director Roger Denny said in a statement. “After multiple conversations with the league office, [SEC] Commissioner [Greg] Sankey informed us of his decision to move our game to Sunday, over our strong objection. After continued discussions, he further informed us that our failure to play on Sunday at the directed time would result in a forfeit.”

Denny’s statement added: “Rescheduling the game has a significant impact, particularly on our fans. Those who have made travel arrangements, accommodations, and personal plans around a Saturday game now face unnecessary disruption and hardship. Their time, commitment and investment deserve greater consideration than they were afforded in the conference’s decision tonight.”

No major issues for the NBA and NHL

A few NBA teams — such as the Cleveland Cavaliers and the Chicago Bulls — had to reschedule flights from Friday night to Saturday morning, but otherwise it’s largely business as usual for the league.

An NBA source confirmed to NBC News all games would take place as scheduled as of Saturday morning, though noted there were a lot of moving parts.

“Flights are late, get stuck on the runway, just like it does in the normal commercial world of flight, so it’s just part of it,” Cavaliers coach Kenny Atkinson said before the team’s game Friday. “We’ve all been part of it. You just adapt.”

Atkinson’s star guard Donovan Mitchell was not enthused about the new plan, as Cleveland has a quick turnaround to another game Saturday.

“This is unprecedented,” Mitchell said Friday, per Cleveland.com’s Chris Fedor. “Back-to-back. Three-hour flight. It was already going to be a tough one. But if they say we have to play then we have to play.”

Mitchell added he would have liked for the game to be canceled.

The NHL, meanwhile, has not announced any changes to its schedule. The league had only two games on Friday night, allowing most teams to travel for their road games prior to the stoppage, according to The Athletic.

World.title: Democrat Mary Peltola is likely to win Alaska’s Senate race, as vote counting continues
World.content:
Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola is likely to win Alaska’s Senate race, according to an NBC News Decision Desk analysis, as vote-counting continues in the state.

Peltola has expanded her narrow lead over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan with each new batch of votes reported this week. A “likely” characterization indicates that the NBC News Decision Desk has at least 95% confidence that Peltola will win the race.

See live results here.

Alaska’s is the only remaining 2026 Senate race in which the NBC News Decision Desk has not yet made a projection.

If Peltola wins, Democrats will have a 56-44 majority in the Senate next year.

The race remains uncalled a week after polls close as votes continue to be counted. Alaskans vote heavily by mail and ballots postmarked by Election Day are counted as long as they arrived by Nov. 13 — and a few days later than that for valid overseas voters.

In a race with such a narrow margin, these final votes are important, especially given Alaska’s ranked-choice rules.

If no candidate wins a majority of the vote on the first ballot, the lowest-placed candidate is eliminated and second-choice votes from that candidate’s supporters are counted. The process then repeats until someone gets a majority.
