World.title: The death of the night out? How Mexico City’s youth are socializing
World.content:
What if the problem isn’t that young people have stopped going out, but that we’ve been getting the night out wrong all along?

For decades, the formula seemed pretty straightforward: Friday night meant getting dressed up, meeting friends, drinking too much, dancing until the early hours and spending Saturday recovering. Going out was practically a weekend obligation.

But for a growing number of young people, getting wasted is losing its appeal. And the traditional clubbing experience is no longer the default way to socialize.

Instead, think dinner with friends, a long walk, a fitness class, a coffee that turns into a three-hour conversation, or a night at someone’s apartment. Alcohol hasn’t disappeared, and neither has the desire to have fun. But the priorities seem to be shifting.

So, is the night out dying? Or are we simply learning to have a good time differently? In Mexico City, where nightlife has long been part of the city’s appeal, I wanted to find out.

Is Gen Z drinking less?

There is evidence that young people are drinking less in several countries, although the trend isn’t universal. According to the European School Survey Project on Alcohol and Other Drugs, the proportion of European students who reported drinking alcohol in the previous month fell from 55% in 1995 to 43% in 2024. The figures concern school students across participating European countries, not all young adults worldwide.

Mexico offers another interesting example. The country’s 2025 National Survey on Drug, Alcohol and Tobacco Consumption (ENCODAT) found that the percentage of adolescents aged 12 to 17 who had consumed alcohol in the previous month fell from 16.1% in 2016 to 7.5% in 2025. That’s a substantial decline among teenagers, although it doesn’t tell us exactly how much Mexico City’s 20-somethings are drinking.

So, what’s behind the change?

Health consciousness is an obvious place to start. Fitness has become part of everyday life for many young adults, from Pilates and running clubs to strength training and early morning workouts. When your Saturday plans involve a long run rather than nursing a hangover, Friday night suddenly looks different.

There’s also a growing awareness of alcohol’s health risks. We know more about its relationship with sleep, physical performance and long-term health, including cancer. And when social media is full of people sharing their workouts, wellness routines and carefully curated lives, waking up feeling terrible can seem like a particularly bad trade-off.

But there’s a contradiction: The same social media that encourages us to go to bed early also makes us feel as though we should be doing something worth posting about. The perfect workout, the perfect job, the perfect group of friends and the perfect weekend have become another set of expectations to keep up with.

I still tell my friends to send me pictures when they travel. Increasingly, though, they would tell me they can’t wait to see my stories when it’s my turn to go somewhere. Sometimes it feels as if an experience isn’t quite complete until you’ve posted about it.

Could the pandemic have played a part, too? Young people who spent months isolated during formative years may have developed different social habits. But it would be too easy to blame COVID for an entire generation’s changing relationship with nightlife. Technology, money, work, wellness culture and shifting social norms may all be part of the picture.

And there’s another question worth asking: If drinking less is becoming more acceptable, does that mean we’re becoming less social, or simply less dependent on alcohol to socialize?

Everything in moderation

I’ve been doing Dry January for four years. Back in 2022, only one of my friends had even heard of it. She was the one who introduced me to the idea.

At the time, not drinking seemed strange unless you were taking antibiotics. How could you possibly go out and not drink? Every January, I’d find myself explaining why I was doing it and why taking a break from alcohol appealed to me. Most people weren’t particularly interested. They only wanted me to have a glass in my hand.

This year was different. By the end of January, I realized I didn’t really feel like drinking. I didn’t miss it at all, and when the month ended, I didn’t see a reason to start again.

I’d already been going out less, drinking fewer cocktails and mostly having wine when I went to restaurants. My first alcoholic drink of the year eventually came in May, at a friend’s wedding. I had a few cocktails, enjoyed myself and moved on.

What surprised me most wasn’t how easy it was to say no to alcohol. It was how much I enjoyed the mornings afterwards. Waking up after a fun evening with no hangover, enough energy to exercise, go for a walk or visit a museum felt like getting an extra day back.

Mexico City has also made it easier to experiment. There are bars and restaurants where alcohol-free drinks feel like a genuine part of the menu rather than an afterthought. A good mocktail can be just as enjoyable as a cocktail, without the alcohol.

Still, I don’t think everyone needs to give up drinking. If I go to Italy with my best friends, I’ll be more than happy to have a Spritz. At Christmas, I’ll gladly share a bottle of wine with my family.

For me, the shift has been about choice rather than restriction. I don’t want to drink just because everyone else is drinking, or because I’ve convinced myself that a night out requires alcohol. And I don’t think there’s anything wrong with someone who feels differently.

Perhaps that’s the real change: Not that drinking has become unacceptable, but that not drinking is becoming less of a big deal.

What do young people actually want from a night out?

To understand what’s happening in Mexico City, I asked young people about their habits, what they do instead of going out, and what would make them want to go out more often.

In my survey, 55% said they go out less frequently than they did three years ago. Respondents also described drinking less when they do go out. Their explanations were revealing.

Several said their friends simply weren’t interested in going clubbing as often. Instead, they preferred daytime plans, relaxed dinners or meeting at someone’s home. These gatherings felt more intimate and made it easier to catch up, have proper conversations and spend time together without feeling rushed.

Sports and wellness came up, too. For young adults juggling work, studies and other responsibilities, a weekend workout or an early start the next morning can take priority over a late night.

What stood out in my conversations was that the issue wasn’t always a lack of desire to socialize. It was a lack of enthusiasm for the available ways of doing it.

In my survey, respondents talked about wanting clubs closer to home, shorter queues and friends who were more willing to go out. Some described asking their friends to make plans and feeling as though they were begging.

That last detail stayed with me. Imagine wanting to go dancing, getting a group together and feeling as though you’re asking everyone for a favor.

But we should be careful not to confuse a preference for smaller gatherings with a rejection of nightlife altogether. People can want fewer nights out without wanting nightlife to disappear. They may simply be more selective about when they go, who they go with and what makes the evening worthwhile.

In fact, 65% of respondents in my survey said they still went to bars, clubs or parties at least once a week. That complicates the idea of a dying night out. Going out less often doesn’t necessarily mean giving it up.

Are bars noticing the shift?

If young people are changing their habits, what does that mean for the places where they spend their evenings?

I spoke to young people about what they drink and to bar and club owners in La Roma about what they have noticed since the pandemic.

In my survey, respondents described drinking less hard liquor and fewer cocktails, such as gin and tonics or rum and Coke. Beer and wine remained popular, while some said they alternated alcoholic drinks with water or delayed their first drink until later in the evening.

Others admitted that they didn’t particularly enjoy the taste of alcohol. For them, drinking was more about loosening up, feeling more sociable and having fun with friends.

Alcohol-free options therefore have an obvious appeal. But mocktails aren’t a complete replacement for the drinking experience: Some respondents said they found it boring to spend an entire evening drinking sodas or alcohol-free cocktails, particularly when everyone else was drinking.

The message isn’t necessarily that young people want bars without alcohol. They want more choice, a good atmosphere and a reason to stay.

The owner of a bar in La Roma that also serves food offered another perspective on the experience of running a venue where people can eat, drink and socialize. His observations, alongside those of a local club owner, suggest that the relationship between nightlife and the pandemic deserves a closer look.

The club owner described a shift after COVID, with fewer young people going out, while holidays and days off could still bring busy nights, including crowds of international visitors.

These are individual observations, not proof of a citywide decline. But they raise an interesting question for Mexico City’s nightlife industry: If people still want to meet friends, what kind of venues and experiences will persuade them to leave home?

The answer might not be another club with louder music and more expensive cocktails. It could be a place where the music is good but conversation is still possible, where food is as important as the drinks, or where people can spend an entire evening without feeling pressured to keep ordering alcohol.

What does the perfect night out look like now?

For many of the young people I spoke to, the ideal evening sounded surprisingly simple: dinner and drinks with friends, either at a restaurant or at someone’s home. Good food, music they actually like, an intimate atmosphere and, crucially, music that isn’t so loud they have to shout to hear one another.

They still enjoy dancing, meeting new people and discovering new places. But they also want to talk, catch up and feel comfortable.

Perhaps the problem with the traditional night out is that it sometimes asks us to choose between the things we want from socializing. We want music, but we also want conversation. We want to meet new people, but we also want to feel safe. We want spontaneity, but we don’t necessarily want to spend hours queuing or traveling across the city.

And Mexico City has no shortage of alternatives.

The night isn’t dead; it’s simply being redefined.

What if the best place to read were also the last place you’d expect to find a book?

From Tokyo to Amsterdam, book raves have been bringing reading into clubs and cultural venues, turning it into a collective experience. The idea is simple: a book, some music and the pleasure of being together, without the pressure to talk. Less noise, more pages. Silence, too, can bring people together.

Mexico City has its own version of this quieter pleasure. The city’s audioramas, including those in Parque México and Chapultepec, offer spaces where people can sit among the trees and listen to music. I discovered them recently and was fascinated by the idea of spending an afternoon there reading or even learning Italian, as I did on my last visit. Just watch out for the person beside you who might have decided to take a nap and start snoring…

Then there are running clubs, which have turned exercise into a social activity in its own right. From themed runs and coffee meet-ups to longer races that bring strangers together, the possibilities go well beyond a night at the club.

These activities aren’t necessarily replacements for nightlife. They’re reminders that socializing doesn’t have to revolve around alcohol, a late bedtime or a particular kind of venue.

Think about your own life for a moment. When you meet your friends, does it always involve drinking? Could it be a museum, a fitness class, a walk through Chapultepec, dinner somewhere new or a Sunday morning spent running and getting coffee afterwards?

None of these plans is inherently better than going dancing until sunrise. And there’s no reason we can’t enjoy both.

Maybe the death of the night out is really the death of the idea that there’s only one way to have a good time.

Young people still want connection, excitement, music, romance and stories to tell the next morning. They just seem increasingly willing to decide for themselves what those things look like.

So, no, I don’t think the night out is dead.

But perhaps the best night out is no longer the one you barely remember. It’s the one that leaves you with a good story, people you feel closer to and a Saturday morning you’re actually excited about.

And you? What’s your perfect night out?

Marta Delgado is a Spanish writer and marketing professional from Galicia, Spain, currently based in Mexico City. She writes about culture, lifestyle, and what it means to build a life abroad, drawing from her own time living in different countries.

World.title: I grew up watching Mexican stereotypes. Hollywood hasn’t changed much
World.content:
William Nericcio, like most of the roughly 500 million residents living in Mexico, the United States and Canada, grew up watching popular television shows and consuming major media outlets.

As a Chicano raised in Laredo, Texas — one of the most densely populated Latino cities in the U.S. — Nericcio regularly saw himself and his community reflected in popular media. Often, however, those portrayals weren’t very accurate or authentic, instead relying on repetitive tropes and one-dimensional stereotypes that Hollywood has been recycling for generations.

#NewProfilePic https://t.co/lbCa4WKiVl — William Nericcio (@eyegiene) July 6, 2026

Nowadays, as a professor of English and comparative literature at San Diego State University and co-author of “Talking #browntv: Latinas and Latinos on the Screen,” Nericcio’s work largely focuses on the historical depictions and evolving complexities of his community on the screen.

Predictable stereotypes

“There are particularly demented representations of your average Mexican (as being) violent, dirty, lazy,” Nericcio tells Mexico News Daily. “If they’re a woman, they like good sex. They’re gonna take things from you. They’re a spitfire. Temptresses (who) carry daggers. That’s the signifier of our violent deviance as Mexicans.”

While Nericcio admits that he likes shows such as “Breaking Bad” and “Narcos” — two popular series featuring prominent Latino characters — he says that representations of Latin Americans have largely remained stagnant and predictable.

“I watched ‘Better Call Saul’ (the ‘Breaking Bad’ spinoff) and after that, even I would cross the street (after seeing a Mexican person in public),” he jokes. “They don’t just kill. They kill with the artistic vision of Salvador Dalí. It’s killing cubed, masterful.”

Century-old tropes still being used

Of course, those kinds of derogatory character oversimplifications have existed for more than a century, going back to 1894, when the short film “Mexican Knife Duel” premiered, marking one of the earliest known forms of Mexican protagonists in U.S. media.

Quoting the scholar Gary D. Keller, the Library of Congress notes that “These films villainized Mexican men and sexualized Mexican women, a pattern that would recur all throughout the 20th century.”

My childhood through Hollywood’s Mexican lens

As a California-raised Mexican American myself, who came of age in the 1990s and 2000s, I can relate. For decades, Mexican characters have too often been minimized in U.S. media, flattened into binary archetypes. Think Speedy Gonzales, who’s portrayed as charming, quick-witted and brave, or his familial counterpart, Slowpoke Rodriguez, slow but cunning and dangerous.

Some of my earliest memories of action flicks are films like “Desperado” with Antonio Banderas and Salma Hayek. In it, Banderas plays El Mariachi, a stone-cold assassin who packs firearms in his guitar case. Hayek’s Carolina, meanwhile, causes car accidents when crossing the street because of gawking men.

Like Nericcio, however, I’ll admit that “Desperado” was one of my favorite movies growing up.

I can also recall films like “The Sandlot,” which featured the character Benny “The Jet” Rodriguez, a baseball-loving kid who, in retrospect, is arguably one of the most fleshed-out Chicano characters ever portrayed. Rather than focusing on his cultural differences or moral deficiencies, Benny is just a regular kid who dreams of making the big leagues. It felt relatable to me back then, and in many ways still does. Benny’s heritage is neither a strength nor a weakness, and besides the name on the back of his jersey, his latinidad was never a factor.

A.C. Slater, played by Mario Lopez in the popular TV series “Saved by the Bell,” was similarly down-to-earth in the ’90s.

Profit over authentic representation

But those examples of wholesome, fully dimensional Chicano and Chicana figures were hard to come by, in my memory.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Paul Shipper 🎨 (@paulshipper)

“It’s called show business, not show ethnography,” Nericcio says. “It demands a profit. What gets a profit? What has worked before. Hollywood is about rebroadcasting images that are tried and true: the criminality of the Mexican.”

Nericcio goes on to say, “It’s how Trump blasted his way into office. He hoodwinked Latinos by saying he’s good for the economy (and fueling media stereotypes about the threat of Mexican immigrants). Folks fall for this.”

In that sense, what’s shown on the screen has real-world consequences and larger implications. It’s not simply about wanting to see more diverse representations of Chicanos and Chicanas in popular media; it’s about how, by not diversifying characters, beliefs can be formed and popularized to negative ends.

Amongst this deluge of negative portrayals, there have been several authentic representations that, unlike A.C. Slater or Benny Rodriguez, also reflect on the lived experiences of Latin populations.

Nericcio points to two of his favorite examples: 2006’s “Children of Men” and 2008’s “Sleep Dealer.”

Both films are set against a dystopian backdrop, allowing social commentary about immigration, exploitation and labor to be at the core of the films’ messaging.

Perhaps more importantly, though, each film was directed by Latinos, with Alfonso Cuarón helming “Children of Men” and Alex Rivera crafting “Sleep Dealer.”

View this post on Instagram A post shared by CALÓ News Arizona (@calonewsaz)

“It’s sci-fi about the future,” Nericcio says of “Sleep Dealer.” “It follows a cyber-bracero who plugs into the matrix and sells his labor by staying in Mexico. The film broadcasts corporate America’s biggest wet dream. Labor without the Mexicans. We don’t want their bodies; we want their food and their labor … we don’t want to hear them speaking. The film is a brilliant portrayal of Mexican subjectivity on the border in its complexity.”

The push for change in writers’ rooms

Those films, though, don’t often generate as much box office success. “Children of Men” was considered a commercial disappointment and was unable to recover its production budget during its theater run. This, despite receiving fairly critical acclaim and a cult following, including three Academy Award nominations, while being retroactively lauded as one of the best thrillers of its time.

“Latino filmmakers are making stories that feature Latino and Mexican actors, but with storylines that aren’t ripped from the tabloid headlines,” Nericcio says. “But most people don’t watch. The progress that will come, if it will come, will come from numbers. Are more Chicanos in film school? Are more of them breaking into creative spaces? The key is the writers’ rooms.”

In that case, the present and future look as grim as the past.

Under-representation in the film industry

In 2021, the Los Angeles Times reported that “Latino representation among film writers is even worse than Latino representation on screen: Since 2008, Latinos have never constituted more than 5% of employed Writers Guild of America (WGA) film writers, according to the available data.”

Earlier this year, the University of California, Los Angeles shared statistics from the LA Times’ De Los, which found that “in 2024, only 1% of leading roles went to Latinos; less than 5% of directors were Latino; and approximately 2% of writers were Latino. Latinos make up nearly 20% of the U.S. population.”

Same old Hollywood

In 2015, Nericcio attempted to do his part by developing his own show, “Mextasy,” that sought to “rewrite televised borders, rethink televisual borders or fronteras, revealing the pulsing, growing body of Latin America alive and thriving within and outside of Uncle Sam’s unknowing body to celebrate the Latino experience throughout the world.”

The show never took off. But the concept — and the intent — remains as urgent today as it did more than 10 years ago, when Nericcio pitched his idea to networks.

“I’m a Chicano from Laredo, Texas, who thinks I’m Anthony Bourdain,” Nericcio jokes. “But it didn’t get picked up. Hollywood will crush your soul.”

As ever, it’s up to consumers to dictate, through our wallets and watching power, what we do or don’t want to see.

It’s something I think about whenever I have the urge to watch the latest hit show or visit a theater (rare for me as the dad of a toddler, but still). Putting our money behind genuine creatives in the communities we’re from is one of the only ways we have to shift the tides.

Until then, Hollywood will continue Hollywood-ing when it comes to its interpretations of Mexican and Mexican Americans.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: What exactly is the ‘real’ Mexico? A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
Last week we published an article written by Sarah Devries asking the question: “Is the beach the real Mexico?” It resonated with me for a number of reasons.

To begin with, I think Mexico has some of the best beaches in the world and have frequented many of them now for over 30 years. I even convinced my wife to get married on one of them (near Playa del Carmen) many moons ago in a wild Indian/Mexican/American cultural mashup. It was a wonderful experience to see our guests, who were from all over the world, falling in love with the beaches in the same way we had years earlier. I have always told people that when you take into account the sheer beauty, variety and atmosphere of Mexico’s beaches, no other country can come close to competing.

Where else can one find the raw beauty of the beaches of Baja — from Playa Balandra to Todos Santos to those of the Bahía Concepción near Mulegé? The party atmosphere of beaches in Acapulco, Puerto Vallarta, Mazatlán and Manzanillo? The crystal clear waters of beaches in Cancún, Playa del Carmen and Tulum? The incredible nature of the beaches in Oaxaca? And all in one country!

So it resonated with me when Sarah took a bit of offence to her friends and family questioning if the beach was, in fact, “the real Mexico.” I have been told by many foreigners that it is not, despite nearly 10% of the Mexican population living on or near the nearly 7,000 miles of coastline in the country. Going back as far as our wedding, people remarked that they had the time of their lives, but that Playa del Carmen and Tulum aren’t “the real Mexico.” I have heard people raving about their vacations to places as diverse as Cancún, Acapulco, Puerto Vallarta and Los Cabos — only to feel the need to confirm to me that those places, in their opinion, aren’t the “real Mexico.”

I have found myself in a similar situation far from the beach, in my adopted hometown of San Miguel de Allende. Well over a hundred friends and family members have come to visit us over the past few years, and without exception, they have a great time. At some point of their visit, however, a comment is always made that, “You guys aren’t really living in the ‘real Mexico.'” They have told me that I live in a “Mexican Disneyland” or a “Mexican Epcot Center.” It frustrates me, as I am pretty sure that the 200,000 Mexicans living here consider themselves “real Mexicans” who really live in Mexico. It seems like most foreigners seem to consider the places in Mexico that they visit to be somehow less “real.” How weird.

The whole “real Mexico” concept really hit home with me again in just the past few weeks. Two weeks ago, my wife, some friends, and I did the Camino Copalita hike in the mountains of rural Oaxaca. (I will be writing more about this incredible experience soon — stay tuned!)

For five days and nights, we lived off the grid. No electricity, no internet or cell phone signal, no running water (except rivers), sleeping outside, eating what was grown or raised within a few hundred meters of where we slept, and just being in the awesomeness of nearly undisturbed nature along with the few hundred residents that make up the towns along the trail.

Then, immediately after the hike, we spent a week in Mexico City, mostly in the Polanco neighborhood, where my wife was having an art exhibit. Polanco is just about as far from rural Oaxaca as you can get: fancy hotels, international cuisine, high-end boutiques, and both residents and tourists from around the world. As you might imagine, such a quick change in environment was intense — quite jarring actually.

But it brings me back to the “real Mexico” question. Was our time in the rural Oaxacan mountains the “real Mexico”? Was our time in posh Polanco the “real Mexico”? Was neither? Were both? Before answering, think about how you would answer the question in your home country. In the United States, for example, what is “the real U.S.”? I would contend that there is no such thing, that it’s an impossible question, as each state and even each city has such tremendous diversity in its nature, food, people, culture and architecture.

So my answer to the “real Mexico” question is that ALL of it is the real Mexico. The beaches, the colonial mountain towns, the rural south and the big cities. We foreigners need to stop thinking about the country in terms of what is “real” and what is “not real”. The country has an incredible diversity and each place, in its own way, ultimately makes up the fabric of the “real Mexico.” I am thrilled to see an increasing number of travelers venture out from a few tourist areas and start to see for themselves firsthand what the “real Mexico” really means. I am certain that they will find it to be incredibly rewarding.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: Ready to host another World Cup? Mexico-US-Costa Rica-Jamaica joint bid for 2031 women’s tournament likely
World.content:
Mexico appears set to host another World Cup in less than five years after FIFA green lighted a joint hosting bid of which the Mexican Soccer Federation is a part.

FIFA, soccer’s international governing body, announced on Wednesday that the bid to host the 2031 Women’s World Cup submitted jointly by Mexico, the United States, Jamaica and Costa Rica “has a strong foundation” and will be voted on at the Extraordinary FIFA Congress on Nov. 23.

If approved (as the lone bid, it is expected to pass with little difficulty), it would mark the second FWWC to be hosted jointly after Australia and New Zealand co-hosted the 2023 tournament.

The Congress will also be considering the joint bid to host the 2035 FIFA Women’s World Cup (FWWC) submitted by England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

Next year’s FWWC is to be hosted by Brazil and will feature 32 teams and 64 matches. The 2031 tournament will be expanded to include 48 teams and 104 games.

The joint 2031 bid proposes 20 host stadiums across the four countries, with 14 in the United States, four in Mexico and one each in Jamaica and Costa Rica. Mexico’s proposed host cities are Mexico City (Estadio Azteca), Guadalajara (Estadio Akron), Monterrey (Estadio BBVA-Bancomer) and Torreón, Coahuila (Estadio Corona).

Following a thorough assessment of the proposal, including inspection visits to the prospective host countries, FIFA published an evaluation report indicating that the bid exceeded its minimum requirements.

“While certain commitments require further engagement, there is a sound basis for confidence that continued dialogue and collaboration with the relevant government agencies should support the successful organization and delivery of the tournament,” FIFA said.

In endorsing the bid, FIFA acknowledged the success of this year’s men’s World Cup which Mexico and the U.S. co-hosted alongside Canada.

FIFA also praised Mexico’s “longstanding record as a FIFA host, having staged the FIFA World Cup in 1970 and 1986, the FIFA Confederations Cup in 1999 and multiple youth competitions, including the FIFA U-20 World Cup 1983 and FIFA U-17 World Cup 2011.”

The technical evaluation focused on “defined priority areas, including the event vision, infrastructure, services and commercial considerations” as well as FIFA Fan Festival sites, while the risk assessment considered “safety and security, sustainability, human rights and environmental protection.”

As co-host, Mexico’s women’s team would be participating in its fourth FWWC after qualifying for the 1999, 2011 and 2015 tournaments. The El Tri Femenil also participated in the unofficial 1971 Women’s World Cup hosted by Mexico. The first FWWC was held in 1991.

With reports from Reuters, Fox Sports, FIFA and ESPN

World.title: New faces and old favorites: Mexico’s 2026 Latin Grammy wins
World.content:
Mexican and Mexican American artists won in at least 10 categories at the Latin Grammys in Las Vegas on Thursday — from 22-year-old Xavi collecting his first two trophies to hitmaker Edgar Barrera becoming the awards’ most decorated winner ever.

Nominated in six categories, Silvana Estrada won one award with her song “Dime,” while Texan Bobby Pulido followed his election to Congress last week with his third Latin Grammy — then announced his retirement from music.

The 27th annual ceremony at Las Vegas’ MGM Grand Garden Arena also featured a first win for Guadalajara-born mariachi singer Camila Fernández and a big centennial tribute to the late Mexican singer-songwriter and ranchera legend José Alfredo Jiménez.

Barrera, born in McAllen, Texas, to a Mexican family, converted a leading 10 nominations into two awards: producer of the year and best regional song for “No Capea.” The two wins brought his career total to 31, breaking the all-time Latin Grammy record he had shared with Puerto Rican rapper Residente.

Xavi, Grupo Frontera – No Capea (Official Video)

Watch this video on YouTube

Barrera, 36, shared the songwriting award with five co-writers, including Xavi and Grupo Frontera singer Adelaido “Payo” Solís III. The prize recognizes the writers, not every member of the performing group.

Xavi won both his nominations, also taking best contemporary Mexican music album for “Dosis.” Born Joshua Xavier Gutiérrez Alonso in Arizona, Xavi was raised largely by his grandparents in Nogales, Sonora, before moving to Phoenix at age 15 with his father.

Grupo Frontera, a Mexican-American band that formed in Texas in 2022, won best norteño album for “Lo Que Me Falta Por Llorar.”

Fernández won best ranchero/mariachi album for “La Fernández.” The 28-year-old is the daughter of ranchero star Alejandro Fernández and the granddaughter of the late Vicente Fernández, one of Mexico’s most famous entertainers of all time.

Edén Muñoz, 36, the former Calibre 50 frontman from Los Mochis, Sinaloa, won best banda album for “Piedras a la Luna.” He was also nominated for best regional song as the writer of “Osadía,” his duet with Cristian Castro.

Estrada, 29, recently named the Los Angeles Philharmonic’s first creative chair for Latin music, received six nominations, including album of the year for “Vendrán Suaves Lluvias” and record and song of the year for “Dime.”

Silvana Estrada — Dime (Video Oficial)

Watch this video on YouTube

The ballad about heartbreak and the liberating power of anger didn’t win in those two categories, but it did garner best singer-songwriter song. The native of Coatepec, Veracruz, now has two Latin Grammys, following her best new artist award in 2022.

Alejandra, Daniela and Paulina Villarreal — three sisters from Monterrey, Nuevo León, who make up the hard-rock trio The Warning — shared best rock song honors for “Ego” with three co-writers.

Mexico City singer Marco Barrientos shared best Spanish-language Christian album for “Eterno” with two others.

Pulido, who has Mexican heritage, won his third Latin Grammy, taking best Tejano album for “Bobby Pulido & Friends: Una Tuya y Una Mía (Vol.2/En Vivo).”

“I want to tell you that I’m retiring from music, and I’m leaving with so much gratitude,” Pulido said in Spanish while accepting the award. He missed the traditional group photo for incoming House members while traveling to Las Vegas, according to The Hill.

Afterward, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries congratulated his fellow Democrat in a social media post: “Felicidades and what a month for Congressman-Elect Pulido.”

¡Felicidades! @bobbypulido425 Mejor Álbum de Música Tejana 🎶👏👏👏 #LatinGRAMMY https://t.co/e39HDhTISH — The Latin Recording Academy / Latin GRAMMYs (@LatinGRAMMYs) November 12, 2026

Chilean Mexican singer Mon Laferte, who has a house in Tepoztlán, Morelos, performed “Femme Fatale” — a week after a concertgoer threw a cellphone that struck her in the face — but went winless in six categories.

Carín León lost both his nominations, for record and album of the year.

Arath Herce from the city of Veracruz went winless in four categories: best new artist, singer-songwriter album, singer-songwriter song and pop/rock song.

Spanish singer Rosalía won five awards, including album of the year for “LUX (Complete Works)” and song of the year for “La Perla.” Argentine singer Milo J took four, including record of the year for “Niño.”

Colombian singer Aria Vega won best new artist, besting a field that included Mexicans Herce, former street sweeper Macario Martínez and Sofía Monroy.

In all, Mexican and Mexican American artists won across all six regional Mexican categories, an umbrella grouping for styles including mariachi, banda and norteño. For the full list of winners, see Billboard.

With reports from Billboard, Uno TV, Infobae and Hola!

World.title: Colombia Arrests Two Over Police Bomb Attack
World.content:
Colombian authorities announced on Saturday 14 November 2026 that police had arrested two suspected members of a rebel splinter group, two weeks after a motorcycle bomb killed two police officers in the southern town of Algeciras. The attack, on the night of Saturday 31 October, struck a busy nightlife area as the town celebrated Halloween.

For US readers, the case shows that armed groups left over from Colombia’s old FARC guerrilla army can still hit towns far from the capital. That matters for anyone travelling in the countryside, working in security or tracking Washington’s anti-drug partnership with Bogotá.

Key Facts •Attack. A motorcycle bomb hit police in Algeciras, a town in Huila department, on 31 October; two officers died. •Arrests. Police announced on 14 November that they detained two suspects, presumed members of the Frente Iván Díaz, a dissident faction of the former FARC rebels. •Group. The Frente Iván Díaz is a dissident faction of the former FARC guerrillas. •Presidency. President Abelardo De la Espriella confirmed the captures on 14 November. •Legal status. Both are suspects; responsibility must be established in court. •Power Index. Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index, with 51.1 points (November 2026 edition).

What We Know

The bomb exploded late on the night of Saturday 31 October in the centre of Algeciras, a town of the department of Huila in southern Colombia. Two patrol officers of the National Police died: Julián Esmith Castaño López at the scene, and Jaime Andrés García Moreno later of his injuries in a hospital in Neiva, the regional capital.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Algeciras (Colombia) Email address Follow

On Saturday 14 November the national police director, General Alejandro Barrera, gave details of the operation that led to the arrests. Police intelligence, criminal investigators and the GAULA, the police anti-kidnapping and extortion unit, took part in it.

Police say the first suspect, known by the alias Araña or Gato Negro, was an explosives expert and an attack coordinator in Huila. They say he helped prepare the motorcycle used in the attack.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Colombia ranks 6th of 14 with 51.1 points. Strongest pillar: military means (91); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (28). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB-); 26 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.8 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The second suspect, alias Mary, is accused of watching police routines and passing the details on to the group. Both are presumed members of the Frente Iván Díaz, and police have not said they confessed.

Investigators seized three firearms, 114 cartridges of different calibres, 34 pamphlets of the Frente Iván Díaz and a stolen motorcycle. President Abelardo De la Espriella publicly confirmed the captures the same day.

Why a Small Town Attack Reaches Far

The Frente Iván Díaz is a dissident faction of the former FARC, the guerrilla army that signed a peace deal with the state in 2016. Groups that rejected that deal kept their weapons and still run extortion, drug routes and attacks on police in parts of Huila, Cauca and nearby departments.

A bomb in a busy street is aimed at the police but hits residents first. That is why officials treat such cases as terrorism, and why the arrests of the planners and lookouts matter more than the capture of foot soldiers.

For US readers, the link is practical. Colombia remains a main partner of Washington in the fight against cocaine trafficking, and insecurity in rural departments feeds the criminal economy behind that trade.

What Is Not Known

Police have not said whether the two suspects will face charges beyond the attack. They have also not published a court date, so it is not yet known what the Fiscalía, the state prosecutor’s office, will argue.

It is also unknown whether the seized weapons and pamphlets are tied to this bomb or to other actions in southern Huila. Investigators say that link still has to be established.

What It Means for You

Travellers should note that the attack hit a town centre on a festive night, not a remote area. Check your government’s travel advice for Huila before visiting, and expect more police checks in the south of the department.

Investors in Colombian assets should treat this as a local security story for now. Nothing so far shows an effect on markets or on the pace of the government’s talks with armed groups.

Frequently Asked Questions

When did the Algeciras attack happen?

A motorcycle bomb exploded late on Saturday 31 October 2026 in the centre of Algeciras, Huila. Two police officers died, one at the scene and one later in hospital.

Who was arrested?

Police detained two suspects, known by the aliases Araña and Mary, on 14 November 2026. They are presumed members of the Frente Iván Díaz and remain suspects until a court rules.

What is the Frente Iván Díaz?

It is a dissident faction of the former FARC guerrillas, which rejected the 2016 peace deal. Police link it to the Algeciras attack.

Is it safe to travel in Huila?

Huila is a popular tourist department, but this attack hit a town centre. Check your government’s travel advice and follow local police guidance before going.

Sources: Policía Nacional de Colombia, statement of 14 November 2026 by Director General Alejandro Barrera; Presidencia de la República, announcement of 14 November 2026.

World.content:

Key Facts Who Esther Dweck, Brazil’s minister of public-service management, defended Tarciana Medeiros, chief executive of Banco do Brasil.

Esther Dweck, Brazil’s minister of public-service management, defended Tarciana Medeiros, chief executive of Banco do Brasil. What Dweck said doubts about Medeiros’s competence should not be raised “just because we are women”.

Dweck said doubts about Medeiros’s competence should not be raised “just because we are women”. Why it matters The state-controlled bank’s third-quarter profit fell 66.5%, and its shares dropped 8.35% in one day.

The state-controlled bank’s third-quarter profit fell 66.5%, and its shares dropped 8.35% in one day. As of Saturday 14 November 2026

On Saturday 14 November 2026, Esther Dweck, Brazil’s Minister of Management and Innovation in Public Services, defended Tarciana Medeiros, chief executive of state-controlled Banco do Brasil, in a post on the social network X. The bank had reported a sharp third-quarter profit fall on Wednesday 11 November.

What Dweck Said

Dweck wrote: “Our competence cannot be put in doubt in a reckless and disproportionate way just because we are women.” She added that debate about results is legitimate but “cannot serve to normalise personal attacks on women in leadership positions”, in her post of 14 November.

World.title: Ghana Ruling Party Ousts Its Accra Chairman
World.content:
Politics: Ghana

Key Facts —Result. Benjamin Danso unseated incumbent Ashie Moore as Greater Accra chairman of Ghana’s governing National Democratic Congress (NDC), in the region around the capital. A delegate vote in Accra has replaced the man who led Ghana’s governing party in the capital region since 2022.

Benjamin Danso won the chairmanship of Ghana’s governing party in the Greater Accra Region on Saturday 14 November 2026. He unseated Emmanuel Nii Ashie Moore, who had held the post since November 2022.

The regional chairman runs the party’s organisation across the region, so the result matters to members of the National Democratic Congress (NDC) in the capital ahead of the 2028 general elections. The party is reorganising nationwide before its national executive elections.

What Happened

The NDC scheduled its Greater Accra regional executive elections for Friday 13 and Saturday 14 November 2026. The youth and women’s contests were set for Friday, and the main regional conference and chairmanship vote for Saturday.

Four candidates stood for chairman: Ashie Moore, the incumbent, Michael Tetteh Kwetey, Ibrahim Jajah and Benjamin Danso. In all, 77 candidates were due to contest 15 regional executive positions.

Ashie Moore first won the post in November 2022, when he beat the then chairman, Joseph Ade Coker. The term lasts four years.

Delegates, the party members entitled to vote, were expected to number more than 1,200, the party said before the vote. Theophilus Tetteh Chai, the party’s Greater Accra regional secretary, gave the schedule ahead of the election.

The Electoral Commission, Ghana’s national election authority, was due to print the election materials and supervise the vote. Police were due to provide security.

Before the vote, Ashie Moore said: “I’m very confident the delegates today will reward hard work.” Delegates then voted on Saturday 14 November.

Other regional chairmen were also chosen on Saturday 14 November, among them Mark Oliver Kevor, re-elected in the Eastern Region, and Nana Kojo Toku, re-elected in the Western Region. Results in several of the NDC’s 16 regions were still pending that evening.

In the Central Region, sitting regional chairman Richard Asiedu has demanded a recount after reports that he lost. No Central Region result had been declared at last report.

Central Accra, Ghana. Photo: Francisco Anzola / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

Who Is Benjamin Danso

Danso is a former NDC chairman of the Krowor constituency, one of the local party units in the regional structure. In his campaign he pledged to lead with service, integrity and commitment to the party’s grassroots.

He also promised a strong, united structure across all 34 constituencies of the region. He set the goal of helping the NDC win the 2028 general elections.

Why It Matters

The regional chairman organises the party across the region’s 34 constituencies, the number Danso cited in his pledge. The vote replaced the man at the top of the capital region’s party.

That choice came during the NDC’s nationwide internal reorganisation. National officers are due to be elected on 19 December.

What Happens Next

The NDC has announced that its National Delegates Conference, which elects national officers, will take place on Saturday 19 December 2026. That is the next fixed checkpoint.

The Central Region result is the other open item, and no recount date has been announced. Results in other regions were also still pending on Saturday evening.

What We Do Not Know

No vote counts for the chairmanship had been published as of 14 November, so the margin is unknown. The final delegate turnout is also not confirmed.

What It Means for You

For readers following Ghana’s politics or business, party chiefs shape candidate selection ahead of 2028. A new chairman in the capital region is therefore worth tracking as the NDC picks its national officers.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who won the NDC chairmanship in Greater Accra?

Benjamin Danso won on Saturday 14 November 2026, unseating incumbent Emmanuel Nii Ashie Moore. No vote counts had been published as of that day.

Who voted in the election?

More than 1,200 delegates were expected to vote, the party said before the vote. They were party members entitled to vote at the regional conference.

What does a regional chairman do?

The regional chairman organises the party across the region, which has 34 constituencies. The post is held for four years.

What happens next in the NDC elections?

The National Delegates Conference to elect national officers is on Saturday 19 December 2026. The Central Region chairmanship result is not declared, and a recount date is not confirmed.

Sources National Democratic Congress of Ghana (regional results and 2026 election timetable, 14 November 2026); Electoral Commission of Ghana

World.title: Colombia Coal Mine Blast Kills Two Miners
World.content:
A gas explosion inside a coal mine in Chita, a mountain municipality in Colombia’s Boyacá department, killed two miners on Friday afternoon, 13 November 2026, and left two more trapped underground. Colombia’s National Mining Agency (ANM), the national mining regulator, said on Saturday 14 November that its rescue teams were still working at the site.

The four men were inside the tunnel when the blast struck, and the agency says the explosion caused a collapse that is slowing the search. This report sets out what officials have confirmed, and what they have not, with respect for the families of the dead and of the men still missing.

Key Facts •Deaths. Two miners died after a gas explosion in a coal mine on Friday 13 November 2026. •Missing. Two more miners remain trapped in Chita, a municipality in Boyacá department. •Rescue. Teams from the National Mining Agency (ANM) are ventilating the tunnel and reinforcing its supports. •Cause. Authorities point to methane gas building up underground, and the cause is still being investigated. •Power Index. Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index, with 51.1 points (November 2026 edition).

What We Know About the Chita Explosion

The explosion happened on Friday afternoon, 13 November 2026, in a mine in the village of La Playa, in the municipality of Chita in Boyacá, according to the ANM. Four workers were inside the shaft, and the agency confirmed that two bodies had been recovered by Saturday.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Colombia Email address Follow

The other two miners were still unaccounted for on Saturday 14 November, when the ANM said its mine-rescue teams were working without pause. Crews from the agency’s rescue stations, including the one at Nobsa, a town in Boyacá, worked through the night on ventilation and on reinforcing the mine’s supports.

The ANM links the blast to a presumed build-up of methane, the natural gas that collects in coal seams. It said the explosion then brought down part of the tunnel, which makes the rescue slower and more dangerous.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Colombia ranks 6th of 14 with 51.1 points. Strongest pillar: military means (91); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (28). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB-); 26 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.8 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The agency also said the mine sits under title FI6-144 and works under a formalisation subcontract. This is a state scheme that lets small miners work legally under a larger title holder while they bring their operations up to standard.

Why Methane Makes Mine Rescue So Slow

Methane is colourless and has no smell, and it ignites when it mixes with air in the wrong proportion. Miners and rescuers manage it with a steady flow of fresh air, which is why ventilation is the first job after an explosion.

The ANM said crews were injecting air into the tunnel without interruption. Rescuers cannot safely push forward until the air is clear enough to breathe and the roof and walls are propped up, so progress is measured in short stretches.

A collapse adds a second hazard to the first. Each reinforced metre protects the rescue crew, but it also takes time that the trapped men may not have.

The ANM has not published a time estimate for reaching the two miners. Rescue crews in Colombia’s coal belt have responded to similar accidents before, and the agency keeps permanent rescue stations in the region for that reason.

What Is Not Known

Officials have not said whether the two trapped miners are alive, and they have not given the exact time of the blast or how far underground the men are. The cause is a working hypothesis, methane, and the official investigation has not reported.

We could not confirm a statement from the governor of Boyacá or from the national disaster-risk agency (UNGRD) in a primary source. The agency has not named the mine’s owner or the men, so we do not publish names.

What It Means for You

For most readers abroad this is a human story rather than a market one. The people affected are miners and their families in rural Chita, and the first test of the response is whether the two trapped men are reached.

Readers who follow Colombian energy or mining investments should watch for the ANM’s findings on ventilation and gas monitoring in small formalised mines. Our

Colombia news hub tracks the story as the rescue continues.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where did the Colombia coal mine explosion happen?

The blast struck a coal mine in the village of La Playa, in Chita, Boyacá. The ANM, Colombia’s mining regulator, said rescue teams were still working there on Saturday 14 November 2026.

How many miners died in the Chita explosion?

Two miners died and two more were trapped, according to the ANM. The agency confirmed two bodies had been recovered by Saturday.

What caused the explosion?

The ANM points to a presumed build-up of methane gas, which then caused a collapse. The investigation is open, so the cause is not final.

Who is leading the rescue?

The ANM’s mine-rescue teams are leading the work, including crews from Nobsa. They are ventilating the tunnel and reinforcing its supports so they can reach the trapped men.

Sources: Agencia Nacional de Minería (ANM), statements on the Chita emergency (14 November 2026); Gobernación de Boyacá (the regional government) and Alcaldía de Chita (the town hall), institutional channels (read 14 November 2026).

World.title: Wilfrido Vargas Ordered to Pay US$231,000
World.content:
Published Saturday 14 November 2026. Source: the court ruling and the parties.

A Santo Domingo court has ordered merengue bandleader Wilfrido Vargas and his company to pay RD$14 million (Dominican pesos, about US$231,000) to a fellow musician over the dance song “El baile del perrito”. The first-instance ruling says Juan Valdez Ybet helped write part of the song and went unrecognised as a co-author for more than 30 years.

Key Facts Free daily brief — no card needed Get every Dominican Republic story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Love it? Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time. ·Ruling. Vargas and his company must jointly pay RD$14 million (about US$231,000) to musician Juan Valdez Ybet. ·Song. “El baile del perrito” (the dog dance) is a merengue dance song. ·Finding. The court found Valdez helped write the lyrics and melody of part B, one section of the song, beyond arranging. ·Status. This is a civil, first-instance judgment dated Wednesday 28 October 2026, not a criminal case. ·As of 14 November 2026, 20:00 GMT

A Dominican Court Rules on a Merengue Hit

The trial-level civil court in Santo Domingo has ordered Dominican merengue bandleader Wilfrido Vargas and his company, Corporación Wilfrido Vargas, S.R.L., to pay RD$14 million (about US$231,000) to musician Juan Valdez Ybet. The ruling is dated Wednesday 28 October 2026, was reported on 14 November, and concerns the song “El baile del perrito”.

The case touches a question few dancers ask: who wrote the song? Credit disputes like this show how a court weighs old recordings and testimony when authorship is contested.

The court ordered both defendants to pay jointly RD$12 million (about US$198,000) in moral damages and RD$2 million (about US$33,000) in patrimonial, or lost-income, damages. The US$ figures use 60.59 pesos per dollar, the close of market-data provider RT on 14 November 2026.

Valdez had claimed RD$100 million (about US$1.65 million), split evenly at RD$50 million (about US$825,000) for each kind of damages. The court awarded 14 per cent of the total he sought.

The Ozama River and the bridges of Santo Domingo seen from the Alcazar de Colon, pictured in August 2022. Photo: AlonsoRiveraM / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Dominican Republic Email address Follow

What We Know

The Second Chamber of the Civil and Commercial Chamber of the Court of First Instance of the National District heard the case. Judge Nidia Victoria Jorge Taveras decided it in Judgment No. 035-2026-SSEN-01198, dated Wednesday 28 October 2026.

The court found that Valdez took part in creating the lyrics and the melody of part B of the song. It held that he was not only the arranger.

The court heard testimony from musicians Ramón Orlando, Alejandro Abrahán Martínez Rodríguez and Santiago Delgado Veloz. It also reviewed audiovisual material and a recording, first made on cassette and later digitised.

On that recording, Vargas, Valdez and a third person, Frantoni Santana, talk while the song takes shape. According to the ruling, Vargas voices dissatisfaction with an initial melody and asks Valdez for a new proposal.

Vargas’s 2018 memoir, “Me volviste loco, Wilfrido”, was also cited as evidence. It names Valdez among the composers who contributed.

Orlando put Valdez’s share of the song at about 70 per cent. The court did not adopt that percentage.

The court also ordered the defendants to publish the operative part of the ruling in a national newspaper at their own expense. They must also pay court costs.

The court rejected a daily penalty, known as an astreinte. It also found inadmissible a request to register Valdez as co-author with publishers and platforms, because it was raised late.

What the Defence Argued

Vargas’s lawyers argued in court that Valdez was only a paid arranger, credited on the album “Itinerario”. They said arranging does not give anyone rights over the composition itself.

They also argued that the claim was time-barred after more than 30 years. The court rejected that argument, citing Law 65-00, the Dominican copyright law.

Under article 17 of that law, moral rights are imprescriptible (they never expire), inalienable and perpetual. Under article 21, as the court applied it, patrimonial rights last for the author’s life plus 70 years.

The judge said exact lost royalties since the 1990s could not be established. The amount was therefore set under article 177, paragraph III.

The RD$12 million (about US$198,000) in moral damages reflects, in the court’s reasoning, the lack of recognition for more than 30 years. The RD$2 million (about US$33,000) patrimonial award stands in for lost income the court could not calculate exactly.

Why the Ruling Matters

The mechanism is simple: Law 65-00 treats the right to be named as an author as one that never expires. That let a claim more than 30 years old end in RD$12 million (about US$198,000) in moral damages.

For listeners anywhere, the case is a reminder that a dance-floor favourite can carry a contested authorship story. It also shows a Dominican court weighing old tapes, witness accounts and a memoir, not only album credits.

In Plain English Moral damages are payment for harm to an author’s name and recognition. Here they reflect more than 30 years without recognition as a co-author. Patrimonial damages are payment for lost money. Here the court set them itself, because exact lost royalties could not be proved. An arranger shapes how an existing song is played, such as its instruments and structure. A co-author helps write the lyrics or melody, which is what the court found for part B.

What Is Not Known

No comment from Vargas or his company on the ruling was found, so it is not known whether they will appeal. It is also not known whether the ruling can be appealed, or what the deadline would be.

The reported terms of the ruling do not say how royalties will be handled from here. That question remains open.

What It Means for Readers

Readers who follow Latin music should note that this is a first-instance civil ruling, not a final word. It settles a dispute over credit and compensation and does not accuse anyone of a crime.

In the Dominican Republic, the decision shows how a court treats an arranger who claims to be an author. The test here was evidence of creative contribution to lyrics and melody, not the label on an album credit.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who must pay whom?

Wilfrido Vargas and his company, Corporación Wilfrido Vargas, S.R.L., must jointly pay musician Juan Valdez Ybet RD$14 million (about US$231,000). The first-instance ruling is dated 28 October 2026.

What is “El baile del perrito”?

It is a merengue dance song known as the dog dance. The court found Valdez helped create the lyrics and melody of its part B.

Is this a criminal case?

No, it is a civil dispute over credit and compensation. The court ordered payment and publication of the ruling, not any criminal penalty.

Will Vargas appeal?

It is not known whether Vargas or his company will appeal, and no comment on the ruling was found. The ruling is a first-instance decision, and no appeal deadline has been confirmed.

World.title: Nyala Commander Dies of Drone Strike Wounds
World.content:
SUDAN · CONFLICT

Ahmed Abdullah Bashar Katir, known as Abu Tonqa, chief of staff of a Darfur armed group that local reports place in an alliance led by Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF, a paramilitary force), has died of earlier wounds that local reports link to a drone strike on his home in Nyala. The group, the Sudan Liberation Forces Gathering (the Gathering), announced his death on Saturday 14 November 2026.

The strike hit a house in the Al-Nahda district of Nyala, the capital of South Darfur, in the early hours of Monday 19 October. Local sources say it killed five people, including his wife.

The group has not said when or where its chief of staff died, and no army account of the strike was available.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Sudan Email address Follow

What We Know About the Death

The Sudan Liberation Forces Gathering, led by its chairman Al-Taher Hajar, announced on Saturday 14 November that its chief of staff had died of an earlier injury. The statement mourned him but did not say where or when he died, or describe the wound.

The chief of staff was wounded when a drone struck a house in Al-Nahda, a district of Nyala, in the early hours of Monday 19 October. Local sources said five people died, including his wife, two children and two bodyguards, and that others were hurt.

A commander of the movement said the drone belonged to the Sudanese army and that the house was not a military site. No Sudanese army statement on the strike was available at the time of writing.

Women selling food at a market in Khartoum, Sudan’s capital. File photo taken in Khartoum: Dr. Ondřej Havelka / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

Who He Was

In plain English Sudan Liberation Forces Gathering: an armed group from Darfur that, local reports say, belongs to the Sudan Founding Alliance. Sudan Founding Alliance: a coalition led by the RSF that runs a rival administration in areas the RSF holds.

The Gathering is led by its chairman, Al-Taher Hajar, who represents it on the presidential council of the Founding Alliance, local reports say. That council is chaired by Hemedti, the nickname of RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo.

Local reports describe Abu Tonqa as one of the movement’s earliest members, with military and field commands. The Gathering’s own statement did not give his career or the cause of his wound.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket is a prediction market where traders stake real money. It priced a Sudan civil war ceasefire by 31 December 2026 at about 11% on 14 November (2:19 p.m. ET).

The event has traded US$119,643 across all its dates. A price is a bet, not a forecast.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Nyala Under Drone Attack

Nyala was struck on Friday 16 October, when the army said it hit RSF command centres and the RSF said a livestock market was hit. A strike on a night market on Monday 26 October killed at least 21 people, a medical source cited by a news agency said.

Doctors Without Borders (MSF), the medical charity, said a Nyala hospital it supports received 36 bodies and saw more than 150 wounded, and Emergency Lawyers, a Sudanese rights group, counted more than 100 dead. Our earlier reports cover the night-market strike and the dispute over its toll.

What Is Not Known

The Gathering has not said when or where Abu Tonqa died, or what his wounds were. His name is written in several ways in Arabic-language reports, including Bashar, Bishr, Katir and Katar.

The army’s account of the 19 October strike is missing, so the claim that it carried out the attack rests on one movement commander. Whether the army regarded the house as a target is not known.

Who Is Affected

This is mainly a story about people living in Nyala under repeated drone strikes: the relatives of the five killed on 19 October, and residents of a city where a market and a home were hit within weeks of each other. A movement commander described the house as a family home, not a military site.

Counting Abu Tonqa, six people have now died from the 19 October strike, according to local sources. More on the war is in our Sudan coverage.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who was Abu Tonqa?

He was chief of staff of the Sudan Liberation Forces Gathering, a Darfur armed group, according to its statement of 14 November 2026. Local reports say the group belongs to the RSF-led Sudan Founding Alliance.

How did he die?

The group says he died of earlier injuries, which local reports link to a drone strike on his home in Nyala on 19 October. It did not say when or where he died.

Who carried out the strike?

A Gathering commander says it was a Sudanese army drone. No Sudanese army statement was available at the time of writing.

Where is Nyala?

Nyala is the capital of South Darfur state in western Sudan. The RSF holds the city.

Sources: statement by the Sudan Liberation Forces Gathering on the death of its chief of staff (14 November 2026); accounts of the 19 October strike from a Gathering commander and local sources; Doctors Without Borders (MSF) and Emergency Lawyers, a Sudanese rights group, on the 26 October Nyala market strike; Polymarket, Sudan civil war ceasefire by 31 December 2026 market, read 14 November 2026.

World.title: Four Miners Trapped in Kassanda Gold Pit
World.content:
UGANDA · MINING

Four artisanal (small-scale, often hand-dug) gold miners have been trapped underground for four days at a mining site in Kassanda District, central Uganda, after a pit collapsed on Tuesday 10 November 2026. Rescue work was still under way on Saturday 14 November.

Police say six men entered a restricted pit at the Kagaba mining site to collect leftover gold ore, and two escaped and raised the alarm. The four who remain trapped are named in local reports as Yoweri Owimaana, Isaac Bijirimaana, Isaac Muneneko and Gasole.

Who Four men are trapped; two others in the group of six escaped.

Where Kagaba site, in Bukuya Town Council (a local authority), Kassanda District, central Uganda.

Status Rescue work continued on 14 November; police have not said whether the men are alive.

Earlier A man died in a pit at the same site on 18 October; officials urged temporary closure of five pits.

Four days after the collapse, the men are still underground at a site where officials had recently recommended closing five pits.

What Happened at Kagaba

Senior Superintendent Lameck Kigozi, spokesperson for the Wamala Regional Police (the police command that covers Kassanda), said six men had entered a restricted pit to scavenge leftover ore. The practice is known locally as okwekyokola, and the pit belonged to a mine owner named as Joseph Kabira.

Two of the men, named as Rukundo and Kaviiri, escaped unhurt and alerted others. Denis Ssekandi, general manager of the Mubende Miners Association (MUMA, a group representing miners in the area), reported the incident to Kassanda Police Station, the local station.

Warnings Before the Collapse

On 18 October, a man died in a pit at the same site, local reports said. Officials of the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development, which regulates mining in Uganda, then recommended temporarily closing five underground pits.

Excavators had been brought in to backfill the pits, but the work was not finished when the six men entered the mine, according to local reports. Kigozi urged miners to stay out of pits declared unsafe and asked mine owners to tighten security at such sites.

What Is Not Known

Police have not said whether the four men are alive, or what caused the collapse. How the six men got into a pit that was meant to be closed is also not explained.

Whether the mine owner faces any action is not known. Police have not said when the inquiry will report.

Who Is Affected

This is above all a local safety story: the families of the four men, and the miners who work at Kagaba, where the ministry had already recommended closing pits. For readers following Uganda, it follows the Namayingo gold mine collapse in eastern Uganda earlier this year, in which local sources counted six dead.

Our earlier report on Uganda’s gold exports covers the wider trade. Police have urged miners and residents to follow ministry safety guidelines and to stay out of closed pits.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where is Kassanda?

Kassanda is a district in central Uganda. The Kagaba mining site is in Bukuya Town Council.

What happened at the Kagaba gold mine?

A pit collapsed on Tuesday 10 November 2026 with six men inside. Two escaped and four are trapped underground.

Who are the trapped miners?

Local reports name them as Yoweri Owimaana, Isaac Bijirimaana, Isaac Muneneko and Gasole. Police have not said whether they are alive.

What are police doing?

Police opened a General Inquiry File, visited the scene and recorded witness statements. Rescue work was continuing on 14 November.

Sources: statements by the Wamala Regional Police spokesperson, Senior Superintendent Lameck Kigozi, and by the Mubende Miners Association (MUMA), as relayed in Ugandan local reporting of 14 November 2026; Uganda Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development safety measures at Kagaba, October 2026.

World.title: Family Says Chad Freed Sudan Ex-Adviser
World.content:
SUDAN · CHAD

Chad has freed Yousif Ibrahim Ezzat, the former political adviser to the commander of Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF), after about 13 months in custody, his family says. The family’s announcement was reported on Saturday 14 November 2026, and it says the release took place on Thursday 12 November.

The RSF is the paramilitary force that has fought Sudan’s army since 15 April 2023. The family says Ezzat was never charged, and none of the reports available to us carries a statement from Chad’s government.

What We Know About the Release

Ezzat’s family says a decision by Chad’s public prosecution office ordered his release and that no charge was brought against him. The family says he was held in N’Djamena for about 13 months.

The family says Chadian forces arrested him on Saturday 11 October 2025 at the Adre crossing, where eastern Chad meets West Darfur, a state in Sudan’s far west. It names the arresting officer as General Saleh Abdullah Jar, a Chadian general known as Salehi, and says Ezzat was held without contact with relatives.

Who Is Yousif Ezzat

In plain English RSF: the Rapid Support Forces, a Sudanese paramilitary force led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti. It has fought Sudan’s regular army since April 2023. Adre: a border town where eastern Chad meets Sudan’s West Darfur state. West Darfur lies in Sudan’s far west, next to Chad.

Ezzat served as political adviser to Hemedti until the RSF announced his dismissal on Wednesday 10 July 2024. The announcement gave no reasons.

Ezzat said afterwards that he had asked to be relieved, citing differences with Abdelrahim Dagalo, Hemedti’s brother and deputy commander of the RSF. He has not been part of the RSF leadership since that dismissal.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket is a prediction market where traders stake real money. It priced a Sudan civil war ceasefire by 31 December 2026 at about 11% on 14 November (2:19 p.m. ET).

The event has traded US$119,643 across all its dates. A price is a bet, not a forecast.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What Is Not Known

Chad has not said why it arrested Ezzat or why it let him go. According to his family, no charge was ever brought.

In a video, Ezzat said his release followed international and tribal efforts, without giving details. Reports say others were arrested with him, and whether they are free is not clear.

Why It Matters Beyond Sudan

Chad shares a border with Sudan’s Darfur region in the west, and the Adre crossing where Ezzat was seized links the two. Our earlier report on Sudan’s complaints to the UN about RSF supply routes gives more background on the border.

For US readers the Sudan war is a policy matter: on 7 January 2025 the US State Department said RSF members and allied militias had committed genocide, and it barred Hemedti and his immediate family from entering the United States. What Chad does with RSF-linked figures, and the fate of cities such as Nyala, the RSF-held capital of South Darfur, therefore stays in view.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Yousif Ezzat?

He was political adviser to Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti, the RSF commander. The RSF announced his dismissal on 10 July 2024.

When was Yousif Ezzat released?

His family says Chad released him on Thursday 12 November 2026. He had spent about 13 months in custody.

Was Yousif Ezzat charged?

His family says no charge was brought. The reports available to us carry no explanation from Chad’s government.

What is the RSF?

The Rapid Support Forces is a Sudanese paramilitary force led by Hemedti. It has fought Sudan’s army since 15 April 2023.

Sources: statement by Ezzat’s family on his release (14 November 2026); Rapid Support Forces announcement of Ezzat’s dismissal (10 July 2024); US State Department, Genocide Determination in Sudan and Imposing Accountability Measures (7 January 2025); Polymarket, Sudan civil war ceasefire by 31 December 2026 market, read 14 November 2026.

World.title: Costa Rica Falls 2-0 to Ecuador in Quito as the Bryan Ruiz Era Begins
World.content:
Costa Rica opened the Bryan Ruiz era with a 2-0 loss to Ecuador on Friday night in Quito. The team finished the friendly with 10 men and lost a defender to a knee injury, four days before it faces Argentina. Jordy Caicedo put Ecuador ahead in the first half. Moisés Caicedo, the Chelsea midfielder and Ecuador captain, sealed it from the penalty spot late in the second half at Estadio Olímpico Atahualpa, which sits about 2,850 meters (9,350 feet) above sea level.

The result gave Argentine coach Marcelo Gallardo his first win in charge of Ecuador. It was Ruiz’s first match as Costa Rica’s permanent head coach. The former national team captain won both of his games as interim coach, against Nicaragua and Haiti in the Concacaf Nations League, before the Costa Rican Football Federation gave him the job.

Costa Rica set the early tempo. The visitors pressed high and won the ball back quickly in the opening minutes. Striker Manfred Ugalde, back with the squad after serving a suspension, forced a save from Ecuador goalkeeper Hernán Galíndez around the ninth minute. Ecuador struck midway through the half. Jordy Caicedo, who plays for Argentine club Huracán, ran onto a long ball from Piero Hincapié. He went around goalkeeper Patrick Sequeira and finished with his left foot for his fifth international goal.

Costa Rica came closest to an equalizer early in the second half. Andrey Soto shot after a pass from Carlos Mora, and Ecuador defender Jackson Porozo cleared the ball off the line. Ruiz made four changes shortly before the hour mark. Alexis Gamboa, Celso Borges, Josimar Méndez and Kenyel Michel came on for Francisco Calvo, Roan Wilson, Soto and Josimar Alcócer. The changes quickly turned costly.

Gamboa went down after a collision with Ecuador’s John Yeboah a few minutes after coming on and was carried off on a stretcher. The federation said he has a left knee injury and will return to Costa Rica on Saturday for further tests, which rules him out against Argentina. Diego Mesén replaced Gamboa around the 65th minute in his first appearance for the national team. He was sent off a few minutes later for a foul on Jordy Caicedo.

Playing a man down at altitude, Costa Rica could not hold on. Ecuador was awarded a penalty for a foul on Yeboah in the box, and Moisés Caicedo converted with less than 10 minutes left. Ruiz said after the match that he left Quito satisfied with what he saw. He said many of the things the coaching staff asked for were carried out and the team showed personality, and he called the result secondary to what the squad learned. He also acknowledged that the game became an uphill battle and said the team’s style of play still needs fine-tuning.

Gallardo said Ecuador grew into the match after an uncomfortable start and called it a constructive performance. He added that the win was a good way to reconnect with the home crowd. The loss extended Costa Rica’s winless run against Ecuador, which dates back to 1992. Ecuador has now won six straight meetings, including a 3-0 win at the 2006 World Cup in Germany and a 3-1 friendly win in Chester, Pennsylvania, in June 2023.

Costa Rica plays Argentina, the 2026 World Cup runner-up, on Tuesday, Nov. 17, at Estadio Mario Alberto Kempes in Córdoba. It is the team’s last match of the year. The federation tried to call up Kendall Waston as cover, but Saprissa said the veteran defender is still recovering from an injury and will not travel.

For a team rebuilding after missing this year’s World Cup, the night in Quito showed what Ruiz has to work with. There were early signs of the aggressive approach he wants, but also how quickly a thin squad can come apart. Tuesday’s game against the world’s runner-up will show how much of that can be fixed in four days.

World.title: Monteverde Went From 25 Dry Days a Year to Nearly 120, BBC Reports
World.content:
Costa Rica’s best known cloud forest is in the international spotlight this week after the BBC published a lengthy feature on Monteverde, reporting that the clouds that define the forest are pulling away from it and changing the life inside. The piece appeared on November 12 on BBC Future, the British broadcaster’s science and environment section. It was written by journalist Jocelyn Timperley, who reported from the Children’s Eternal Rainforest and other reserves around Monteverde.

The central message will be familiar to anyone who has followed the science here. The BBC reports that the fog bank that once sat on the forest almost year-round is rising with warmer temperatures, leaving the canopy exposed to sun and dry air for much of the dry season.

It leans on the long running records of Alan Pounds, resident scientist at the Monteverde Cloud Forest Biological Preserve, who has counted the days when neither rain nor mist reaches his gauge. There were about 25 a year in the 1970s. His latest figures, which the BBC describes as preliminary, put the recent average near 119.

Much of the feature is devoted to the epiphytes, the orchids, mosses, bromeliads and ferns that cover Monteverde’s trees and drink directly from the mist. The BBC follows ecologists Nalini Nadkarni of the University of Utah and Sybil Gotsch of the University of Kentucky, along with Costa Rican scientist Elenter Cubero Campos, whose experiments are designed to show what the forest loses as those hanging gardens dry out.

The feature also revisits the golden toad, the Monteverde species that vanished after 1989 and is widely cited as one of the first extinctions linked to a warming climate.
