World.title: Washington atribuye el parón aéreo a un problema con un nuevo cableado de fibra óptica
World.content:
El viernes 13 de la aviación estadounidense, que dejó miles de vuelos cancelados y retrasados, fue consecuencia de una falla en el equipo y no de un ataque cibernético, aseguró Bryan Bedford, titular de la Administración Federal de Aviación (FAA, por sus siglas en inglés), durante una conferencia de prensa este sábado. El secretario de Transporte, Sean Duffy, dijo en la misma conferencia que el problema se inició cuando un contratista de la compañía L3Harris, que provee servicios a la FAA, realizaba un mantenimiento de rutina para sustituir el antiguo cableado de cobre por fibra óptica, lo que provocó una saturación en el sistema de control de tráfico aéreo.

El enrutador que se estaba sustituyendo comenzó a saturar a otros enrutadores del sistema de control de tráfico aéreo, indicó Duffy. “Ya fuera por un error del contratista o por un equipo defectuoso, el enrutador que se estaba reemplazando durante la transición comenzó a saturar otros enrutadores de nuestro sistema de control de tráfico aéreo. Concretamente, se registraron más de 1.000 intentos de conexión cada cuatro o cinco segundos; esto provocó problemas en nuestras comunicaciones con las aeronaves y causó interrupciones en la recepción de datos de radar”, detalló.

Al percatarse de la situación, las autoridades ordenaron la suspensión de los despegues en tierra y procedieron a aislar el problema, antes de reabrir el espacio aéreo más tarde ese mismo día.

Bedford, en tanto, insistió en que no se trató de un ataque externo. “No tenemos ninguna prueba de nada malintencionado ni de nada relacionado con la inteligencia artificial. Queremos dejar claro que se trata de un problema de equipamiento; estamos investigando qué pieza específica resultó defectuosa”, afirmó.

Bryan Bedford, administrador de la Administración Federal de Aviación (FAA) de Estados Unidos. Eric Lee (REUTERS)

El funcionario recalcó que el incidente fue tratado como una prioridad por el gabinete de seguridad de la Casa Blanca, con la participación del Buró Federal de Investigaciones (FBI, por sus siglas en inglés). Según Bedford, todas las agencias involucradas concluyeron “que no se trató de un ataque cibernético”.

Las operaciones afectadas

La crisis que sacude el complejo sistema aeroportuario de Estados Unidos se prolongaba este sábado, con más de 4.000 vuelos cancelados y retrasados. La incertidumbre crece a medida que se acerca uno de los periodos de mayor actividad aérea del año: el Día de Acción de Gracias. Bedford, sin embargo, dijo que esperan ver mayores señales de recuperación este domingo. “Creo que ya pasamos lo peor”, aseguró el funcionario.

Varios aeropuertos de la costa este del país figuraban entre los más afectados este sábado. Entre ellos estaban LaGuardia y John F. Kennedy, en Nueva York, así como los de Detroit y Louisville, según el sitio de seguimiento de vuelos Flightradar24. Algunas aerolíneas, como American Airlines, una de las más impactadas, advirtieron que las cancelaciones y los retrasos continuarían a lo largo del día.

Al inicio de la interrupción, alrededor de las 3:45 p.m. del viernes (hora del Este), había unos 50.000 vuelos programados. De ellos, cerca de 30.000 lograron completarse. De los 20.000 restantes, se recuperaron 8.000, mientras que otros 12.000 fueron cancelados, explicó Bedford durante la conferencia este sábado.

El administrador de la FAA estimó que entre 4.000 y 5.000 de los 41.000 vuelos programados para este sábado serán cancelados. “Esto nos permitirá lograr una recuperación total para mañana”, afirmó.

Pasajeros observan el panel de salidas en el Aeropuerto Nacional Ronald Reagan de Washington. EMILY CURIEL (EFE)

El parón en los aeropuertos

En primera instancia, se informó que un problema en el sistema informático que gestiona las comunicaciones obligó a la FAA a cancelar todas las operaciones nacionales en los aeropuertos del país durante más de cuatro horas, la suspensión del tráfico aéreo más larga desde el fatídico 11 de septiembre de 2001. Las autoridades justificaron el parón “debido a circunstancias extraordinarias y por motivos de seguridad”. El incidente provocó un colapso en los aeropuertos, dejando más de 6.500 vuelos cancelados, cerca de 10.000 retrasados y cientos de miles de pasajeros afectados.

Los problemas en la red informática comenzaron sobre las 15.36 de la tarde (hora de la costa este), según detalló horas más tarde el secretario de Transporte, Sean Duffy. Los operadores detectaron “inestabilidad” en las comunicaciones de radar de los centros de control de tráfico aéreo. El problema surgió “cuando se estaban realizando ajustes parciales en el sistema, incorporando nuevos equipos y tecnología; sin embargo, estos elementos no resultaron adecuados. Terminaron sobrecargando el sistema antiguo”, precisó el secretario de Seguridad Nacional, Markwayne Mullin, que compareció junto a Duffy en una conferencia de prensa en la Casa Blanca.

Mullin descartó desde el viernes que el incidente se debiera a un sabotaje, a ciberataques o a actos malintencionados. “No hay indicios de actividad sospechosa. No hemos encontrado rastros ni identificaciones de personas que hayan accedido al sistema. Al parecer, todo fue un proceso automatizado”, aseguró el secretario de Seguridad Nacional. “Sin embargo, seguimos buscando, así que no lo descartamos”, agregó.

Las autoridades aseguraron que durante el incidente ningún vuelo estuvo en peligro y que tomaron la decisión de parar por precaución. Cerca de cuatro horas y media más tarde permitieron reanudar las operaciones. Eran ya las 8.15 de la tarde. Para entonces, el sistema aéreo estadounidense era ya un caos que tardará días en normalizarse. “Será un proceso lento”, dijo el responsable máximo de la FAA. “Creo que volveremos a estar operativos cuando llegue el momento álgido de los viajes durante el Día de Acción de Gracias”, indicó Duffy.

La orden de suspensión de todos los vuelos nacionales es algo poco habitual en Estados Unidos. La orden del viernes paralizó casi todas las salidas de viajes nacionales. Algunos vuelos internacionales pudieron despegar, así como otros con material médico o de primera necesidad. Decenas de miles de pasajeros quedaron atrapados en aeropuertos de todo el país. No se sabe exactamente el número de personas afectadas, pero cada día pasan algo más de dos millones de personas por los controles de seguridad de los aeropuertos estadounidenses, según la Administración de Seguridad del Transporte (TSA).

Pasajeros de Delta Air Lines recogen su equipaje de una pila de maletas no reclamadas en el Aeropuerto Nacional Ronald Reagan. EMILY CURIEL (EFE)

La Administración achacó el problema a la obsolescencia de los sistemas. “Los parches no funcionan. Necesitamos un sistema integral; requerimos que alguien desarrolle el sistema en su totalidad. Intentar construirlo mediante parches parciales no funciona, y esto es precisamente lo que ocurre cuando se procede de esa manera”, indicó Mullin. “Es necesaria una renovación completa del sistema”, insistió.

“Va a seguir fallando”, advirtió el secretario de Transporte en referencia a la tecnología desfasada de hace varias décadas que la FAA quiere modernizar, lo que a la postre provocó el fallo en las telecomunicaciones que causó el incidente. “Lo que tenemos es un sistema de control de tráfico aéreo increíblemente antiguo”, dijo Duffy antes de aprovechar para reclamar nuevos fondos al Congreso para la renovación de todo el sistema. “Durante el último año, el presidente ha estado pidiendo al Congreso que financie por completo la construcción de un sistema de control de tráfico aéreo totalmente nuevo”.

Los dos ministros del gabinete de Donald Trump reclamaron “fondos de emergencia” por un total de 50.000 millones de dólares para modernizar el sistema de control de tráfico aéreo. El secretario de Transporte ya había presentado una solicitud previamente para aumentar la financiación en 30.000 millones. “Yo he pedido, el presidente ha pedido 30.000 millones de dólares. Pero yo quiero 50.000 millones”, afirmó Duffy. “¿Qué hay más importante que tener un sistema de control de tráfico aéreo que funcione de verdad?”, apostilló para explicar que hay que renovar el hardware, el software y los sistemas de telecomunicaciones.

World.title: Zelenski asegura que EE UU sugiere admitir a Ucrania en la OTAN a cambio de entregar el Donbás a Rusia
World.content:
El yerno y enviado especial de Donald Trump para Ucrania, Jared Kushner, saludaba el viernes al presidente Volodímir Zelenski en Dublín, en una imagen oficial ucrania.

El presidente de Ucrania, Volodimir Zelenski, ha asegurado que los mediadores de Estados Unidos para ese conflicto han planteado la posibilidad de aceptar al país en la OTAN a cambio de que renuncie al Donbás y se lo entregue a Rusia. Esta es la primera vez que se pone sobre la mesa una posible vinculación del deseo de Ucrania de ingresar en la Alianza con concesiones territoriales, según las declaraciones de Zelenski difundidas por su oficina este sábado.

“Los estadounidenses plantearon una pregunta: “¿Y si Ucrania se une a la OTAN? ¿Se retiraría Ucrania de Donbás?”, ha afirmado el presidente sobre esa posibilidad, que surgió tras la última ronda negociadora entre Rusia y Ucrania, bajo mediación estadounidense, que concluyó el miércoles en Abu Dabi, la capital de Emiratos Árabes Unidos.

“Por eso creo que la OTAN vuelve a estar sobre la mesa. Pero también habéis oído las declaraciones de (el presidente ruso Vladimir) Putin, y se trata de una conversación extremadamente difícil”, ha aseverado el presidente ucranio.

Putin lleva tiempo afirmando que la adhesión de Ucrania a la OTAN es una línea roja para Moscú, y ha citado esta cuestión como una de las razones que a sus ojos justifica la invasión a gran escala de Ucrania que comenzó en 2022.

En sus declaraciones, Zelenski reitera su postura de que Kiev no está dispuesta a ceder territorio. Sin embargo, el presidente ha matizado luego que, si esta propuesta se concreta dentro de un paquete integral que incluya garantías de seguridad, el derecho a un ejército ucranio fuerte y bien financiado, y fondos para la reconstrucción, la sometería a un referéndum nacional. “No tengo derecho a decidirlo yo solo. Necesito concreción, que aún falta, y todo esto se está debatiendo”, ha señalado.

Los enviados estadounidenses para el conflicto en Ucrania, Jared Kushner y Steve Witkoff, viajaron el jueves a Dublín, donde se celebraba una cumbre europea, para reunirse con Zelenski tras los contactos mantenidos el día anterior con el presidente ruso, Vladimir Putin.

Hasta ahora Washington había descartado el ingreso de Ucrania en la OTAN, mientras que Moscú exige neutralidad y límites a las fuerzas militares ucranias, además de la renuncia a territorios, como base para cualquier acuerdo.

Zelenski ha indicado además que los estadounidenses han trasladado a Kiev que Rusia quiere “otra estructura de seguridad diferente” para Europa. “Yo creo que puede ser peligroso (...) Creo que los americanos han planteado esto por influencia rusa”, ha argumentado. Y ha recordado que en 2021 Putin planteó a Joe Biden “la redistribución de fuerzas en Europa y en todo el mundo, debilitar o retirar tropas de la OTAN y la retirada de tropas estadounidenses”.

El mandatario ha corroborado luego los comentarios de los líderes europeos que participaron en la cumbre de Dublín el viernes y rechazado la petición de Rusia de alcanzar un acuerdo sobre ese diseño de la arquitectura de seguridad europea sin poner fin antes a la guerra en Ucrania.

“No podemos dar un vuelco a todo y empezar hablando de cambiar el marco de seguridad en el mundo o en todo el continente en general, y solo entonces poner fin a esta guerra. Primero hay que acabar con la guerra”, ha declarado Zelenski.

El presidente rechaza asimismo la sugerencia de Putin de un alto el fuego humanitario local en Kostiantynivka, una ciudad que ambos contendientes se disputan en la región oriental ucrania de Donetsk, en Ucrania. En opinión de Zelenski, los civiles de esa localidad ya han tenido la oportunidad de salir de ella, por lo que acusó a las fuerzas rusas de enmascarar su incapacidad de tomar la urbe militarmente lanzando la idea de un alto el fuego para así poder apoderarse de la ciudad.

“Putin simplemente quiere que abandonemos Kostiantynivka para que ellos puedan entrar y ocupar toda la ciudad de esa manera”, ha dicho.

“He trasladado mi postura a los negociadores americanos: la gente que hay allí son solo ciudadanos de Ucrania con armas y ciudadanos de Rusia, ocupantes, también con armas”, ha explicado Zelenski.

Ucrania ha facilitado una lista de otros siete u ocho asentamientos en primera línea del frente donde hay civiles, incluidos niños, atrapados, con vistas a una posible tregua humanitaria, pero, ha acusado Zelenski, Rusia prefiere utilizarlos como objetivos militares, una acusación que Moscú niega.

El presidente ucranio además ha puesto como ejemplo la tregua de Oleshki que permitió la evacuación de la población, pero también habilitó a Rusia para reforzar sus posiciones militares.

Por último, ha destacado que durante el mes de octubre Rusia tuvo 54.000 muertos y heridos graves en lo que supone el peor mes para el país desde que empezó la escalada bélica, hace ya casi cinco años.

Abu Dabi

La última ronda negociadora entre Rusia y Ucrania, bajo mediación de Estados Unidos, concluyó el miércoles en Abu Dabi sin ningún avance significativo, aunque las partes acordaron un intercambio de prisioneros que afectará a más de 1.000 personas, según afirmó Zelenski, que precisó que las cifras definitivas del intercambio de prisioneros aún se estaban negociando.

Los enviados estadounidenses Witkoff y Kushner se habían comprometido a plantear a Putin un alto el fuego para detener los ataques a infraestructura energética en su reunión en Moscú el jueves, según afirmó el presidente ucranio, pero tampoco sobre esa cuestión se han divulgado progresos.

Zelenski se reunió con Witkoff y Kushner el jueves en Irlanda tras sus conversaciones en Moscú. En Dublin afirmó que los negociadores estadounidenses le habían comunicado que todas las partes habían acordado que Europa tuviera un puesto en la mesa de negociaciones en las próximas conversaciones de paz.

En Abu Dabi, los representantes de Europa —que es ahora el mayor apoyo financiero y militar de Ucrania— mantuvieron conversaciones con funcionarios estadounidenses y ucranios, pero no se sentaron a la mesa con Rusia. En la cumbre de Irlanda, los líderes de la UE acordaron que el equipo europeo para cualquier ronda de negociaciones de paz sobre Ucrania estaría compuesto por cinco grandes potencias militares —el Reino Unido, que no es miembro de la UE, además de Francia, Alemania, Italia y Polonia— así como por altos funcionarios de la UE.

World.title: Jetten cabinet survives crisis talks for now, deadlock continues
World.content:
The Dutch cabinet’s crisis talks ended in deadlock on Friday after more than seven hours, and the coalition will survive for the time being, though talks will continue over the weekend.

Prime minister Rob Jetten met right-wing liberal VVD leader Dilan Yesilgöz and Christian Democrat CDA deputy prime minister Bart van den Brink on Friday morning, following Thursday night’s vote on the tax plan, which the VVD says broke the coalition agreement.

Yesilgöz, speaking at a press conference after the talks, said the political situation cannot continue as things stand. She described the current minority coalition as a “failed experiment” and said that a government collapse was a “possible solution”, while acknowledging no one wants to plunge the country into another election.

Jetten, who spoke before her, said that “things have not gone well recently, and that is affecting mutual relations”. “That can and must be better: substantively, politically, and personally.”

While the cabinet has not yet collapsed, VVD sources told the Telegraaf that no progress had been made and the impasse continues.

If the talks had ended on Friday, “it could have gone wrong”, Jetten said.

Health insurance companies are set to increase premiums in 2027, pushing up the cost of a basic package up by as much as €17 a month.

Companies were required to announce the cost of their premiums by midnight on Thursday and the cost will rise sharply across the board next year.

Insurer DSW, traditionally the first to publish its rates, announced in October that the price for its premium will go up by €14.75 a month.

The most popular basic insurance at Zilveren Kruis is rising by €5.70 euros to €164.95 euros, while at CZ the basic insurance will soon cost €177.25, an increase of more than €17 compared to last year.

Last year, premiums were able to remain virtually unchanged due to more money in the health insurance fund.

Health insurance companies attribute the rise to the aging population, which has more health care needs, as well as the increase in wages for healthcare employees and gas prices.

World.title: Two arrested for Prinsjesdag train sabotage
World.content:
Police have arrested two people in connection with the sabotage on the railway during Prinsjesdag, the public prosecution service (OM) announced on Friday.

A 49-year-old man and a 41-year-old woman from Drenthe were arrested on Thursday. According to the OM, the pair remain suspects but there was not enough evidence to keep them in custody.

Train services across the country were disrupted in September in what network operators described an act of coordinated sabotage. The attacks took place during Prinsjesdag, the state opening of parliament in The Hague and one of the biggest days in the Dutch political calendar.

Steel pipes were attached to the tracks at multiple locations across the country, disrupting rail service nationwide.

It is not yet known who was behind the attacks. On the same day, tractor tires, hay bales, and pallets were lit on fire at various locations. Some of those incidents were tied to farmer activists.

The Farmers Defence Force, responsible for recent motorway disruptions, said it was not responsible but that “wild actions” by individual farmers had been expected on budget day.

The two suspects are the first to be arrested in the case.

World.title: The Hague is the tile “whipping” champion
World.content:
No city has done more to whip their gardens into shape than The Hague, which took home the Golden Tile prize for removing the most paving stones from its gardens, totalling a record 507,000 citywide, breaking the previous record by nearly 50,000.

The NK Tegelwippen, or Dutch National Tile Removal Championship, pits councils against one another to see who can free up the most green space.

According to the organisation, this makes neighbourhoods more attractive, combats flood and rising temperatures and gives children more areas for play.

“It is fantastic that we are still breaking records. It shows that perseverance pays off and that residents consider greenery in the city increasingly important,” Joris Wijsmuller, the director of Duurzaam Den Haag, said in a statement.

Some 150,000 tiles were taken out by residents, schools, sports clubs, and companies participated in the event, according to the council. The remainder were removed by the city in public spaces.

The Hague also won the title in 2021 and 2022.

World.title: Three’s a crowd: Will Jetten’s tax bill kill the cabinet?
World.content:
There is an old medical joke about a surgeon who declares: “The operation was a complete success, but the patient died.”

After months of chaotic, gruelling negotiations, Rob Jetten achieved a majority in parliament for his tax bill on Thursday night, but his coalition is in tatters. The right-wing liberal VVD were so incensed by the deal the other two partners, Jetten’s D66 and the Christian Democrats (CDA), struck with the left-wing Pro that they voted against the entire plan, which had been extensively drafted and redrafted by the VVD finance minister, Eelco Heinen.

The party’s leader, Dilan Yesilgöz, denounced it as “a bad deal for the Netherlands” and demanded a “fundamental reset” of the centre-right coalition. Essentially, she wanted the prime minister to switch his cabinet off and switch it on again.

The millionaires’ tax knife twist

Strikingly, the amendment that D66, CDA and Pro agreed on Wednesday afternoon was a milder version of one that the VVD had seemed willing to tolerate earlier in the week. Pro wanted to raise an extra €1.5 billion in wealth taxes in order to pay for an income tax cut for the lowest earners. D66 and CDA had negotiated the amount down to €1 billion and built in counterbalancing measures to protect people with modest savings – at an earlier stage one of the key concerns for the VVD. Its impact, even on the private investors it was aimed at, was marginal.

But none of that mattered. For the VVD, the deal was unacceptable because it crossed a red line – raising taxes on successful, hard-working entrepreneurs – and it was drawn up behind their backs between their coalition partners and Pro.

Jesse Klaver, the leader of Pro, then twisted the knife by describing the measure as a “millionaires’ tax”, a phrase that went down like cold gravel in the throats of not just the VVD, but CDA leader Henri Bontenbal.

The seeds of the crisis were sown around 10 days earlier, as a reconstruction in AD.nl has found, when the coalition parties agreed to enter what commentators immediately called an “open marriage”. After months of abortive attempts to strike a collective deal with a divided opposition that balanced the interests of left and right, the three parties would try to form separate majorities for their own priorities. It would allow D66 and CDA to pair up with Pro and Volt while the VVD could court the right-wing opposition block of JA21, the farmers’ party BBB and the orthodox Protestant SGP. As a last resort, they could even vote on opposite sides when the amendments were tabled in parliament, if it meant that the tax bill and the coalition survived.

Unagreed terms

The problem was, none of the parties had agreed on the terms of the open marriage. And what the VVD hadn’t reckoned with was that D66 and CDA would go all the way with Pro and produce an amendment that seemed calculated to hurt them. D66 and CDA protested that they had kept their partners informed throughout the negotiations and even invited them to the table. But the VVD’s whole reason for joining the coalition in the first place was to keep the left-wing Pro out of power, as D66 and CDA knew all too well.

For Yesilgöz, the amendment represented the very outcome that she had entered the partnership to avoid, and Klaver’s press conference and Instagram reel to celebrate the millionaires’ tax were simply rubbing salt into the wound. To extend the analogy, it was like agreeing to an arranged marriage only to see your partner immediately phone up the ex-girlfriend he told you was no threat and take her for dinner at the Ritz.

None of this should obscure the extent to which the VVD engineered their own downfall. The minority cabinet was built on unstable foundations because the VVD wanted to shut out the opposition party that would have the strongest hand in the upcoming negotiations. When the coalition agreement was published, they took out billboards to parade their achievements, such as retaining mortgage interest tax relief.

The final betrayal

From the outset the VVD have focused more on defending their red lines within the coalition than finding the opposition votes they need to pass their legislation. It allowed Pro to exploit the deadlock to torpedo key VVD policies such as the €6.5 billion of welfare cuts. The budget amendment was the final betrayal for the VVD, but it was also the inevitable outcome of a process in which the party had refused to build any kind of constructive relationship with Pro, while D66 and CDA had reached out to unlikely partners such as Gidi Markuszower’s far-right DNA. And when the VVD decided to reject its own budget deal, its partners delivered a final humiliation by salvaging it with the support of a pair of fringe parties on the left: Denk and the animal rights party PvdD.

What happens next is unclear. The VVD, stung by what they see as a deep betrayal, want the coalition to renew its vows. Jetten prefers to talk about a “restart”, the language usually used for businesses that have called in the receivers. Yesilgöz almost goaded the other parties to try their luck with Pro in a new combination, but that would leave the cabinet still nine votes short of a majority and a hostile opposition dominated by the right. Jesse Klaver may well have overplayed his hand with his “pick me” posts on social media.

But new elections are an equally risky option for three parties whose standing in the opinion polls has been further damaged by the tax plan saga. And if the coalition survives in its current form, it will be as a marriage of inconvenience. Not for the first time, politics and matrimony have turned out to be a toxic mix.

Nine people have been arrested in Rotterdam as part of a major drug dealing investigation, according to regional broadcaster RTV Rijnmond.

Raids were carried out on Monday and led to the seizure of cars, cash and drugs.

Eight of the men are Rotterdam residents and one is from The Hague; they are being charged with membership of a criminal drugs organisation and three are are also suspected of money laundering.

What types of drugs were involved has not been disclosed. All suspects are between 27 and 40 years old, and police have reportedly not ruled out further arrests.

World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

A novel about a Dutchman living in Austria during the interwar period has been awarded the 2026 NS Public Prize.

Narcis by Judith Fanto follows Manno, who moves from Haarlem to Vienna following the death of his mother and finds a circle of friends, bonds that are tested as Hitler rises to power.

Fanto described the honour as “wonderful” during a ceremony on Thursday evening. “This appreciation from the readers is the exuberant culmination of years of work in silence,” she said.

She takes home €7,500 and a sculpture in recognition.

The award, now in its 25th edition, is a collaboration between the Foundation for Collective Promotion of the Dutch Book and Dutch railway operator NS.

More than 131,000 readers cast their votes and Narcis beat five other works, including The Superfluous by Herman Koch.

World.title: Polish president vetoes law on removing harmful online content, warning of “censorship”
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki has vetoed a government bill creating new powers to block harmful online content. Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, argued that the measures were too far-reaching and could be abused to introduce “censorship”. Government figures have strongly criticised the president’s decision, arguing that it will leave young people in particular more exposed to dangerous content. It also means that Poland still has not fully implemented the European Union’s Digital Services Act (DSA). ❌ Nie dla cenzury Internetu! pic.twitter.com/WusnK7LImD — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) November 13, 2026 Previously, in January this year, Nawrocki had vetoed an earlier bill intended to implement the DSA, describing the measures as “Owellian”. That prompted the government to split the legislation in two. In September, Nawrocki agreed to sign one of those bills, which appointed the president of the Office of Electronic Communications (UKE) as Poland’s digital services coordinator, responsible for overseeing enforcement of the DSA. A second bill was then needed to introduce the actual powers to block harmful online content. It was approved by the government’s majority in parliament in October, with the right-wing and far-right opposition either voting against it or abstaining. Among the new powers included in the legislation were authorisation for the heads of UKE and the National Broadcasting Council (KRRiT) to order the blocking of online content containing violence or threats based on race, nationality, ethnicity, religion or political affiliation. It also allowed the immediate blocking, at the request of a prosecutor or the police, of content involving the acceptance of a contract to commit murder or inciting or assisting in suicide or self-harm. “Perpetrators of serious crimes should not be allowed to use the internet to spread violence and threats,” said digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski. “The state must have effective tools to quickly respond to such threats. The safety of internet users must transcend political divisions.” The government also argued that last month’s series of stabbings in schools and this month’s deadly terrorist attack in Kraków – which have raised concern about the online radicalisation of young people – have emphasised the importance of tough controls over digital content. There are "strong traces of right-wing extremism" in the activity of the man who carried out the mass shooting in Kraków, says Poland's justice minister. His search history included websites relating to Anders Breivik, the Norwegian far-right terrorist https://t.co/UhVbkWSaCq — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 10, 2026 However, on Friday, the final day by which the president had to make a decision on the bill, Nawrocki announced that he was vetoing it. He argued that “the government has clearly mixed up European obligations with its own political interests”. The measures in the bill threaten to create a “censorship official” and “essentially give the government arbitrary control and the ability to decide what we can and cannot say, write or publish, said the president. Decisions on whether content is permitted or not should be “the exclusive competence of the justice system and independent judges”, he argued. Nawrocki also said that the powers in the vetoed bill were “disproportionate”, allowing an entire domain to be blocked due to a single example of illegal content. “The security of citizens cannot be a pretext for weakening their freedoms,” said Nawrocki. “We must not create a false choice: either the security or the freedom of its citizens. A responsible state must ensure and balance both.” Dlaczego Prezydent RP Karol Nawrocki zawetował ustawę o DSA? ⬇️ pic.twitter.com/1BUJVFEftl — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) November 13, 2026 Deputy digital affairs minister Dariusz Standerski, however, said that the president was “not defending free speech” but instead “once again siding with global [digital] platforms and allowing them to decide what users see”. “The vetoed provisions concerned illegal content, not opinions or views expressed online,” added the ministry, which also noted that all decisions on blocking content were subject to appeals and judicial review. Prime Minister Donald Tusk, meanwhile, accused Nawrocki of “waging war on the government at the expense of Polish children and Polish security”, which would both be threatened by the absence of the vetoed measures. Ochrona dzieci przed internetowymi przestępcami. Trudno wyobrazić sobie ważniejszą sprawę, która powinna łączyć ponad politycznymi podziałami. A jednak zawetował. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) November 13, 2026 Aleksandra Wójtowicz, an analyst on new technologies at the Polish Institute of International Affairs (PISM), told the Fakt newspaper that the measures do “not in any way relate to alleged censorship”. They are intended to force digital platforms to remove illegal content, she explained. Wójtowicz added that the measures would actually have protected free speech by giving Polish users whose accounts were unjustly deleted by social media platforms the right to appeal against those decisions outside of the platform itself. However, Nawrocki’s veto was praised by Przemysław Czarnek, deputy leader of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s largest opposition party. Czarnek told TV Trwam that the proposed measures had been intended to “fight the opposition” rather than actual hate speech. A new hub has opened at the University of Oxford to support research cooperation with Poland, offering grants for academic projects, visits, training and workshops. The Oxford Poland Hub, which its organisers describe as Poland’s first initiative of its kind anywhere in the world, will also hold public events exploring Polish history, language and culture. We’re proud to have worked on the Oxford-Poland Hub & helped make it a reality together with great partners 🇵🇱🇬🇧 Huge thanks to: 🔹 @UniofOxford & @JesusOxford, esp. Prof Paulina Kewes & Dr Marek Naczyk 🔹 Ministry of Science and Higher Education & Minister @MarcinKulasek 🧵 pic.twitter.com/LghfpOhptC — Polish Embassy UK 🇵🇱 (@PolishEmbassyUK) November 12, 2026 “The launch of the Oxford-Poland Hub is an exciting new chapter in Oxford’s longstanding relationship with Poland,” said the University of Oxford’s vice-chancellor, Irene Tracey. “[It] will create new opportunities for academic exchange, collaborative research and partnership between Oxford and Poland.” The centre is initially funded for three years by Poland’s National Agency for Academic Exchange (NAWA), with support from the science and higher education ministry. It will operate within The Oxford Research Centre in the Humanities (TORCH). “The Oxford Poland Hub…gives us a permanent institutional presence at one of the world’s leading academic centres,” said Wojciech Karczewski, NAWA’s director general. “We see it as an investment in long-term partnerships that will enable researchers from Poland and Oxford to tackle increasingly ambitious research challenges together.” The University of Oxford is the oldest university in the English-speaking world and one of the most prestigious. It ranked first globally in the latest Times Higher Education World University Rankings. The new centre will offer grants of up to £5,000 (26,400 zloty) to support research projects or academic visits and up to £10,000 for academic workshops. Training scholarships are due to be introduced from the hub’s second year. All researchers affiliated with the University of Oxford will be eligible to apply for funding if their work involves collaboration with researchers based in Poland. The hub will focus on humanities and social sciences as well as cooperation with Oxford’s libraries and museums. The hub will also organise public lectures, exhibitions and events related to Polish history, language and culture for the academic community and Oxford’s residents, including its Polish community. 🇵🇱🇬🇧 Oxford-Poland Hub oficjalnie otwarty! Polska nauka zyskuje nowe możliwości współpracy z Uniwersytetem Oksfordzkim. W uroczystym otwarciu wziął udział minister nauki i szkolnictwa wyższego Marcin Kulasek. Centrum powstało dzięki współpracy Ministerstwa Nauki i Szkolnictwa… pic.twitter.com/bZaCdM3Y53 — Ministerstwo Nauki i Szkolnictwa Wyższego (@MNiSW_GOV__PL) November 10, 2026 The hub was inaugurated on Monday at Jesus College, one of Oxford University’s colleges, with Poland’s science and higher education minister, Marcin Kulasek, and Rafał Wiśniewski, chargé d’affaires at the Polish Embassy in London, among those attending. “Poland and the United Kingdom have for many years developed strong cooperation in science and higher education through joint research projects, academic mobility programmes and institutional partnerships,” Kulasek said. “The Oxford–Poland Hub opens a new chapter in this cooperation.” The centre is directed by Paulina Kewes, a professor of English literature at Oxford who was born in Poland. Professor Norman Davies, the renowned historian of Poland and an honorary fellow at St Antony’s College, Oxford, attended the launch. The inaugural lecture, given by Dariusz Wójcik, a professor at the National University of Singapore and honorary research associate at the University of Oxford, discussed Maria Czaplicka, the renowned Polish academic who in 1916 became Oxford’s first female lecturer of anthropology. World.title: Belgian court overturns seizure of Polish air-traffic agency’s funds in Pfizer legal battle
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A Belgian court has overturned an order to seize funds from Poland’s air-traffic control agency, PANSA, as part of pharmaceutical giant Pfizer’s efforts to enforce a €1.3 billion claim for COVID-19 vaccines Poland ordered but later refused to receive and pay for. The ruling, issued on Thursday, followed a legal challenge by PANSA to the freezing of its funds. It argued that it was not a party to the dispute between Pfizer and the Polish state. ❗️Dziś Francuskojęzyczny Sąd Pierwszej Instancji w Brukseli wydał korzystny dla strony polskiej wyrok w sprawie zajęcia opłat trasowych należnych @PANSA_PL , pobieranych za pośrednictwem EUROCONTROL. Sąd uznał zajęcie za bezzasadne i uchylił postanowienie, na podstawie którego… pic.twitter.com/EHvHZnL6ab — Ministerstwo Zdrowia (@MZ_GOV_PL) November 12, 2026 In July this year, PANSA announced that it had been cut off from the fees paid to it by the European Organisation for the Safety of Air Navigation (Eurocontrol), which manages air traffic in Europe. Around 80% of PANSA’s revenue comes from those fees. Eurocontrol is based in Belgium, which is where Pfizer has been fighting its legal battle against Poland over the unpaid vaccines. The move to freeze PANSA’s funds was part of Pfizer’s efforts to claim money it had been awarded from Poland by a Belgian court in April this year. Prime Minister Donald Tusk pledged government support to ensure PANSA had sufficient funds to maintain its operations and assured that air safety would not be compromised. Poland’s air-traffic control agency has been cut off from most of its revenue as part of efforts by pharmaceutical giant Pfizer to enforce a Belgian court ruling requiring Poland to pay €1.3bn for Covid vaccines it ordered but then refused to receive https://t.co/Nd9IyLqmmf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 11, 2026 On Thursday this week, PANSA announced that its legal challenge to the seizure of its assets by bailiffs had been successful, though it noted that the ruling can still be appealed. Poland’s health ministry, which has been involved in overseeing the legal battle with Pfizer, said that the Belgian court had confirmed that PANSA’s funds belong to the agency itself, not to the State treasury. “The agency is a separate legal entity; it possesses its own assets and manages its own finances independently. It is not liable for the obligations of the State treasury; therefore, its funds cannot be used to satisfy Pfizer’s claims against Poland,” wrote the ministry. In comments to Polish Radio, PANSA chief Magdalena Jaworska-Maćkowiak said the agency had become a hostage in a case “that did not, in fact, concern us”. “It stemmed from an entirely separate dispute,” she noted. “This created extreme difficulties, as we were relying on a ‘bridge’ financing arrangement that, under current law, could not provide us with long-term stability.” Pfizer, meanwhile, said Thursday’s court decision affected only one avenue of its efforts to enforce payment of the April ruling. “We are taking ​appropriate steps through ​established legal ⁠and contractual mechanisms to ensure compliance with the court’s [April] decision,” it added, quoted by Reuters. Sąd w Brukseli uznał sprzeciw PAŻP wobec zajęcia komorniczego dokonanego na wniosek Pfizer za zasadny i uchylił postanowienie z 25 czerwca 2026 r., stanowiące podstawę zajęcia komorniczego. Rozstrzygnięcie jest zatem korzystne dla PAŻP, ale wyrok nie jest jeszcze prawomocny. — PANSA (@PANSA_PL) November 12, 2026 The dispute stems from Poland’s refusal in 2022 to accept and pay for COVID-19 vaccine doses ordered from Pfizer under European Union procurement agreements. In April 2022, the then health minister, Adam Niedzielski, invoked a force majeure clause following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 Poland, which by then had already sold or donated some of its surplus vaccines, argued the mass influx of Ukrainian refugees strained its public finances, while its cases of Covid infections had dropped. Romania later made a similar decision to not comply with the contract. In 2023, Pfizer sued both countries in Belgium, the country where the contracts were signed. Over the course of the case, Poland also argued that Pfizer had potentially abused its market position. A Belgian court has ordered Poland to pay US pharmaceutical giant Pfizer around €1.3 billion for Covid vaccines ordered by the European Commission on behalf of member states during the pandemic but which the Polish government later refused to receive https://t.co/1ZtPgl8Y3o — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 2, 2026 But in April, a Belgian court rejected those arguments and ruled in Pfizer’s favour, ordering Poland to accept approximately 64 million vaccine doses and pay more than 5.6 billion zloty, plus interest and legal costs. Poland appealed against the judgment in August 2026. The health ministry said on Thursday it would not disclose details of its legal arguments or planned procedural steps while the proceedings remain ongoing. World.title: Temporary no longer: Ukrainian refugees in Poland confront the long term
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Leo Greenberg Speaking to Fox News in late October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky admitted a widely known but uncomfortable truth: Ukraine needs its refugees back. “We need 9.5 million people – who lost their homes, who are abroad, everywhere – we need them to come back to Ukraine…to rebuild their country,” he said. Zelensky: We need 9.5 million people who lost their housing, who are abroad everywhere — we need them to come back to Ukraine, just to live and to build their country. pic.twitter.com/Xu2Ld4eGOu — Clash Report (@clashreport) October 21, 2026 Unfortunately for Ukraine, all signs point in the opposite direction: Ukrainians abroad are deferring or abandoning thoughts of return. A large proportion of those refugees – almost one million of them – live in Poland, where Ukrainians, including migrants who arrived before 2022, have provided an economic and demographic boon. But their continued stay has also posed social and political challenges, as a country with no history of mass immigration grapples with the new reality of a sizable non-citizen minority. This has left the refugees themselves in a state of limbo: torn between a homeland that wants them back, and to which many would like to return, but where conditions do not allow for it; and an adopted home where they have created new lives but where social tensions and logistical hurdles have meant persistent uncertainty. A new reality sets in When Solomiia Pischana, a Ukrainian woman in her late twenties, fled from Kyiv to Poland in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, she hoped to go back that same year. When Kyiv was secured by Ukrainian forces, a return seemed possible. In late 2022, Pischana started travelling back home to see family and friends. “I was really living between two countries. I thought a lot about going back.” Yet quickly, a new reality set in on her visits: “In winter it became basically impossible to stay there – the constant explosions.” In Poland, by contrast, “everyone put the emphasis on helping me, on helping Ukrainians.” In a photo essay, we look at the lives of three of the million or so Ukrainian refugees who remain in Poland one year on from Russia's invasion: Liudmyla, a mother; Vlad, an amputee soldier; and Viktoria, a high-school student https://t.co/kdOpEgt2LB — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 21, 2023 For many Ukrainians, Pischana’s story will feel familiar. When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Poland became the main waystation for Ukrainians on their way out. Millions crossed the border, and while many went on to other destinations in Europe and beyond, initially more than one million remained in Poland. The Polish state reacted quickly, assigning more than a million special identification numbers for Ukrainian refugees – known as “PESEL-UKR” – and enrolling them in the same housing and benefits systems used by Polish citizens. So too did Polish society, with a majority of Poles working in some way to assist Ukraine or arriving refugees, and many hosting refugees in their homes. Around 77% of Poles have been involved in helping refugees from Ukraine, for which purpose they spent around €2 billion out of their own pockets, a new study by @PIE_NET_PL has found https://t.co/xWu8JWNMui — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 28, 2022 For Ukraine, the exodus of around six million refugees meant a raft of problems. Some 650,000 military-age men left the country, while schools had to figure out how to provide remote instruction for two million children abroad. Most of all, the refugee crisis worsened Ukraine’s demographic challenges. Before 2022, Ukraine’s population of 42 million had already been shrinking and ageing. Now, Ukraine’s minister for social policy estimates that just 22-25 million people remain in Ukrainian-controlled territory. Two thirds of Ukrainian businesses are short of workers. Initially, many hoped for a brief war. But, as the reality of a long, grinding conflict dawned, it became clear that Ukraine could no longer plan for an imminent influx of able-bodied adults: surveys by Kyiv’s Centre for Economic Strategies show that the proportion of refugees intending to return dropped from 74% in November 2022 to 43% in January 2026. “Rather chaotic” attempts to connect with refugees This reality has meant that, while Ukraine needs its people back, it also knows that it cannot compel people to return to a life defined by rolling blackouts and the ever-present threat of drones and ballistic missiles. As a result, Ukraine’s efforts to encourage and support refugee return have been haphazard and limited. Ukraine has one deputy minister, Ilona Havronska, who is armed with just 150 million hryvnia (13.1 million zloty, €3 million) in this year’s state budget to maintain connections with refugees abroad and support their return. Havronska has sought to create a network of “Unity Hubs,” paid for by foreign governments, where Ukrainian refugees can confer with trained consultants about returning home. Such facilities have opened in Stockholm, Prague and Berlin, with the latter receiving 5,000 visits since opening in May. ⚡️Ukraine, Germany agree to open 'Unity Hub' for Ukrainian refugees in Berlin. "This is a professional space that brings together community, business, and cultural initiatives," National Unity Minister Oleksii Chernyshov said.https://t.co/rlTq3MpOd0 — The Kyiv Independent (@KyivIndependent) February 15, 2025 So far, however, no hub has opened in Poland, whose interior ministry told Notes from Poland: “To be frank, the Ukrainian side, Minister Havronska, they haven’t approached us much about this recently.” Ukraine’s other major effort, a digital platform called “Dodomu” (“Homeward”), allows users to make a return plan and check off items on a digital to-do list, such as transferring medical files, verifying IDs, and registering children in Ukrainian schools. Since launching in June, Dodomu has been used by 4,500 people in Poland, of whom 600 have completed a questionnaire about their possibility of return. Ukraine’s efforts to reach out to refugees abroad have been “rather chaotic”, according to Olena Babakova, a Polish-Ukrainian journalist and researcher who studies migration. However, a survey by the UNHCR suggests that it may not make much difference: Ukrainian refugees ranked “support for return” as less important to their decision-making than security, economic opportunities, and housing in Ukraine. Nevertheless, for older refugees and those from now-occupied territories in eastern Ukraine, large numbers cited additional information as one of their key needs. Valentina Bryl, a Ukrainian who has lived in Poland since before 2022 and is now an HR specialist in Wrocław, notes that returning to Ukraine would mean she would have to “start everything from the beginning – my job, my life. It’s not just about safety.” So while Bryl says that she visits Ukraine often – taking the 25-hour rail journey from Wrocław to Kharkiv to see her husband, who is serving at the front – she hasn’t made use of Dodomu or thought about the Unity Hubs. She has no intention of moving back. From welcome to wariness in Poland Yet for the million or so Ukrainian refugees in Poland, as well as the hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian economic migrants who came before 2022, a growing consideration is not only the conditions in Ukraine, but also the environment they face in their adopted homeland. Poland welcomed refugees in 2022 and has supported them since. It has also benefited economically from their presence, with Ukrainian refugees estimated to have raised national GDP by 2.4% in 2025. Ukrainian refugees boosted Poland’s GDP by 2.4% in 2025, the equivalent of €21.5bn, according to a report by the UN @Refugees agency and @Deloitte At the same time, their growing presence in the labour market had no negative impact on employment or wages https://t.co/lcsuIwBzpy — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 8, 2026 However, there have been growing social and political tensions. During the 2025 presidential election, even liberal candidates proposed restricting child benefits for Ukrainian refugees. The eventual winner, right-wing candidate Karol Nawrocki, in one of his first acts as president, vetoed an extension of Ukrainians’ temporary protections, before signing a revised extension that restricted benefits. Those political changes reflect shifting attitudes in society. A June 2026 report from the Institute of Political Critique (IKP) described last year’s election campaign as a “Rubicon”, citing testimony from Ukrainian refugees that the public environment had become more hostile and historical issues had surfaced. Pischana told Notes from Poland that, while she is “surrounded by good people” in Poland, she has noticed that “old topics like the Volhynia massacre are coming up much more”, referring to the mass slaughter of Poles by Ukrainian nationalists in World War Two. “Just walking down the street and speaking Ukrainian, it’s started to feel a bit more dangerous,” she added. Police data show that the number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland was 30% higher in the first half of this year than in the same period of 2025. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show. The figures come following recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are Poland's largest immigrant group https://t.co/pcTsJddDz7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 Myroslava Keryk, who leads Ukraiński Dom, a hub that provides services to Ukrainian refugees in Warsaw, told Notes from Poland that her staff have faced growing harassment. She described a slew of AI-generated videos depicting them demanding Poles pay greater taxes to support refugees, as well as sexualised, fake accounts made of her employees on online apps. Poland’s government has condemned the recent spate of hate crimes and accused the opposition and Nawrocki of stirring up such social vitriol. Meanwhile, it has begun preparing for Ukrainian refugees’ longer-term stay. Ukrainian refugees’ current PESEL-UKR status is tied to the EU’s temporary protections, now set to expire in March 2028. So this year, the government introduced a new “CUKR” status, valid for three years of residence after it is granted. Some 75,000 Ukrainians have already submitted applications. President Nawrocki has signed into law a government bill ending the special status granted in 2022 to Ukrainian refugees, who will now be treated on the same legal basis as other foreigners. Nawrocki said he is "ending the era of unconditional privileges" https://t.co/BzY7wrdl49 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 20, 2026 This new status, however, is only a step on the path to long-term stability. CUKR, unlike most refugees’ current “UKR” status, counts toward the five years of legal stay required to apply for long-term EU resident status. However, its three-year duration means holders need to secure two additional years of legal protection in Poland before applying for long-term residency. Polish state policies have not always made things easy for refugees. New restrictions on benefits and on travel outside of Poland have made refugees careful. Despite that, many appreciated the legal and logistical clarity of Poland’s approach, typified by the new CUKR status. Refugees’ primary fears have concerned their social environment, not their legal status. Babakova put it neatly: “Ukrainians in Poland feel very connected to Ukrainian society, but not the state. At the same time, they have come to trust the Polish state, but not Polish society.” The citizenship question At the same time, a growing number of Ukrainians are thinking of obtaining citizenship, which would allow them to travel more freely and vote in Polish elections. An August survey of Ukrainian refugees in Poland found that a plurality (35%) listed obtaining citizenship as the “most desired form of assistance” to make their lives easier. In 2025, a record 19,000 foreigners, more than half of whom (10,000) were Ukrainian, were granted citizenship in Poland. Poland granted citizenship to a record 19,135 foreigners in 2025, up 17% from the previous year and almost five times higher than a decade ago. Over half of recipients were Ukrainians, followed by Belarusians, Russians, Vietnamese and Turks https://t.co/FoyWd5UPJx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 15, 2026 But since then, Poland has moved to restrict access to citizenship – to make it “an earned privilege, not a formal certificate”, in the words of the interior ministry. The plans include extending the required period of legal residence from five to eight years, requiring a loyalty declaration, mandating advanced knowledge of Polish, and introducing an exam on Polish history and values. Pischana wants to become a Polish citizen: “I’ve thought that it would be logical […] I’ve lived for years in Poland. I know the language.” She added that her university thesis focuses on Polish history: she’s writing a comparison of Ukrainian and Polish songs with political or social themes, from the 1980s to the present day. Kamil Kisiel, deputy director for the department of internal affairs and migration at Poland’s interior ministry, told Notes from Poland that the new citizenship laws, soon to be announced, will be tough: “For now, being more restrictive is the way to go, so that we can manage people’s expectations”. The proportion of Poles who hold a negative view of relations with Ukraine has risen to the highest level ever recorded by state research agency CBOS Meanwhile, the proportion who believe reconciliation with Ukraine is possible is at its lowest ever level https://t.co/YYBCFkVxNr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026 Kisiel was also up front that the Polish government does not envision many Ukrainians in Poland becoming citizens. No more than a few tens of thousands of Ukrainians have obtained Polish citizenship in the past decade, and those who arrived in 2022 are not yet eligible to apply. Instead, Kisiel highlighted, “long-term EU residence is…the sort of stability people should expect”. Karina, a Ukrainian woman who has been in Poland since she was 15 and did not want her surname published, says that she wants Polish citizenship as it offers “a chance to travel around the European Union, go to Spain. You can also go to America, because a Polish passport gives you visa-free travel; unfortunately, with a Ukrainian one you can’t.” Head in Poland, heart in Ukraine Barring a major change in the course of the war, Ukraine may even become one of the countries, including Ireland and Armenia, whose diasporas are as large or larger than their domestic population – a scenario that Havronska, the Ukrainian deputy minister, told Notes from Poland she is planning for. At the same time, social tensions and citizenship restrictions in Poland reflect the fact that refugees are challenging Poland’s identity: since the eradication and movement of Jews, Ukrainians and Germans during and after World War Two, Poland has been a largely monoethnic nation, accustomed to one language, one faith, and one national identity. The approximately 1.5 million Ukrainians in Poland have changed that. For Pischana, her head is in Poland while her heart remains in Ukraine, saying that she feels more attached to the culture of her homeland. “It’s a pity I can’t develop in my own country, because there’s room to do it there,” she says. For Bryl, it’s been harder to keep close to Ukraine: “I have work, I have other responsibilities…You no longer want to read, you don’t want to get angry at some bad news”. At the beginning, she said, she felt she had a fully Ukrainian life – just one that was put on pause. But, she adds, “when it’s already been going on for five years, and it’s still unknown how long it’ll go on, well, it’s hard to keep it on pause.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland dismisses Russia’s claim of breaking up Polish spy network as “disinformation”
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. After Russia announced that it had dismantled a Polish spy network and arrested two alleged agents, Poland has dismissed the claims as “disinformation” and a “provocation”. On Wednesday, while Poland was celebrating its national Independence Day, Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) announced that it had “disrupted the activities of an intelligence network of the Polish special services operating in Kaliningrad”, a Russian exclave that borders Poland. It claimed to have detained two “agents”- one working for Poland’s Military Intelligence Service (SWW), the other for the Internal Security Agency (ABW) – who had been “collecting and transmitting information about military personnel and facilities” and “the socio-economic situation in the Kaliningrad region”. The FSB added that seven Polish citizens and three Russians who had had contact with Polish intelligence agencies had been “officially warned”, and that the Polish citizens had been banned from entering Russia. The agency also published a film containing images of alleged suspects being detained and various documents and telephone messages in Polish. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the arrests would not further worsen relations with Poland given ties between the two countries “essentially do not exist right now,” reported the RIA news agency. In a statement on Wednesday morning, Jacek Dobrzyński, the spokesman for Poland’s security services, said that he regarded the Russian announcement “as yet another provocation and act of disinformation”, especially as it had been released on Polish Independence Day. He added that he would not comment further and “appealed to everyone not to amplify hostile narratives or play into Russian propaganda”. Speaking to news website Wirtualna Polska, Maciej Wewiór, the spokesman for Poland’s foreign ministry, said that Poland was working to verify the information announced by the FSB. However, he urged “extreme caution” when dealing with such claims from Russia. “Let’s not fall for Russian propaganda and become pawns in this game,” he said. Jako rzecznik ministra koordynatora służb specjalnych nie komentuję materiałów zamieszczanych w sieci przez rosyjskie służby. 🛑 W dniu Narodowego Święta Niepodległości traktuję je szczególnie jako kolejną prowokację i dezinformację. 🛑 Apeluję o niepowielanie wrogiej narracji i… — Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) November 11, 2026 Polish fact-checking and investigative journalism service OKO.press also raised doubts about the material shared by Russia. It notes that the alleged Polish-language phone messages released by the FSB have unnatural wording and appear to have been translated from Russian. It also points out that the footage showing the alleged detentions appears to have been recorded much earlier, judging by the green folliage on trees. This assessment was echoed by Stanisław Żaryn, who served as spokesman for the security services from 2016 to 2022. He said that “fabricated propaganda materials” were clearly “prepared in advance” and “fit the Russian security services’ ongoing campaign against Poland”. “It should be assumed that, in its operation against Poland, Moscow will resort to fabricated evidence, and today’s FSB statement will be used to legitimise earlier accusations against Poland of preparing an attack on Kaliningrad,” he added. #InfoAlert. Kolejna rosyjska prowokacja. FSB twierdzi, że rozbiła polską siatkę szpiegowską pracującą w Obwodzie Królewieckim. Analiza komunikacji rosyjskiej wskazuje, że mamy do czynienia z zaplanowaną sekwencją działań informacyjnych. Wpisuje się ona w stałe oddziaływanie… pic.twitter.com/s6bTV9pIK8 — Stanisław Żaryn (@StZaryn) November 11, 2026 The FSB’s announcement came a week after Poland announced that it had detained and charged six people – five Poles and one Russian – suspected of running an operation to illegally supply Russia with military components, which were smuggled over the border into Kaliningrad. Poland also sent additional security personnel to its regions along the Russian border this month following intelligence reports suggesting a planned act of sabotage or other provocation there. Prime Minister Donald Tusk later claimed that “individuals with flashlights” had been spotted at the border but “we very quickly mobilised the appropriate forces and managed to prevent a provocation”. Poland recently launched a special operation along the Russian border after receiving information that acts of sabotage may take place there in the coming days. For more, see our report from yesterday:https://t.co/RVaXb6SQJI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 3, 2026 Poland has seen a sharp rise in cases of espionage and sabotage carried out on behalf of Moscow in recent years. The ABW launched 48 investigations related to espionage last year, more than twice as many as in 2024. In those two years taken together, there were more espionage investigations than over the previous three decades combined. Earlier this year, the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism published a report identifying Poland as the “primary focus” of Russia’s campaign of sabotage in Europe. In response, Poland has successively closed down all of Russia’s consulates on its territory, prompting Russia to do the same with Polish consulates in a tit-for-tat move. World.title: Poland indicts Ukrainian man for assisting in rail sabotage on behalf of Russia

Polish prosecutors have filed an indictment against a Ukrainian man accused of working on behalf of Russian intelligence and assisting in last year’s sabotage of a rail line in Poland. The accused, who can be named only as Volodymyr B. under Polish privacy law and is pictured above, will stand trial for espionage, sabotage and causing the risk of a major transport accident. He could face up to life in prison if convicted. Prokurator z mazowieckiego wydziału PZ PK skierował do Sądu Okręgowego w Warszawie akt oskarżenia przeciwko Volodymyrowi B. w śledztwie dotyczącym aktów dywersji na torach kolejowych, do których doszło jesienią 2025 r. w miejscowości Mika i Gołąb. ⬇️https://t.co/N2vK7thpKe — Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) November 12, 2026 In November last year, the Polish authorities discovered acts of sabotage on two sections of a rail line running between Warsaw and the eastern Polish city of Lublin. In one case, a device containing military-grade C4 explosive was detonated in an apparent attempt to derail a freight train near the village of Mika. However, it caused only minor damage to the floor of the train. The following day, in the nearby town of Puławy, a passenger train carrying 475 people had to brake suddenly due to damage to the line. However, no one was injured. Soon after, Prime Minister Donald Tusk announced that the perpetrators had been identified as two Ukrainian citizens working on behalf of Russia. They had entered Poland from Belarus and then fled back across the border immediately after the incident. In December, Interpol issued red notices for the men, identified as Yevhenii Ivanov and Oleksandr Kononov. However, the pair remain at large. Meanwhile, a third Ukrainian man, Volodymyr B., was detained in Poland a few days after the sabotage and was charged with assisting in carrying out the attack. In their statement regarding the indictment of Volodymyr B., published on Thursday, the National Prosecutor’s Office says that he assisted Yevhenii Ivanov in conducting reconnaissance of the area, selecting a place to plant the explosives and installing recording devices and metal elements on the rails. “These actions created an imminent threat of a disaster, threatening the lives and health of many people and significant property damage,” wrote prosecutors. “Their goal was to seriously intimidate many people and influence public opinion.” They also say that Volodymyr B. was “participating in the activities of Russian intelligence”. The most serious charge he faces is for acts of sabotage on behalf of foreign intelligence, a crime that carries a minimum prison sentence of ten years, ranging up to life. Interpol has published red notices for two men that Poland says were responsible for carrying out the sabotage of a rail line last month on behalf of Russia The pair immediately fled to Belarus after the incident and their current location is unknown https://t.co/RnahHDQkC8 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 18, 2025 Earlier this year, the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism published a report identifying Poland as the “primary focus” of Russia’s campaign of sabotage in Europe. Such actions have often been carried out by Ukrainians and Belarusians. Last month, the trial began of four men – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders. This week, Poland announced that it had detained and charged two Ukrainians accused of carrying out espionage and acts of sabotage on behalf of Russia. World.title: Polish deputy foreign minister charged over alleged misappropriation of millions of zloty
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A Polish deputy foreign minister has been charged with misappropriating millions of zloty entrusted to him and taking steps to prevent creditors from recovering money owed to them. Prosecutors say that Władysław Teofil Bartoszewski used the money for personal expenses and to buy three apartments in Warsaw. His wife has also been charged in the case. Both of them deny the allegations, and Bartoszewski says he “will defend the truth and my good name”. Prokurator z mazowieckiego wydziału PZ PK przedstawił posłowi na Sejm RP Władysławowi Teofilowi Bartoszewskiemu dwa zarzuty: przywłaszczenia powierzonych mu środków pieniężnych znacznej wartości oraz udaremnienia zaspokojenia wierzyciela. Komunikat: ➡️ https://t.co/EXZ3NsovBh pic.twitter.com/Lmp2f3Bw2r — Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) November 10, 2026 The case dates back to before Bartoszewski had entered politics. In 2019, he became an MP for the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL). In 2023, after PSL became a junior partner in the current ruling coalition of Prime Minister Donald Tusk, he was made deputy foreign minister. From 2004, say prosecutors, Bartoszewski was entrusted with managing the assets of Polish art collector and philanthropist Andrzej Ciechanowiecki, who was Bartoszewski’s godfather and a friend of his late father, Władysław Bartoszewski, a former Polish resistance fighter, Auschwitz prisoner, and later foreign minister. From 2005, Władysław Teofil Bartoszewski, who has waived his right to anonymity in the case, also managed funds belonging to the Non Omnis Moriar Foundation, linked to the collector. According to prosecutors, Bartoszewski used some of the money to buy and renovate three apartments in Warsaw between 2005 and 2006. From 2009, Ciechanowiecki began asking Bartoszewski to account for the funds, but he allegedly failed to do so and began avoiding contact with Ciechanowiecki. In 2012, Ciechanowiecki and the foundation terminated their agreements with Bartoszewski and demanded the return of funds, say prosecutors. The following year, they filed a lawsuit demanding that Bartoszewski pay them around £1 million, 7.2 million zloty, €650,000 and $76,000, plus interest. According to prosecutors, Bartoszewski then took steps to prevent the money from being recovered. A company owned by him and his wife sold three apartments in Warsaw, after which the couple disposed of their shares in the company. His wife also donated a property to their underage children. “As a result of these actions, Władysław Teofil Bartoszewski and his wife possess no assets from which the creditor’s claims could be satisfied,” prosecutors said. In March 2024, a Warsaw court ordered Bartoszewski to pay the foundation more than 13.2 million zloty, plus interest. Prosecutors note that the judgment is not yet binding as an appeal is still pending. Od półtora roku sąd nie wyznaczył terminu apelacji w sprawie Władysława Teofila Bartoszewskiego — dowiedział się Onet. Sąd pierwszej instancji nakazał wiceministrowi spraw zagranicznych zwrot aż 13 mln zł, jakie powierzył mu jego chrzestny https://t.co/JzPwcJG4KU — Kamil Dziubka 🟡🇵🇱🇺🇦 (@KamilDziubka) November 4, 2025 Meanwhile, in 2023, representatives of the Ciechanowiecki Collection Foundation at the Royal Castle in Wawel, which now holds the assets of Ciechanowiecki (who died in 2015), filed a notification to prosecutors of alleged crimes committed by Bartoszewski and his wife. Earlier this year, the prosecutor general, Waldemar Żurek, asked parliament to lift Bartoszewski’s immunity so that prosecutors could bring charges against him. However, he voluntarily waived it on 6 October. At the time, Bartoszewski told newspaper Fakt that he “absolutely does not feel guilty” and “the evidence confirms this”. He also claimed that there is “a political element to my case”, though he did not elaborate further. Sejmowa komisja regulaminowa opowiedziała się we wtorek za uchyleniem immunitetu posła PSL Władysława Teofila Bartoszewskiego w związku z wnioskiem prokuratury w sprawie podejrzenia popełnienia przez niego między innymi przestępstwa przywłaszczenia mienia.https://t.co/ydA0jNNUQ8 — tvn24 (@tvn24) October 6, 2026 On Tuesday this week, prosecutors announced that they had charged Bartoszewski with misappropriation of funds of significant value – £1 million, €405,000 and 6,683,705 zloty – entrusted to him by Ciechanowiecki and the foundation. The offence carries a prison sentence of between one and 10 years. A second charge concerns allegedly taking steps to prevent or reduce the recovery of money owed to a creditor. It carries a prison sentence of between three months and five years. Prosecutors say that, on the same day, they “brought similar charges” against Bartoszewski’s wife and that both of the accused denied guilt. Wiceszef MSZ Władysław Teofil Bartoszewski oświadczył, że nie przyznaje się do popełnienia zarzucanych mu przez prokuraturę czynów. Zapowiedział, że będzie bronił prawdy i swojego dobrego imienia "tak długo, jak będzie to konieczne". https://t.co/tGodfs9Gzi — Interia (@Int_Wydarzenia) November 10, 2026 In a statement issued later on Tuesday, Bartoszewski issued a statement rejecting the allegations and saying that he “will defend the truth and my good name in every instance, for as long as necessary”, reports the Polish Press AGency (PAP). “I am convinced that both the criminal proceedings and the ongoing civil proceedings will confirm my arguments and rights to my property,” he added. “I consistently maintain that all actions related to the acquisition of the real estate were consistent with the original will of Andrzej Ciechanowiecki expressed at the time of their purchase, and the premises were intended to constitute permanent financial security for my family.” Asked whether the prime minister would dismiss Bartoszewski following the charges or wait for a court ruling, government spokesperson Adam Szłapka said that the deputy minister “is currently on leave and decisions regarding this matter will be made upon his return”.
