World.title: Heydar Aliyev Foundation VP Leyla Aliyeva holds series of meetings at COP31 (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 15. On November 14, Leyla Aliyeva, Vice-President of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation, founder and head of the IDEA Public Union, met with Salim bin Mohammed AlMalik, Director-General of the Islamic World Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (ICESCO), on the sidelines of the 31st session of the Conference of the Parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31).

During the meeting, the sides discussed opportunities for expanding cooperation between the IDEA Public Union and ICESCO. In this regard, the sides touched upon creating new opportunities for Azerbaijani youth to gain international experience in environmental protection and sustainable development.

The parties exchanged views on implementing joint initiatives aimed at promoting environmental education in schools, greening, waste sorting, water conservation, and energy efficiency.

Discussions also focused on opportunities for organizing international environmental summer camps in Azerbaijan with the participation of youth and implementing joint awareness-raising projects in the field of biodiversity conservation.

The sides discussed the prospects for supporting youth activities in environmental innovations and carrying out joint efforts aimed at developing innovative solutions for air pollution, waste management, water resource protection, and climate change adaptation.

X X X

On November 14, Leyla Aliyeva also met with Max Bello, Global Ocean Expert at the Blue Marine Foundation, and Michael Fishbach, Co-Founder and Executive Director of the Great Whale Conservancy.

The meeting featured discussions on the impacts of the declining water level of the Caspian Sea on the marine ecosystem, biodiversity, and coastal areas, as well as enhancing international cooperation to address existing environmental challenges.

They also exchanged views on expanding marine protected areas in Azerbaijan, conserving Caspian seals and other rare marine species, protecting their natural habitats, and exploring opportunities for international experience exchange and cooperation in this field.

X X X

The same day, Prime Minister of Tonga Lord Fatafehi Fakafānua visited the Azerbaijan pavilion at COP31. The Prime Minister of Tonga was briefed on the stands set up and the projects presented there.

World.title: Heydar Aliyev Foundation VP Leyla Aliyeva attends event on "Women and Climate Investments: Empowering Women Leaders in the Turkic World to Contribute to Climate Action" (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 14. Leyla Aliyeva, Vice-President of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation, founder and head of the IDEA Public Union, attended a panel session on the theme "Women and Climate Investments: Empowering Women Leaders in the Turkic World to Contribute to Climate Action", held at the Azerbaijan pavilion at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye.

Addressing the event, Leyla Aliyeva highlighted the vital role women play in the life of society and the importance of their empowerment. She also emphasized the necessity of expanding cooperation among Turkic states in this area.

Noting women’s active participation in the projects of the IDEA Public Union, Leyla Aliyeva said that initiatives implemented particularly in the regions create new opportunities for women.

Speakers at the panel included Bahar Muradova, Chairperson of the State Committee for Family, Women and Children Affairs of Azerbaijan; Mahinur Özdemir Göktaş, Minister of Family and Social Services of Türkiye; Umayra Taghiyeva, Deputy Minister of Ecology and Natural Resources of Azerbaijan; and Sakina Babayeva, Chairperson of the Board of the Association for Women's Entrepreneurship Development in Azerbaijan.

Discussions focused on increasing women's economic activity in combating climate change, expanding access to climate investments, and ensuring their participation in decision-making processes as key priorities.

The speakers stressed the importance of expanding cooperation, experience exchange, and joint innovative initiatives among women entrepreneurs across the Turkic world.

World.title: Azerbaijan faces risk of failing to secure $411.8M foreign loan in 2027
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 14. Azerbaijan is facing the risk of failing to secure 700 million manat ($411.8 million) in foreign loan next year.

The the opinion issued by the Chamber of Accounts on the draft law "On the state budget of the Republic of Azerbaijan for 2027" noted that, given the low execution rate of foreign loans in the current year, the allocation of a significant share of foreign borrowing to finance the state budget deficit for the coming year, combined with the fact that the projects intended to be financed through these funds aren't substantiated within the "Budget package", increases the risk that the planned borrowing won’t be fully realized.

According to the opinion, 2.73 billion manat $1.6 billion) is expected to be raised through government borrowing in 2027 to finance the state budget deficit. This is projected to account for 86.8% of total financing.

"According to information provided with the 2027 state budget draft, 700 million manat is expected to be raised through foreign loans. However, the 'Budget package' doesn't provide information on the projects to be financed through these funds or the amounts allocated to them.

Although more than 1.71 billion manat ($1.01 billion) was projected to be received through domestic and external borrowing in 2026, no funds had been received during the first nine months of the reporting year. Meanwhile, 125 million manat ($73.5 million) was received through externally borrowed loans, equivalent to 14.7% of the annual forecast of 850 million manat ($500 million) for 2026," the opinion pointed out.

World.title: Azerbaijani banks' Bloomberg deals approach $34B in nine months
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 14. Azerbaijani banks executed 1,648 transactions worth 57.6 billion manat ($33.9 billion) on the Bloomberg trading system from January through September 2026, the Central Bank of Azerbaijan’s (CBA) latest data on monetary indicators says.

According to the data, the total volume of transactions in the unsecured interbank money market increased by 11% compared to the same period last year. In terms of maturity structure, transactions with maturities of one to three days accounted for the largest share, representing 95% of the total volume.

During the reporting period, interest rates in the unsecured money market followed a downward trend across the quarters. Specifically, the average interest rate on transactions stood at 6.58% in Q1, 6.44% in Q2, and 6.28% in Q3.

Overall, the average interest rate in the unsecured interbank money market amounted to 6.54% from January through September, down 0.68 percentage points compared to the same period last year.

Similar trends were observed in the repo market.

Specifically, 4,404 repo transactions totaling 25.2 billion manat ($14.8 billion) were concluded during the first nine months of 2026. Banks accounted for 84% of the total transaction volume.

In terms of maturity structure, the vast majority of repo transactions had maturities of six to eight days, accounting for 91% of the total volume.

The weighted average interest rate on repo transactions also declined across the quarters. Specifically, it stood at 6% in Q1 2026, falling to 5.68% in Q2 and 5.17% in Q3.

At the end of the nine-month period, the weighted average interest rate on repo transactions amounted to 5.71%, down 0.9 percentage points compared to the same period last year.

Thus, from January through September 2026, transaction volumes remained high in both the unsecured interbank money market and the repo segment, while interest rates followed a downward trend across the quarters. These figures reflect an easing of interest rate conditions in both major segments of the money market, alongside sustained interbank trading activity.

World.title: Role of innovative technologies in climate resilience discussed at COP31 (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 14. A panel discussion on the topic "A Just and Inclusive Technology Development For Climate Resilience” was held on the sidelines of the 31st session of the Conference of the Parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, co-organized by the Islamic World Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (ICESCO), the Heydar Aliyev Foundation, and the IDEA Public Union.

The event, organized at the Azerbaijan pavilion, was moderated by Issam Krimi, Head of the Innovation and Creativity, Science and Environment Sector at ICESCO.

Speakers at the discussions included Kuanysh Yergaliyev, Head of the Science and Environment Sector at ICESCO; Hakima El Haite, Member of the COP31 Advisory Board, COP22 High-Level Climate Champion, and former Minister of Environment of the Kingdom of Morocco; Romina Khurshid Alam, Coordinator to the Prime Minister of Pakistan on Climate Change and Environmental Coordination; Mansur Oshurbaev, Vice Minister of Ecology and Natural Resources of Kazakhstan; Elnur Safarov, Caspian Research Expert at the IDEA Public Union; Hatim Aznague, Climate Policy Expert at the Union for the Mediterranean; and Wissam Chehade, Expert at ICESCO.

During the panel, participants discussed the application of innovative technologies in addressing challenges posed by climate change, the efficient water resources management, and strengthening resilience against natural disasters. The speakers emphasized the importance of ensuring equitable access to climate technologies, as well as expanding cooperation and experience exchange, particularly among developing countries.

World.title: Carpenter leads Chelsea to victory against Manchester City
World.content:
Ellie Carpenter has continued her thunderous campaign for Chelsea, helping set up the winner in the Blues' table-topping Women's Super League (WSL) victory over champions Manchester City.

By assisting on Sandy Baltimore's stunning goal that sealed the 1-0 win at Stamford Bridge on Saturday (Sunday AEDT), the on-song wing back also earned the bragging rights over Matildas' teammate Mary Fowler, who was taken off by City with half an hour to go after a much more ineffective afternoon.

By inflicting City's first league defeat of the season, Chelsea went back to the top, leapfrogging the champs to go a point clear after 10 matches.

And as usual this season, the energetic 26-year-old Carpenter, who has looked one of the best players in the WSL this term, was at the heart of the win, already having caused plenty of problems with her crossing from the right flank even before her key contribution deep into stoppage time in the first half.

Carpenter found Baltimore in the box with a short pass and then sped off to take the return pass while dragging her defender with her.

That simply opened up more space for French international Baltimore, who had time to set her sights and curl home a superb left-footed strike beyond keeper Ayaka Yamashita.

It was Carpenter's first assist of her exceptional league season to go with her four goals.

However, across all competitions she's the club leader with nine goal involvements, five goals and four assists.

City looked as if they could eke out an equaliser but their hopes were finally dashed with a quarter of an hour left when Yamashita was sent off, losing out in a race to the ball with Alyssa Thompson and clumsily bringing her down.

Fowler, whose recent form has helped her really nail down a starting spot at City, had already been taken off by that point, replaced by fit-again WSL legend Vivianne Miedema, but the visitors still could not find an equaliser, Lauren Hemp missing a sitter from point-blank range in the 64th minute.

It was City's first defeat in any competition since April 25.

Elsewhere, Manchester United captain Maya le Tissier marked her 150th appearance for the club with a goal in a 2-0 victory at Crystal Palace that moved them to fourth, while Tottenham drew 0-0 at home to Everton and Liverpool won 3-0 at Brighton.

AAP

World.title: A slowing economy could mean higher youth unemployment, economist warns
World.content:
Young people struggling to find work can be the canary in the coal mine for the rest of the jobs market.

And a recent rise in the youth unemployment rate could be a sign of things to come.

Australian Bureau of Statistics data from September showed youth unemployment at 11.1 per cent compared with the overall unemployment rate of 4.7 per cent.

While still lower than before the pandemic, a slowing economy could mean youth unemployment rises further in the coming months.

"We tend to see younger workers affected more heavily when there is a slowdown," chief economist at jobs website SEEK, Blair Chapman, said.

Commonwealth Bank economist Harry Ottley said the youth unemployment rate was "definitely rising more quickly than other cohorts".

Hundreds of applications, constant rejection

Lachlan Riddell has experienced what he describes as "job hunting depression".

"I started to fall into a bit of a slump, [asking myself], 'why am I even doing this'," he said.

The 24-year-old estimated he had applied for hundreds of jobs over the past three years, from collecting supermarket trolleys to retail and hospitality roles.

"I feel like there is a mentality that … generation Z don't want to work, that they're very selective about what they want to do, which is simply not true," he said.

Lachlan Riddell says without a permanent job, he's struggling to make ends meet. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Mr Riddell has a Diploma of Music and works casually as an audio-visual technician, but shifts are sporadic.

He said that despite having wide-ranging work experience, he rarely received a response from employers, and most job applications were online.

" I've seen a lot of companies now use AI for their job hiring process. I'm not even talking to a real human. "

He has concerns that success in Tasmania's small jobs market can depend less on what you know than who you know.

Lachlan Riddell has applied for jobs, including in hospitality. (ABC News: Sam Ikin)

As he continues his search for more permanent work, Mr Riddell said he was struggling to make ends meet on his Jobseeker payment and relied on support from his fiancee.

" It's pretty hard financially to survive. "

Graduate jobs

Graduate job ads have been trending down after post-pandemic highs, according to SEEK.

"There is anecdotal evidence that several larger firms have reduced their graduate intakes in recent years," Mr Chapman said.

"The big four accounting firms are a good example of this as they reduced their intakes in response to declines in demand."

Blair Chapman says the number of graduate jobs has been trending down. (ABC News: John Gunn)

He said he suspected a slowdown in demand for graduates would continue in Australia as the economy softened.

But it is not all bad news.

The rise in youth unemployment has come alongside continued job growth for young people.

Harry Ottley says there are more young people in the labour market looking for work. (Supplied)

"The share of young people in work [the employment-to-population ratio] is 63.6 per cent, down from a peak of 66.7 per cent in November 2022, but well above its 2019 average of 59.7 per cent," Mr Ottley said.

He said youth participation was also high at 71.4 per cent compared with 67.7 per cent in 2019.

"So more young people are in the labour market looking for work," he said.

Blair Chapman says younger workers are often more heavily affected when there is an economic slowdown. (ABC News: Jake Grant)

AI disruption and multiple job holders competing with young people for work

There have been fears that the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) could lead to a jobs apocalypse, particularly for young people and white-collar workers.

But a study by the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations found the technology was not yet causing broad disruption to Australia's labour market.

The study, released in July this year, also found that jobs for people aged 20 to 24 had grown slightly faster than those for people aged 25 and over since the introduction of ChatGPT, while young graduate outcomes remained resilient.

But the report did cite evidence from the US suggesting young people have experienced slower employment growth than older people since the introduction of generative AI tools, especially in occupations more exposed to AI.

Qantas last week announced 850 job cuts and plans to accelerate its use of AI.

Qantas is cutting jobs. (ABC News: Evelyn Manfield)

"We do think there'll be some job disruption at the margin, let's say, over the next five years," Mr Ottley said.

Federal Skills and Training Minister Andrew Giles said AI was mostly augmenting jobs, "so changing the way in which a job is done rather than completely automating a job".

"We've got to really focus on our skill to make sure workers are equipped to manage this transition," Mr Giles said.

Young people are also facing increasing competition for positions from existing job holders.

One million people in Australia have multiple jobs.

World.title: Young Victorian voters torn between disillusionment, optimism
World.content:
Young voters across regional Victoria say the issues that matter most to them are close to home, but they are getting little information about state politics, often relying on social media and word of mouth.

Many the ABC spoke to said they were not satisfied with the political status quo and were turning to alternative parties.

The Victorian Electoral Commission (VEC) said people aged between 18 and 44 would be pivotal to the outcome of this month's state election, making up 44 per cent of the vote.

Mildura Rural City youth council deputy mayor Ollie Edens wants the youth voice to be heard.

The recent high school graduate said that while a generation ago, young people voted in line with their parents, "very few" of his peers will do so.

The key policies on offer from parties in the 2026 Victorian state election Political parties are laying out their visions for the state's future, as voters prepare to head to the polls on November 28.

He said social media was driving young people to make their own voting choices.

"I've seen young people getting more of an independent conscience when it comes to politics, and they're very determined on that," he said.

Mr Edens is travelling to Melbourne as he has not found the training course he needs in Mildura, and would like to see a greater focus on supporting young people to stay in regional areas.

Ollie Edens says local education options are limited, with the local university campus offering few courses. (ABC Mildura-Swan Hill: Alexandra Treloar )

Wodonga student Jack Dumsday relies on his wheelchair to get around and said he was concerned about Wodonga's public transport system.

"Wodonga is not a small town by any means, and we have an abysmal bus network. I'd love to see that improve," he said.

Picking the 'lesser of evils'

Charlie Bradbury, who lives in the Ovens Valley electorate in north-east Victoria, said she would be "picking the lesser of the evils".

The 22-year-old is on the youth advisory committee at the North East Support & Action for Youth (NESAY) community agency, which works with young people and families to provide safe housing, education and employment.

Despite her dissatisfaction with the political landscape, Ms Bradbury said the Greens' policies around rent freezing and publicly owned local supermarkets were appealing.

She said she would approach her vote with a "gender-based" focus.

"[That's] purely because the present violence against women epidemic is absolutely abysmal," she said.

Charlie Bradbury says some issues are not being properly addressed by political parties. (ABC)

Since 2025, One Nation has surged in polls across Australia, recently claiming four lower house seats in the South Australian election.

Ms Bradbury said she had seen this rise and while she noticed it more in "older generations", it was not limited to that demographic.

"It does kind of feel like we've taken a step backwards — the younger generation," she said.

Young voters to have 'huge impact' on election outcome

Monash University associate professor of politics Zareh Ghazarian said there would be "thousands" of first-time voters who will have a "huge impact" in determining the outcome in this election.

Dr Ghazarian studied how young and first-time voters approached their first time at the ballot box.

Zareh Ghazarian says young and first-time voters could have a "huge impact" in determining the outcome of November's Victorian state election. (Supplied)

"We identified that, of course, young people have rich and many different reasons as to who they decide to vote for," he said.

"And they do reflect in broad ways the sorts of strategies and preferences older voters demonstrate."

He said young voters could be divided into two categories: those who research candidates, their policies and ideas, and those who look at how their parents and friends voted.

"When you have such a high proportion of young people in Victoria, the decisions they're going to make may potentially be the key to the major parties or any party, any candidate in any electorate winning the seat," Dr Ghazarian said.

Young voters still have faith in politics: GetUp

Conal Feehely, the Victorian campaign director for GetUp, which is an independent movement of more than one million people aiming to bring participation back into our democracy, said young people were "frustrated".

"Young Australians are facing the prospect of having a lower standard of living than their parents had, and that's a really heavy burden," he said.

"They're [also] facing enormous student debt … enormous increases to their rent and still don't see a prospect of owning a home."

Conal Feehely says young voters are frustrated with a range of issues heading into this year's state election. (ABC)

Mr Feehely said young people "want a type of politics that's hopeful and gives them answers and they're not seeing a lot of that right now".

Youth have long played vital role in political activism: analyst

Dr Ghazarian said it was unsurprising young people were tackling the current political landscape through protests, saying this had long been the case in Australia and abroad.

"Many young people are leading figures in international movements such as those concerned with environmental protection, conservation and social justice," he said.

Not only did young people lead political debate, but they also responded to it, he added.

"Young people are using their ability to protest, their ability to have their say in public views and they're having a go," Dr Ghazarian said.

Hamish Knight and Dylan Stockwell organised a rally against One Nation last month, which saw about 100 students march through Bendigo.

Hamish, 17, is concerned the party is dividing Australia and believes people need to "start fighting back".

Mr Feehely said he believed young people tended to be "a bit more blank canvas than other demographics".

He said this "opens the door" to influence, especially online, where young people were spending "more time … being influenced by algorithms".

But NESAY youth advisory committee's Sarah Clayton has a different take.

The 21-year-old Benambra voter said she felt uninformed about politics and saw that reflected among her peers.

Victoria election 2026 live updates: For all the latest news from the campaign trail, read our blog.

Ms Clayton did not watch television and often received information through social media or word of mouth.

"I think the biggest reason [for a lack of knowledge on politics] is within my social media algorithms. It's not something that pops up very much," she said.

She said the donkey vote had become "popular" in her generation and she wanted to see more education in schools about politics.

Young people often receive election information via social media. (ABC News)

Ms Clayton said it was common for young people to be on the receiving end of smart remarks from mates when politics was brought up.

"You're not supposed to talk about politics — it's meant to be a private thing, and it frustrates people — but I think that's exactly why it needs to be spoken about," she said.

"People are passionate about things, and this is how we get and make changes in our world. I think there is a huge lack of understanding within youth and a lot of the Australian population in general about the importance of voting."

World.title: The Brisbane buildings made from sandstone touched by dinosaurs
World.content:
Some of Brisbane's oldest heritage-listed buildings are harbouring clues about the prehistoric past.

Fossilised footprints belonging to 230-million-year-old dinosaurs have been unearthed in Brisbane, indented into the same sandstone that constructed the city's most recognisable buildings, like the General Post Office.

"These buildings certainly capture my eye, and I do glance twice to see what evidence might be hidden within their own architecture," Palaeontologist Dr Anthony Romilio said.

Iconic Brisbane landmarks like the General Post Office were built with sandstone from the same quarry. (ABC News: Lucy Loram)

Dr Romilio said two separate pieces of Brisbane-mined sandstone handed over to the University of Queensland's Dinosaur Lab, appear to display the tread-marks of the Sauropodomorph.

"Instead of walking on all four legs, they walked on their back legs. They still retained a very long neck and tail, but they were more ancient than the more typical than the brontosaurus," he said.

One of the footprints was discovered by a teenager over six decades ago at Petrie's Quarry.

Palaeontologist Anthony Romilio identified the footprints as likely belonging to a sauropodomorph. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

The history of Petrie's Quarry

Before the inner-north neighbourhood of Albion became the sought-after suburbia of today, it was Petrie's Quarry.

Educator Sue-Belinda Meehan said the Petrie family opened the quarry in the 1860s, 30 years after the family settled in Brisbane, which was then known as the Moreton Bay Penal Colony.

"If the Petrie's hadn't recognised the quality of that sandstone, we wouldn't have the sandstone that literally built Brisbane," she said.

A woman at Petrie's Quarry, which would one day become the suburb of Albion. (Supplied: State Library of Queensland)

The General Post Office, All Hallows School, and the Old Customs House were all made up of the creamy, white stone.

"When you think about the number of buildings that were constructed from it, it's quite extraordinary … it's probably easier to mention buildings that weren't made from it, then buildings that were," Ms Meehan said.

St Stephen's Cathedral, St John's Cathedral, and St Paul's Presbyterian Church are among the other builds that feature Petrie sandstone.

Sue-Belinda Meehan says the quarry supplied the sandstone that "literally built Brisbane". (ABC News: Lucy Loram)

"They were very much equal opportunity builders. It didn't matter what brand of religion you were, the Petries would build you a church," she said.

All the while, they were working with stone that had been touched by dinosaurs.

" The thing that really tickles me is that there were stone masons looking at big blocks of sandstones going, 'oh heaven's there's a flaw in it, there's a footprint' … and cutting it out. "

The General Post Office, located on Queen Street, was built in 1875. (Supplied: State Library of Queensland)

Aquatic Albion

As quarrying ceased, the site was often visited by adventurous school children and aspiring geologists, before the suburb of Albion slowly started to build around it.

But Ms Meehan said remnants of the once active quarry remained today.

"If you go out to Albion and drive down Crosby Road, and look up to St Margaret's, you can see the scar in the mountain that was Petrie's Quarry."

Layers of white sandstone are still visible in Albion today. (ABC News: Liz Pickering)

Dr Romilio said the white hills of Albion are made up of layers of sand that were deposited when the landscape was traversed by dinosaurs.

"If you were to travel 230 million years ago, you would find a very flat area. There wouldn't be much in the way of trees in that immediate area, because you're looking at a very wide river," he said.

"It would have been shallow enough for a two-legged dinosaur to walk past."

But the Sauropodomorph was not the only pre-historic creature walking the now streets of Albion.

"It would have also been an environment in which aquatic creatures lived as well. So giant salamander like animals are known to have existed in that same time as well," Dr Romilio said.

Before: University of Queensland palaeontologist Anthony Romilio created a 3D map of the fossil. . . After: This helped determine what kind of dinosaur the footprint belonged to. . . Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition Before and after images SLIDE University of Queensland palaeontologist Anthony Romilio created a 3D map of the fossil. / This helped determine what kind of dinosaur the footprint belonged to.

Fossil discoveries

Both pieces of sandstone etched with the dinosaur footprints were discovered during the 1950's.

Dr Romilio said he is often approached with information about Brisbane's Petrie Quarry site.

"It may seem unusual in a capital city, that we find evidence of dinosaurs, but really all you need is the right aged material and a keen eye, and some conviction to investigate," Dr Romilio said.

St Stephens Cathedral today, sitting in a forest of modern buildings. (ABC News: Lucy Loram)

Ms Meehan said not all dinosaur discoveries are reserved for outback Queensland.

"Queensland is just awash with wonderful dinosaur relics from the past, and to know that we have them here in Brisbane, just makes it an even more fabulous city," she said.

World.title: Nurse offers 'out of the blue' to have surrogate baby for colleague
World.content:
When Amanda Lewis gave birth to a surrogate baby girl, her role did not end when she handed her over to her biological parents.

Ms Lewis, who has two teenage daughters, has continued to occasionally breastfeed baby Evangeline and has spent hours expressing milk for her since she was born on August 3.

The little girl was delivered after a seven-hour labour at the Ipswich Hospital, west of Brisbane, where Ms Lewis worked with the baby's biological mother Bec Vallee for years as nurses.

Amanda Lewis with Bec Vallee and newborn Eva. Amanda gave birth to Eva on August 3. Eva is Bec's biological child. (ABC News: Janelle Miles)

Known as Eva, she weighed 3 kilograms after being born almost three weeks early.

Ms Vallee was diagnosed with nephrotic syndrome, a kidney disorder, at age 12.

She has had two kidney transplants — one donated by her mum at 17 and another about three years ago.

The second kidney came from a living, altruistic donor — a stranger who willingly gave up a kidney — as part of the Australian and New Zealand Paired Kidney Exchange Program.

Doctors warned about pregnancy risks

Growing up, doctors warned her about the high risks to her of pregnancy with her medical condition.

After Bec married Ryan Vallee, they talked about adoption and becoming foster parents.

But about eight years ago, her older sister Sarah offered to be a surrogate for the couple and gave birth to their first daughter Ambrosia — who they call Bo — in 2019.

Sisters Eva and Bo Vallee were both born through surrogacy. (Supplied)

"We always thought that she would be our only child because of the rarity and incredible sacrifice that surrogacy is, especially in Australia, because it has to be an altruistic act," Ms Vallee says.

"I just never thought we would find someone willing to go again for us."

Unexpectedly, about three years ago, Ms Lewis phoned Ms Vallee to begin the conversation about becoming a surrogate to give Bo a sibling.

Amanda Lewis and Bec Vallee at their baby shower before the birth of Eva. (Supplied )

"We were work friends, but not intimate close friends. We didn't see each outside of work," Ms Vallee recalls.

"It was quite an emotional thought that I'd had someone step forward and offer me this completely, really completely, out of the blue.

"So, it was one of those life-changing phone calls. That's how the journey began."

At three months old, Eva wears a smocked dress that once belonged to her biological mum.

Baby Eva wearing a dress that belonged to her biological mum. (Supplied)

Ms Vallee, 37, says there are few gifts that can compare to someone carrying and giving birth to your child — except organ donation.

"It's a highly emotional experience," she says.

"I feel the two greatest sacrifices that another person can make for a friend or a relative or a person is to give an organ or to sacrifice their body to have a baby for someone else to grow their family.

"I have the incredible blessing of experiencing both things twice."

Ryan and Bec Vallee, with their daughters Bo, 7, and newborn Eva, and Eva's surrogate mum, Amanda Lewis. (ABC News: Janelle Miles)

Surrogate births in Australia are rare

Statistics from the Australian and New Zealand Assisted Reproduction Database (ANZARD) reveal just how rare the gift of surrogacy is across the two countries.

Out of about 360,000 babies born in Australia and New Zealand annually, only about 100 are delivered to surrogate mums — less than 0.03 per cent.

In 2024, the latest data reported by ANZARD, based at the University of NSW, 103 babies were born to surrogates Down Under.

The year Bo was born in 2019, she was one of 73 surrogate babies delivered in Australia and New Zealand.

In the decade between 2015 and 2024, the lowest number of babies born to surrogate mothers in the two countries was 46 in 2016. The highest was 133 in 2022.

Only altruistic surrogacy is allowed in Australia.

Three-month-old Eva Vallee is the product of altruistic surrogacy. Her mother's nursing friend Amanda Lewis gave birth to her. (ABC News: Janelle Miles)

Commercial surrogacy — where a surrogate is paid beyond reasonable expenses — is prohibited in every state and territory.

But the Australian Law Reform Commission is due to report on its review of surrogacy laws in the coming days.

Every year, Australian passports are issued to about 350 to 400 children born through overseas surrogacy, based on Department of Home Affairs figures.

For Ms Lewis, a mother to two teenage girls, her experience of being a surrogate for the Vallee family would not have meant as much had it been a commercial transaction.

Three-month-old Eva Vallee being nursed by the woman who gave birth to her, Amanda Lewis. (ABC News: Janelle Miles)

"I've lived a very normal life and the thought that I've done something that is bigger than myself, internally, just makes me very happy, that I could be part of someone else's story and actually really help their life," she says.

"People are quite self-centred these days, but you can just step out and help someone and do something that's not the norm.

"While I understand that in other countries that people do do it for money, and all of that, I think for me, it would muddy the waters. I wouldn't have got out of it what I got out of it."

Positives for both families

Her whole family has benefited.

The 41-year-old says the experience has facilitated conversations with her teenage daughters Ella, 16, and Grace, 14, and their friends, about helping other people.

Husband Tom was also on board with her decision to become a surrogate.

Tom Lewis with baby Eva Vallee. The Lewis and Vallee families have become close after Tom's wife Amanda gave birth to Eva. (Supplied)

"We have just set the foundations for us to have a really warm and loving friendship and bond through our whole families," Ms Lewis says.

"I would expect that I get to watch Eva grow up and just have that little sense of pride and go, you know, I just played a really nice piece of the puzzle to make that happen.

"For our family it has been so enriching."

Teenagers Ella and Grace Lewis with their mum, Amanda, at a baby shower before the birth of Eva. They're pictured with Eva's biological mum Bec and her seven-year-old sister, Bo. (Supplied)

She describes her relationship with Eva as a bit like being a grandparent.

"You kind of have the fun cuddles, but then you get to go," Ms Lewis says with a smile.

"That's how I think being a grandparent will be like.

"You are really heavily involved, but you don't have to do the nitty-gritties — the 3am waking up and rocking and all of that."

Enjoying maternity leave together

Ms Vallee and Ms Lewis have both been able to enjoy maternity leave together after Eva's birth.

Queensland Health maternity leave and the Federal Government's paid parental leave have allowed Ms Lewis to take six months off, giving her the opportunity to keep intermittently breastfeeding Eva and to express milk for her.

Surrogate mum Amanda Lewis has spent hours expressing breastmilk for three-month-old Eva Vallee, who she gave birth to on August 3. (ABC News: Janelle Miles)

"I think if I would have gone back to work at say, six weeks, which is what a lot of surrogates do, I would not have been ready at all," Ms Lewis says.

"All your hormones, they're all still settling down and I think the feeding really helped with that side of things.

"It just has turned out to be this most amazing phase. It has allowed me to feed her and pump, and she's exclusively had my breast milk. That has been really important to me."

Asked whether she would be a surrogate again, Ms Lewis replied: "If I was 10 years younger, I potentially would. But not at 41."

However, the Vallees, who recently celebrated their 15th wedding anniversary, have not ruled out welcoming more children.

Bec and Ryan Vallee with their daughters Bo, 7, and newborn Eva. They have not ruled out having more children. (Supplied)

"We are just delighted by our two daughters, and we would love to adopt still," Mr Vallee says.

"We're just grateful for each day and the gift it is to have them in our lives."

Seven-year-old Bo is overjoyed to have a sibling.

"When I found out, it was the most amazing thing I ever felt," she says.

"It's incredible."

Dad Ryan Vallee with his two daughters, Bo and Eva. (Supplied)

The Vallees picked the name Evangeline because it means "bringer of good news" and hope their story will inspire others to provide help to someone else in need.

"It might not be an organ donation or a surrogacy but each of us, every day, has the opportunity to say 'yes' to someone or something that we can be part of in healing or bringing life, hope, or even just a small amount of happiness," Ms Vallee says.

"The challenge for me is how to give back in the same way I've been given to."

World.title: Ocean that once covered Flinders Ranges preserved Earth's earliest life
World.content:
Researchers have found new evidence about how ancient sea level changes led to the preservation of some of Earth's earliest complex life forms.

Geological features across South Australia's Flinders Ranges were mapped in the study led by Adelaide University, reconstructing the landscape of hundreds of millions of years ago to investigate how sediment and fossils came to be.

"You have to imagine that the Flinders Ranges … was under the ocean," University of Adelaide associate professor Diego Garcia-Bellido said.

Researchers say the findings give a clearer picture of how the Flinders Ranges landscape changed. (Supplied: Adelaide University)

"Canyons were being carved and creating this accommodation space for a lot more sediment."

The findings focused on the Ediacaran period, about 550 million years ago, "at the time or just before the appearance of the first complex life on the planet".

Diego Garcia-Bellido works at Chace Range in September. (Supplied: Xavier Damiani/Adelaide University)

Looking at Nilpena Ediacara National Park in the Flinders Ranges, researchers noticed unusual rock formations that indicated the presence of submarine canyons.

Dr Garcia-Bellido and his colleagues from the university and the South Australian Museum began finding the canyons "all over the Flinders", up to 280 metres deep and 6 kilometres wide.

The findings suggest that flooding of seawater played a crucial part in the formation of the canyons, and subsequently the preservation of some of the first complex life on the planet.

Earth's earliest life

Knowledge about how the canyons formed could help with the understanding of early evolution.

"The environment is a very important point of reference; you need to know where these organisms started living, and why they settled there," Dr Garcia-Bellido said.

Karol Faehnrich and Jim Gehling map the geological features in the Flinders Ranges in 2024. (Supplied: Diego Garcia-Bellido)

"What we see is that, as the canyons get filled and the sea level rises, this creates in the shallow shelf an environment that is ideal for the shallow water microbial mat to grow.

" This is where this original Ediacara biota began to grow and actually produce the most diverse assemblage of this pre-animal world. "

Fossils of early soft-bodied organisms known as Ediacaran biota were first discovered in the Flinders Ranges in 1946

Fossils like these form an important part of an ongoing bid for UNESCO World Heritage recognition for the Flinders Ranges.

Jim Gehling does some mapping at Chace Range in 2016. (Supplied: Diego Garcia-Bellido)

"The fact that this is so important is because we see how animals arrive on this planet, or start developing on this planet," Dr Garcia-Bellido said.

"With these studies, we're trying to find more about these very earliest complex forms.

"It's glimpsing a world that is probably the most alien we can actually find because we've gone so far back in time that the animals that we see around us today … didn't even exist."

World.title: All Blacks suffer 73-year first in defeat to Wales
World.content:
Wales has ended a 73-year winless sequence against New Zealand with a stunning 35-28 victory in the Nations Championship.

Wales, who last overcame the All Blacks in 1953 and have endured a dismal recent run, outscored the visitors five tries to four on Saturday and produced a defensive performance for the ages to end a run of 34 losses to the three-times world champions.

They caught New Zealand cold with two early tries and two more at the start of the second half, and heroic Welsh defence resisted waves of attacks in the closing stages to hold on for a famous victory.

"It's come from belief. Obviously, we've got the crowd behind us, and the energy and the noise was unbelievable," Welsh man of the match James Botham said.

"We've been training on the defensive side of things, and it shows how training has come on and just how much we have got each other's back."

The Wales players team were in tears at the end amid raucous celebrations at Cardiff's Principality Stadium after Tomos Williams, Dewi Lake, Archie Griffin, Eddie James and Louis Rees-Zammit scored tries and Sam Costelow was immaculate with the boot.

New Zealand were stunned, held up over the line three times in the closing minutes at a raucous Cardiff. (Getty Images: Dan Istitene)

New Zealand's tries were scored by Cortez Ratima, Wallace Sititi, Fehi Fineanganofo and Peter Lakai, all converted by Richie Mo'unga, but were held up over the line three times, with the Welsh defenders making a total of 346 tackles by the end of the game.

It was only the fourth time Wales had beaten New Zealand in 39 meetings.

"A hell of a defensive effort from them," New Zealand coach Dave Rennie said.

"They were excellent tonight."

One consolation for the All Blacks is that the bonus points they have picked up have put them above South Africa in the Northern Hemisphere standings as they seek a place in the new competition's final at Twickenham.

Elsewhere, England thrashed Eddie Jones's Japan 78-15 Nations Championship at Twickenham, with England winger Will Joseph scoring a record-equalling five tries.

Joseph was making only his second appearance for England, more than four years after his debut, and started his return with a try from his first touch inside the opening 65 seconds before adding three more in the first 25 minutes.

The 24-year-old scored a fifth after the interval to equal the record set by Rory Underwood in 1989 and matched by Josh Lewsey in 2003 and Henry Arundell at the last World Cup.

England ran in 13 tries in a record score against Japan, and in the new Nations Championship competition.

And in Genoa, Argentina beat Italy 19-14, condemning the hosts to their fifth defeat in five matches in the competition.

Reuters

World.title: Philippines wins Eurovision Asia, making history
World.content:
The Philippines had made musical history in Bangkok, claiming victory in the inaugural Eurovision Asia Song Contest.

Carmelle Allyza San Juan Collado took home the crown with an electric performance of the original song Sobra-Sobra, a tune she said was inspired by the strength of Philippine women.

"I'm really happy. I'm really grateful that I made history," Collado said.

Carmelle Allyza San Juan Collado claimed the top prize. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

The 19-year-old performer from Bicol comes from a family of entertainers and had been the youngest contestant in the competition.

She is already known in her country after winning the Tawag ng Tanghalan singing competition, participating in Pinoy Big Brother and releasing a self-titled album this year.

"I got singing from my mother's side," she told the ABC.

"My mother sang, my grandmother sang, and also my grandfather. My uncles and aunties, my cousins, they all sang.

Carmelle says she is grateful to have won. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

"I hope that I can leave audiences with a deep sense of connection and I hope I can make them understand that the Filipino music is universally relatable."

Spectators from around the world

Seventy years after Eurovision was created to help unite war-torn Europe through music, the competition has embarked on an ambitious new chapter in Asia.

The original Eurovision Song Contest is the world's longest-running international music competition, and is renowned for its music, spectacle and glamour.

More than 130 million viewers tuned in to watch the contest in Vienna in May.

JUNHEE represented South Korea. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

But the inaugural Asian edition did not generate the same fan following.

Some of the region's largest and most influential nations, including India, China and Japan, were notably absent.

Instead, 11 countries took to the stage, with performers from Bhutan, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Laos, Malaysia, Mongolia, Nepal, the Philippines, South Korea, Thailand and Vietnam competing for the hearts and votes of viewers.

Tóc Tiên is Vietnam's representative at the Eurovision Song Contest Asia 2026 in Bangkok. (Supplied: Eurovision Song Contest Asia)

But what the competition lacked in anticipation, it made up for in spectacle, with everything from colourful tuktuks paraded on stage, to awe-inspiring visual special effects and show-stopping costumes.

Adam Bryers and Lalla Stewart, who were dressed in matching sparkling silver outfits, flew from Perth to watch the musical extravaganza.

"We love Eurovision and we have Eurovision parties in Perth in our house and also with our friends," Bryers told the ABC.

"The glam, the fun, the music, the silliness — it's a really great festival. I think it really suits the culture here, especially in places like the Philippines, so it will do well,."

Adam Bryers and Lalla Stewart travelled from Perth to attend Eurovision Asia 2026. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

Ran Macanang travelled from the Philippines to watch the show live, having followed the original competition for a decade.

"There are thousands of fans in the Philippines for Eurovision already, so knowing that Eurovision is finally coming to Asia, everyone is excited that finally someone from the Philippines can show the world our talents," he told the ABC while waving his nation's flag.

" Asia has what it takes to be as colourful as the main Eurovision in Europe. "

This year's winner will not receive any prize money or automatically gain the right to host the next competition.

The road to Eurovision Asia

Mongolia was one of the 11 countries to compete in the competition.

Behind the lights and carefully choreographed performances, the road to Eurovision Asia was long and, for some contestants, heartbreaking.

For Thinla, the journey began in the rice paddies of south-western Laos, where she grew up singing and dancing while her parents cultivated the land.

In a country where 15 per cent of the population lives below the poverty line, according to the Asian Development Bank, she said it was difficult to carve out a career as an entertainer.

"I started dancing because at the time I just wanted to make money to support my family," the 29-year-old said.

"It's not easy."

Eurovision Asia contestant Thinla represented Laos. (ABC: Haidarr Jones)

Despite the challenges and the upheaval caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, Thinla secured a scholarship to study in China.

But four years ago, shortly after returning to Laos, she lost her biggest fan: her father.

"I hope he can see me growing up like this and can see me perform because he loved it when I sang and performed for him," she said, tears running down her face.

For Nepal's Pratik Himal Rai, the competition carried a profound sense of responsibility.

He was representing not only the dreams of his family, but also a nation still reeling from tragedy.

Pratik Himal Rai represented Nepal in the competition. (Supplied: Eurovision Song Contest Asia)

In August, flash floods devastated communities along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers near the Nepal-Tibet border, killing at least 1,400 people.

More than 5,700 remain missing, including close family members of Rai's friends.

He said he felt a great sense of responsibility. (ABC: Haidarr Jones)

"My message for the world is that love is eternal. To all the lives that we have lost in the floods, we have lost them but their love for us is still there," he said.

Fierce competition

Eurovision has embarked on an ambitious new chapter in Asia. (Supplied: Eurovision Song Contest Asia)

Yet, for all its ambition, Eurovision Asia's launch was mired in questions about public interest and organisation.

The competition's attempt to enter the American market in 2022 fell flat, getting poor viewing figures as it competed against more established shows such as American Idol.

Eurovision Asia has made a tentative start in its bid to capture the region's music fans.

In a market rich in musical heritage and global talent covering genres from K-pop to indie, the potential audience is vast.

World.title: This man is reviving London’s gig culture. His cure offers Sydney’s scene new hope too
World.content:
CultureMusicLive music This man is reviving London’s gig culture. His cure offers Sydney’s scene new hope too Kayla Olaya November 15, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Jon Collins believes the pandemic crippled London’s live music scene, but concedes it was never as moribund as Sydney’s to begin with. Efforts to wind back a decade of NSW lockout laws under a restrictive government were truncated by the global health crisis, leaving behind a dysfunctional music performance ecosystem, the chief executive of the UK’s Live Music Industry Venues and Entertainment said. Jon Collins, chief executive of the UK’s Live Music Industry Venues and Entertainment. Wolter Peeters Collins is in Sydney to speak at a government nightlife conference about how he turned back the clock in London. When he and a coalition of 13 live music organisations looked at how to revive gig culture at a point of crisis in the UK, they realised their ecosystem was out of balance. Large stadium tours were performing well, but artists, promoters and venues at the middle and grassroots levels were struggling.



The result: 43 festivals cancelled and 30 venues permanently closing in 2025 alone. Fans no longer had disposable income to bet on their local gigs. Venues started relying on the predictability of cover shows. “The ability of people to experiment with that £10 ticket (about $20), go to the small local venue – they don’t have as much leeway to take those risks on that band that they don’t know,” Collins said. 17-year-old Lachlan Munro at Orange’s The Gig. His schoolmates helped spike his hair. Audrey Richardson “If you’ve only got limited disposable income, do you want a guaranteed seven out of 10 night out going to see an Oasis cover band … or would you rather go and see that band that you’ve not really heard of that could be a real two out of 10 stinker? Or it could be a nine out of 10, and they’re going to be playing arenas in three years.” The answer to London’s woes is gaining attention in the NSW parliament, after the report from the NSW State of Live Music inquiry was tabled this week.



Related Article Live music ‘Concert-goers pay’: Ticket levy could raise $3m for Sydney’s struggling music scene In the UK, following a parliamentary inquiry, a plan was devised to introduce a £1 levy on tickets for concerts with capacity for more than 5000 patrons, to be placed in a trust to fund the grassroots music scene. Since it began in 2025, it has raised millions of pounds. Artists can choose to add the levy to their concert tickets. When it began, American artists, including Diana Ross, Lynyrd Skynyrd and Bowling for Soup, were the first to participate in the scheme, Collins said. Now, artists such as Olivia Dean, Florence and The Machine, Harry Styles, Lily Allen and Take That have added “the pound,” as Collins calls it. Sam Fender has also committed to the initiative for next year. “We’ve got over 130 tours now carrying the pound,” Collins said.



So far this year, the fund has raised £2.5 million, has another £6 million “guaranteed” with partnered artists and expects to distribute £7 to £8 million in 2027. A board of industry experts distributes the trust’s money in funding rounds. The first round, Collins said, went to seven programs covering artists, venues, promoters and festivals. One helped ease touring costs, another helped venues convert high utility bills into green energy, and there was a boost for small and micro festivals. An AC/DC concert at Accor Stadium, Sydney, in November 2025. Venues NSW/Brett Costello The trust also helps communities in Northern Ireland and Scotland learn how to stage, market, promote and run an event, while also putting young artists on stages for younger audiences. Of the 37 recommendations from the NSW State of Live Music inquiry, a ticket levy is the frontrunner. After three hearings and 105 submissions, the committee found rising operating costs, insurance premiums, user-pays policing charges, changing audience behaviours and limited artist development pathways were stifling the sector.



Committee chair Sarah Kaine said a ticket levy would create sustainable funding to support the next generation of artists and venues. Tame Impala performing in Australia this year. Richard Clifford The Australian Music Venue Foundation, a lobby group representing grassroots music venues in Australia, initially proposed a $1 levy on every ticket for shows with a capacity above 5000 patrons. The organisation estimates that five major Sydney venues alone could generate $3 million to $3.15 million each year. Touring artists or punters would pay the levy through an opt-in scheme. Earlier this year, pop star Olivia Dean donated $1 for each ticket sold on her Australian tour to the organisation. Meanwhile, NSW Greens MP Cate Faehrmann believes consumers already bear various ticketing costs, and multinational corporations should fund the local scene through a tax increase.



Teens at the all-ages Orange festival, The Gig. Audrey Richardson For Collins, the industry’s sustainability, from kids in regional towns having access to music to venues being able to afford insurance, is core to the survival of live music. And he doesn’t see why Sydney can’t have the same. “There’s the opportunity to build a similar coalition here,” he said. “It’s promoters, agents, and managers ... that gives you the momentum.”

World.title: An old copper wire in the bush: why the US had to shut down its airspace
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaAviation An old copper wire in the bush: why the US had to shut down its airspace Michael Koziol Updated November 15, 2026 — 7:16am ,first published 6:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Washington: A routine upgrade to an old copper wire communications network in a remote area of the United States was responsible for bringing the nation’s air traffic to a halt, officials said. They effectively ruled out a cyberattack or the involvement of any artificial intelligence systems, adding that the decision to order a nationwide ground stop was taken out of “an abundance of caution”. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy with Federal Aviation Administration administrator Bryan Bedford on Saturday. AP Photo/Tom Brenner Speaking at a news conference on Saturday morning (US time), Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the instability in the system occurred while telecom contractor L3Harris was undertaking routine maintenance at a remote location to upgrade copper wiring to fibre-optic. “That router that was being replaced as we switched from copper to fibre, it started flooding other routers in our air traffic control system,” he said. “We had over 1000 connection attempts every four to five seconds.”



Those connection attempts began to overwhelm the system, leading to communications issues with airplanes, and disrupted radar feeds. “When we see that, your safety is paramount. We shut down the airspace.” Officials said they did not yet know whether the initial problem was caused by contractor incompetence, a wrong configuration or a faulty new router installed in the system. Passengers at George Bush International Airport in Houston on Saturday. Delays were expected to continue over the weekend. AP Photo/Ashley Landis Duffy said they did not believe any form of nefarious activity was involved. “Once we were able to isolate the work that was being done at that location, all of our systems came back online,” he said. “This was an FAA [Federal Aviation Administration] system that didn’t meet the moment, or a contractor didn’t meet the moment, or equipment didn’t meet the moment.”



L3Harris said it has been modernising the communications infrastructure behind the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA. More than 70 per cent of planned copper to fibre optic conversions have been completed, it said. The company was supporting the FAA investigation, and took the matter and its impact on travellers seriously, L3Harris said. The incident has put the spotlight on America’s ageing air traffic control infrastructure. AP Photo/Ashley Landis FAA administrator Bryan Bedford apologised to the travelling public for the disruption. He said that by the time the ground stop was ordered at 3.45pm Washington time on Friday (Saturday AEDT), about 30,000 of the day’s 50,000 scheduled flights had already landed or were airborne. Of the 20,000 remaining, 12,000 had to be cancelled - 9000 commercial flights and 3000 private. There were significant flow-on effects into Saturday, with another 4000 or 5000 flights expected to be cancelled, but the system was expected to recover by Sunday, Bedford said.



“We see zero evidence of anything nefarious and no evidence of anything AI-related. We have an equipment issue,” he said. Asked why maintenance was being done on a Friday afternoon rather than during a quieter time, Duffy said upgrades in remote areas were done during the day, whereas major airports were done at night. Several thousand flights would also be cancelled on Saturday (US time), officials said, as airlines worked to recover from the shutdown. AP Photo/Ashley Landis Rebecca Guy, the FAA’s acting chief technology officer, said the agency had not realised that a problem at an isolated location could have such wide flow-on consequences. The incident has put the focus back on the US’ ageing air traffic control infrastructure, which still relies in part on copper wires and floppy disks.



Earlier this month, the FAA announced plans to end the use of floppy disks by the end of 2028. The Enterprise Information Display System would replace four systems that date back to the 1980s. Bedford said the system was so old (he described it as “1G”) that it was no longer in production and cost about $US1 billion a year just to sustain. Old Cisco 600 routers were constantly being replaced, he said. Rebecca Guy, acting chief technology officer at the FAA, said the agency had not realised such widespread consequences were possible. AP Photo/Tom Brenner “This is probably one of the worst kept secrets in government - that this [communications] system needs to be replaced.” Last year, Congress appropriated $US12.5 billion ($18.2 billion) for system upgrades, but Duffy had already announced the Trump administration wanted $US30 billion more. He now wants as much as $US50 billion.



“Everyone says they want to do it, and the president is pushing it, but we don’t get the resources,” Duffy said on Saturday. “How long are we going to wait, America and Congress?” Related Article On the ground

Airports Love? No, just thousands of dispirited, stranded passengers, actually On Friday night at the White House, when a reporter pointed out to Duffy that the Republicans have controlled Congress for the past two years, he asked her which news organisation she was with, and suggested she had not properly covered Donald Trump’s fight for funding. Democratic congressman Robert Garcia, who will likely chair the House Oversight Committee once Democrats gain control next year, said there must be “full public transparency” about what happened and why. “We need answers to ensure our systems and technology are funded and upgraded to ensure the safety of the public,” Garcia said.



The major US airlines were still grappling with the fallout on Saturday, with planes and crews out of place from where they would usually be located. Delta encouraged passengers to rebook for Monday if their plans allowed. United Airlines said most flights were operating normally, but some were delayed or cancelled. World.title: How a late father’s early lessons and a mother’s constant presence shaped an AFL draft hopeful
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 How a late father’s early lessons and a mother’s constant presence shaped an AFL draft hopeful Marc McGowan November 15, 2026 — 7:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. There was always someone in Lachie Hicks’ corner when things got tough in his draft year. In a world where sports parents can be overbearing, the talented Western Jets midfielder, who also played for Altona and Wesley College, has had a far more positive experience with his mum and No.1 fan, Christina. Lachie Hicks has a special kind of motivation spurring him on into the AFL draft this month. AFL Photos “Mum’s kind of everything, to be honest,” Hicks told this masthead. “She comes to every single game. She doesn’t say too much – she kind of stays away – but I know she always wants the best for me, and obviously, ideally, she wants me to make it [as an AFL player].



Editor's pick AFL 2026 ‘It stuffs up every club’: Why an AFL move left the likely No.1 draft pick in shock “She’s always been my biggest support, and it’s always been there for me as well – every bad game, every good game.” Hicks averaged almost 29 disposals, five clearances and 1.4 goals for the Jets in an outstanding Talent League campaign this past season, then put his athletic prowess on display with top-10 results in draft combine testing in agility, the two-kilometre time trial and the 20-metre sprint. His late father, Scott, introduced him and his other son, Brodie to football not long after they could walk. Scott played for Essendon’s reserves and under-19 sides, as well as playing 54 VFA games for Box Hill and another eight at Port Melbourne with his older brother Ashley after starting at Doutta Stars, where the Hicks family has a strong legacy.



A serious heart condition brought a premature end to his football career, then tragically his life six years ago while he was sleeping. Doutta Stars and Box Hill each posted their condolences at the time, illustrating the impact Scott – or “Scacs”, as he was known – had at each club, describing him as a “naturally talented, likeable larrikin”. “He’s the reason I started footy,” Hicks said of his dad. “We’d always go for a kick with Dad and my brother. He got a footy in our hands at a young age … it will be the best day of my life if I get drafted after all the work that’s gone in.”



There is plenty of sporting success through the family, beyond just his father. Among Hicks’ immediate family, Christina was a state-league netballer and Brodie represented Australia at the world under-20 athletics championships four years ago, while his cousin, Robbie Hicks, played three games for Richmond in 2010. Hicks (second from left) with fellow draft prospects Mason McGroder, Sam Gayfer and Albert Macgowan at the draft combine. Getty Images “I got lucky with their genetics,” Hicks said. “I got in contact with Robbie, and have been messaging him throughout the year because he’s been through kind of what I’m going through, so he understands it, and has been keeping track of how I’m going.”



Hicks, who models his playing style on that of Swans superstar Isaac Heeney, tried to dodge anything written or said about him this year to maintain his focus in the biggest season of his life. Related Article AFL 2026 ‘An A-plus character’: The prospect from a family of Essendon diehards who could kickstart the Dons He has been a state representative since the under-15s, so being drafted into the AFL has been a long-held and now realistic dream. “There is a fair bit of pressure, and then people writing stuff about you – good, bad, whatever – so that’s when you lean on people you’re close with and talk to them,” Hicks said. “If you’re struggling, or you want to talk about something, that’s when your friends and family are so important. You just have to focus on yourself and listen to your coaches and people who really know you.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

Step off the plane in Cairns and the air hits warm and wet, carrying frangipani and salt. Ten minutes later you’re on the Esplanade at Crystalbrook Riley, five-star and facing the Coral Sea, with seven nights ahead and no real reason to rush them. The reef and the rainforest are a short walk from the lobby for whenever you’re ready. Find your Zen at Crystalbrook Riley. Still water The lagoon sits at the resort’s centre, a sand beach down one side, cabanas the other, a lap lane for those inclined. Because the water is guests-only, it never gets crowded. The poolside menu is Calypso Club’s, carried down to your cabana: Moreton Bay bugs with burnt lime, a Calypso’s Treasure of Havana Club, coconut and kaffir lime. The afternoon is small choices, shaded cabana or open sand, deep end or the shallow edge where the beach slides in. One wild day



Sooner or later, the reef and the rainforest get their day. Your package includes one tour, your pick of four, with the rest bookable on top. The reef day sails on Evolution, a 35-metre superyacht, to two of the outer reefs, Norman, Saxon or Hastings depending on conditions, for five hours in the water and a barbecue lunch of fish, steak and prawns. At Saxon, white-tip reef sharks rest on the sand below the snorkellers and turtles rise for air. Prefer land? A four-wheel drive follows the Bloomfield Track into the Daintree, with a crocodile cruise on the river and a swim at Emmagen Creek. The wildlife option climbs to the Atherton Tablelands for platypus at dusk and a torchlit search for Lumholtz’s tree kangaroos. The fourth rides the Skyrail gondolas over World Heritage rainforest to Kuranda and takes the 1891 railway back down through the Barron Gorge. 



On the days you’re anchored, Eleme Day Spa is on site and a 24-hour gym for anyone with energy to burn. The resort bikes cover the Esplanade boardwalk, past the galleries and night markets, and the reef boats leave from the wharf a short walk south. It is all within reach, and easy to ignore. On the last evening the lagoon empties out and goes gold with the sky, and the only hard part of the week is leaving it. World.title: Community rallies to stop closure of long-standing Brisbane daycare centre
World.content:
NationalQueenslandChildcare Community rallies to stop closure of long-standing Brisbane daycare centre Catherine Strohfeldt November 15, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A community in Brisbane’s south is fighting to stop the closure of a local childcare and kindergarten centre they say has been a community pillar for decades. Western Brisbane local Angelina Tila said she continued to send her children to the YMCA Acacia Ridge Early Learning Centre despite moving away from the suburb years ago. “For my family, this centre has never simply been a childcare facility … our relationship with the centre spans decades,” she said. Angelina Tila and Luke McMahon are among several dozen parents fighting the closure of the YMCA Acacia Ridge Early Learning Centre. Catherine Strohfeldt Parents and staff members at the early learning centre were notified in mid-October Y Queensland (formerly YMCA Queensland) would shutter from December 18, ending more than 40 years of operation at the community organisation’s oldest – and now last standing – childcare centre in the state.



Fellow parent Luke McMahon said the closure meant he was scrambling ahead of Christmas to find a new centre for his daughter. Related Article Exclusive

Schools These schools might have saved the state $456 million: report “It’s not just that, it’s that … it took her about five months before she started feeling comfortable at the centre,” he said. Another parent who expected to keep her son enrolled at the Acacia Ridge Early Learning Centre for kindergarten next year said she was now struggling to find placements at other centres with fewer than three months’ notice. The families have launched several petitions with the Brisbane City Council and online, attracting several hundred signatures.



A Y Queensland spokesperson said the not-for-profit organisation had found it “increasingly challenging” to keep the early learning facility afloat. “The decision to close Acacia Ridge Early Learning Centre was not made lightly,” the spokesperson said. The YMCA Acacia Ridge Early Learning Centre has a scheduled close for December 18. Catherine Strohfeldt “Despite our best efforts, we’ve reached a point where continuing to operate the centre is no longer viable.” The early education facility sits on several blocks leased to Y Queensland until 2050, with the plot also housing sports and recreation fields, a community centre, a special assistance school.



Tila said part of the centre’s appeal was it connection to the community, including the educators’ commitment to children in their care, and the diverse cultural background of the centre’s community. “My children are the only ones who have Fijian heritage in the centre, so [one educator] said to me, ‘how can we celebrate Fiji Day, can we do this?’ – they include everyone,” Tila said. Families were also concerned the early learning centre was subject to conditions laid out in its Brisbane City Council lease more than 50 years ago that would require council approval to change the use of the land to anything but a child care facility. McMahon said he hoped Y Queensland could transfer its lease to another childcare provider, which had occurred for the organisation’s Birtinya centre – which closed down earlier in the year.



The council said decisions concerning the lease fell to Y Queensland. Related Article Early learning Multiple early learning centres to close after failed bid to find buyers The not-for-profit organisation declined to comment on the lease conditions, and could not reveal plans for the site, although a spokesperson said Y Queensland would maintain its presence in the suburb though its other community facilities. Y Queensland said it had checked for vacancies with nearby childcare centres, and emailed families a list of six options in late October.
