World.title: While the past haunts Australian cricket, its future is piling on runs in the Sheffield Shield
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket Opinion While the past haunts Australian cricket, its future is piling on runs in the Sheffield Shield Geoff Lawson Cricket columnist November 15, 2026 — 5:30am

November 15, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

While Pat Cummins conducted his exhausting press conference on Friday in the Cricket NSW indoor centre, shading the dots in a picture more than eight years old in front of a media umbrella field that even Bradman wouldn’t penetrate, a short bounce throw away a more relevant conflict unfolded. A Sheffield Shield match between NSW and South Australia was heading into the third day’s play and a callow experienced youth named Sam Konstas was walking to the crease with a ton under his belt and looking to lengthen the Blues’ lead. Sam Konstas raises his bat after notching another century on Friday. Getty Images Konstas went on to make 173, his second century in four matches. The senior partner in his second wicket stand of 117 was Kurtis Patterson, who averages 144 in Test cricket from two matches. Patterson occupied the crease for 88 balls, making 43. Each is in the frame for a Test recall. Dumped six-Test opener Jake Weatherald scythed a typically rapid 142 in South Australia’s first innings.



Batsmen were suddenly cooking with gas, wind turbine and/or photovoltaic energy at NSW’s Cricket Central at Sydney’s Olympic Park. Shield cricket in Victoria returned home to the MCG, where the groundsman had found the keys to the mower. Ex-Test batsman Peter Handscomb got a patient 323-ball 169 for Victoria, and former Blue Blake Macdonald hit 116. Left-handed Western Australian rookie Corey Wasley, another of the talent-packed 2024 under-19 World Cup team, responded with 179 not out from 337 deliveries, patience being of valuable virtue. Peter Handscomb drives on the way to his latest ton. Getty Images At the ’Gabba Marnus Labuschagne (12) missed out against Tasmania, playing an unbalanced and careless drive, but young guns Jack Clayton (52), Hugh Weibgen (89) and Hugo Burdon (70), also former Australian under-19s representatives, made half centuries. Curators around the country must have read and digested Cricket Australia boss Todd Greenberg’s suggestion that match surfaces need to be a little less like the front lawn and a bit more like the concrete path to the clothesline, although the spinners still aren’t getting a lot of overs.



Nic Maddinson, who was surprisingly summoned to open in the South African series, has been batting in the middle order with modest returns on his reinstatement to state cricket, having been replaced by the exuberant Oliver Davies against the new ball. The bottom line on batting talent and likely Test aspirants has been in the red over the last couple of years as the pitches favoured seam bowling and selectors persisted with failing incumbents while confusing white ball potential with red ball performance. Cooper Connolly is a case in point – his first Test was his fourth first-class game, having never made a century, but 90 on first-class debut. Connolly wore the hi-vis on the bench in South Africa instead of playing the early Shield games at home. He was getting loads of net time when he needed match time. The pathway to the top of the cricket pyramid doesn’t include a statistic for runs and wickets accumulated in the nets and against the “wanger”.



Connolly’s two innings in Cape Town were desultory and no surprise when he failed twice with 29 and nought. Relentless net sessions and full-time drink waiting have never produced improvements in batsmen or bowlers. Australian cricket needs players of his talent to turn potential into performance – one of rugby league super coach Jack Gibson’s sayings, “potential never won nothing,” stands the test of time. Cooper Connolly, dismissed for 27 off 30 balls against England on Friday, will miss the next two rounds of the Sheffield Shield. Getty Images Connolly finds himself in three weeks of white ball cricket, again missing the experience of Sheffield Shield and the opportunity to grow. The reality for Connolly is the young guns mentioned above are edging in front of him in the Test match pecking order at a time when spots are up for grabs.



Twenty-year-old Victorian and much-mentioned left-hand bat Oliver Peake finds himself warming the pine at white ball matches instead of turning out for his home state. He has only played 16 first-class games in his nascent career, averaging under 25, so the proof of the pudding has not yet set. It will be interesting to see over the next two One Day Internationals and five Twenty20s if Peake gets a game for Australia. If not, then his lesson time has been severely restricted. Young gun Ollie Peake in action for Australia in June. Getty Images There are players who see their international careers moulded around 50- and 20-over cricket, and with World Cups and Olympics on the horizon there will be ample opportunities to impress, but choosing Test batsmen on white ball form is bound for trouble. Less so for bowlers, and the debut of Mahli Beardman (6-24) against England is a cause for genuine excitement. Konstas must have confused his format ambitions in the first innings versus South Australia when he charged down the pitch to the challenging pace of Jordan Buckingham and coughed up a simple chance to the infield.



Perhaps he was intoxicated by the uninhibited stroke play at the other end from Davies, or maybe looking for a slot on an Indian Premier League auction list. His second innings sprung from a study in discipline, well-judged strokeplay, then domination; just what you might expect from a Test-calibre batsman. Davies may be a “like for like” choice if Travis Head is unavailable – opening the batting when cannon fire is required on a fiery pitch, or settling in to bruise the old ball and tiring bowlers on peaceful decks. NSW opener Ollie Davies. Getty Images Konstas looks primed to join Matthew Renshaw, taking first guard against New Zealand in three weeks’ time in the first Test in Perth, but the competition for spots all through the order (Steve Smith is safe at four) has found some higher gears thanks to Sheffield Shield performances. The media scrimmage that semi-circled their wagons around Cummins wrote and filmed the explanations and nuances from a cricket match in the dimming past, admittedly a past with few ghosts.



If they wanted to examine the present and get an impression of what the future of Australian cricket is going to look like, then they needed simply to turn their tripods, their gaze and their recording machines 180 degrees to find the newest field of dreams. Or it could be a nine out of 10, and they’re going to be playing arenas in three years.” The answer to London’s woes is gaining attention in the NSW parliament, after the report from the NSW State of Live Music inquiry was tabled this week.



Related Article Live music ‘Concert-goers pay’: Ticket levy could raise $3m for Sydney’s struggling music scene In the UK, following a parliamentary inquiry, a plan was devised to introduce a £1 levy on tickets for concerts with capacity for more than 5000 patrons, to be placed in a trust to fund the grassroots music scene. Since it began in 2025, it has raised millions of pounds. Artists can choose to add the levy to their concert tickets. When it began, American artists, including Diana Ross, Lynyrd Skynyrd and Bowling for Soup, were the first to participate in the scheme, Collins said. Now, artists such as Olivia Dean, Florence and The Machine, Harry Styles, Lily Allen and Take That have added “the pound,” as Collins calls it. Sam Fender has also committed to the initiative for next year. “We’ve got over 130 tours now carrying the pound,” Collins said.



So far this year, the fund has raised £2.5 million, has another £6 million “guaranteed” with partnered artists and expects to distribute £7 to £8 million in 2027. A board of industry experts distributes the trust’s money in funding rounds. The first round, Collins said, went to seven programs covering artists, venues, promoters and festivals. One helped ease touring costs, another helped venues convert high utility bills into green energy, and there was a boost for small and micro festivals. An AC/DC concert at Accor Stadium, Sydney, in November 2025. Venues NSW/Brett Costello The trust also helps communities in Northern Ireland and Scotland learn how to stage, market, promote and run an event, while also putting young artists on stages for younger audiences. Of the 37 recommendations from the NSW State of Live Music inquiry, a ticket levy is the frontrunner. After three hearings and 105 submissions, the committee found rising operating costs, insurance premiums, user-pays policing charges, changing audience behaviours and limited artist development pathways were stifling the sector.



Committee chair Sarah Kaine said a ticket levy would create sustainable funding to support the next generation of artists and venues. Tame Impala performing in Australia this year. Richard Clifford The Australian Music Venue Foundation, a lobby group representing grassroots music venues in Australia, initially proposed a $1 levy on every ticket for shows with a capacity above 5000 patrons. The organisation estimates that five major Sydney venues alone could generate $3 million to $3.15 million each year. Touring artists or punters would pay the levy through an opt-in scheme. Earlier this year, pop star Olivia Dean donated $1 for each ticket sold on her Australian tour to the organisation. Meanwhile, NSW Greens MP Cate Faehrmann believes consumers already bear various ticketing costs, and multinational corporations should fund the local scene through a tax increase.



Teens at the all-ages Orange festival, The Gig. Audrey Richardson For Collins, the industry’s sustainability, from kids in regional towns having access to music to venues being able to afford insurance, is core to the survival of live music. And he doesn’t see why Sydney can’t have the same. “There’s the opportunity to build a similar coalition here,” he said. “It’s promoters, agents, and managers ... that gives you the momentum.”

World.title: An old copper wire in the bush: why the US had to shut down its airspace
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaAviation An old copper wire in the bush: why the US had to shut down its airspace Michael Koziol Updated November 15, 2026 — 7:16am ,first published 6:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Washington: A routine upgrade to an old copper wire communications network in a remote area of the United States was responsible for bringing the nation’s air traffic to a halt, officials said. They effectively ruled out a cyberattack or the involvement of any artificial intelligence systems, adding that the decision to order a nationwide ground stop was taken out of “an abundance of caution”. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy with Federal Aviation Administration administrator Bryan Bedford on Saturday. AP Photo/Tom Brenner Speaking at a news conference on Saturday morning (US time), Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the instability in the system occurred while telecom contractor L3Harris was undertaking routine maintenance at a remote location to upgrade copper wiring to fibre-optic. “That router that was being replaced as we switched from copper to fibre, it started flooding other routers in our air traffic control system,” he said. “We had over 1000 connection attempts every four to five seconds.”



Those connection attempts began to overwhelm the system, leading to communications issues with airplanes, and disrupted radar feeds. “When we see that, your safety is paramount. We shut down the airspace.” Officials said they did not yet know whether the initial problem was caused by contractor incompetence, a wrong configuration or a faulty new router installed in the system. Passengers at George Bush International Airport in Houston on Saturday. Delays were expected to continue over the weekend. AP Photo/Ashley Landis Duffy said they did not believe any form of nefarious activity was involved. “Once we were able to isolate the work that was being done at that location, all of our systems came back online,” he said. “This was an FAA [Federal Aviation Administration] system that didn’t meet the moment, or a contractor didn’t meet the moment, or equipment didn’t meet the moment.”



L3Harris said it has been modernising the communications infrastructure behind the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA. More than 70 per cent of planned copper to fibre optic conversions have been completed, it said. The company was supporting the FAA investigation, and took the matter and its impact on travellers seriously, L3Harris said. The incident has put the spotlight on America’s ageing air traffic control infrastructure. AP Photo/Ashley Landis FAA administrator Bryan Bedford apologised to the travelling public for the disruption. He said that by the time the ground stop was ordered at 3.45pm Washington time on Friday (Saturday AEDT), about 30,000 of the day’s 50,000 scheduled flights had already landed or were airborne. Of the 20,000 remaining, 12,000 had to be cancelled - 9000 commercial flights and 3000 private. There were significant flow-on effects into Saturday, with another 4000 or 5000 flights expected to be cancelled, but the system was expected to recover by Sunday, Bedford said.



“We see zero evidence of anything nefarious and no evidence of anything AI-related. We have an equipment issue,” he said. Asked why maintenance was being done on a Friday afternoon rather than during a quieter time, Duffy said upgrades in remote areas were done during the day, whereas major airports were done at night. Several thousand flights would also be cancelled on Saturday (US time), officials said, as airlines worked to recover from the shutdown. AP Photo/Ashley Landis Rebecca Guy, the FAA’s acting chief technology officer, said the agency had not realised that a problem at an isolated location could have such wide flow-on consequences. The incident has put the focus back on the US’ ageing air traffic control infrastructure, which still relies in part on copper wires and floppy disks.



Earlier this month, the FAA announced plans to end the use of floppy disks by the end of 2028. The Enterprise Information Display System would replace four systems that date back to the 1980s. Bedford said the system was so old (he described it as “1G”) that it was no longer in production and cost about $US1 billion a year just to sustain. Old Cisco 600 routers were constantly being replaced, he said. Rebecca Guy, acting chief technology officer at the FAA, said the agency had not realised such widespread consequences were possible. AP Photo/Tom Brenner “This is probably one of the worst kept secrets in government - that this [communications] system needs to be replaced.” Last year, Congress appropriated $US12.5 billion ($18.2 billion) for system upgrades, but Duffy had already announced the Trump administration wanted $US30 billion more. He now wants as much as $US50 billion.



“Everyone says they want to do it, and the president is pushing it, but we don’t get the resources,” Duffy said on Saturday. “How long are we going to wait, America and Congress?” Related Article On the ground

Airports Love? No, just thousands of dispirited, stranded passengers, actually On Friday night at the White House, when a reporter pointed out to Duffy that the Republicans have controlled Congress for the past two years, he asked her which news organisation she was with, and suggested she had not properly covered Donald Trump’s fight for funding. Democratic congressman Robert Garcia, who will likely chair the House Oversight Committee once Democrats gain control next year, said there must be “full public transparency” about what happened and why. “We need answers to ensure our systems and technology are funded and upgraded to ensure the safety of the public,” Garcia said.



The major US airlines were still grappling with the fallout on Saturday, with planes and crews out of place from where they would usually be located. Delta encouraged passengers to rebook for Monday if their plans allowed. United Airlines said most flights were operating normally, but some were delayed or cancelled. World.title: How a late father’s early lessons and a mother’s constant presence shaped an AFL draft hopeful
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 How a late father’s early lessons and a mother’s constant presence shaped an AFL draft hopeful Marc McGowan November 15, 2026 — 7:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. There was always someone in Lachie Hicks’ corner when things got tough in his draft year. In a world where sports parents can be overbearing, the talented Western Jets midfielder, who also played for Altona and Wesley College, has had a far more positive experience with his mum and No.1 fan, Christina. Lachie Hicks has a special kind of motivation spurring him on into the AFL draft this month. AFL Photos “Mum’s kind of everything, to be honest,” Hicks told this masthead. “She comes to every single game. She doesn’t say too much – she kind of stays away – but I know she always wants the best for me, and obviously, ideally, she wants me to make it [as an AFL player].



Editor's pick AFL 2026 ‘It stuffs up every club’: Why an AFL move left the likely No.1 draft pick in shock “She’s always been my biggest support, and it’s always been there for me as well – every bad game, every good game.” Hicks averaged almost 29 disposals, five clearances and 1.4 goals for the Jets in an outstanding Talent League campaign this past season, then put his athletic prowess on display with top-10 results in draft combine testing in agility, the two-kilometre time trial and the 20-metre sprint. His late father, Scott, introduced him and his other son, Brodie to football not long after they could walk. Scott played for Essendon’s reserves and under-19 sides, as well as playing 54 VFA games for Box Hill and another eight at Port Melbourne with his older brother Ashley after starting at Doutta Stars, where the Hicks family has a strong legacy.



A serious heart condition brought a premature end to his football career, then tragically his life six years ago while he was sleeping. Doutta Stars and Box Hill each posted their condolences at the time, illustrating the impact Scott – or “Scacs”, as he was known – had at each club, describing him as a “naturally talented, likeable larrikin”. “He’s the reason I started footy,” Hicks said of his dad. “We’d always go for a kick with Dad and my brother. He got a footy in our hands at a young age … it will be the best day of my life if I get drafted after all the work that’s gone in.”



There is plenty of sporting success through the family, beyond just his father. Among Hicks’ immediate family, Christina was a state-league netballer and Brodie represented Australia at the world under-20 athletics championships four years ago, while his cousin, Robbie Hicks, played three games for Richmond in 2010. Hicks (second from left) with fellow draft prospects Mason McGroder, Sam Gayfer and Albert Macgowan at the draft combine. Getty Images “I got lucky with their genetics,” Hicks said. “I got in contact with Robbie, and have been messaging him throughout the year because he’s been through kind of what I’m going through, so he understands it, and has been keeping track of how I’m going.”



Hicks, who models his playing style on that of Swans superstar Isaac Heeney, tried to dodge anything written or said about him this year to maintain his focus in the biggest season of his life. Related Article AFL 2026 ‘An A-plus character’: The prospect from a family of Essendon diehards who could kickstart the Dons He has been a state representative since the under-15s, so being drafted into the AFL has been a long-held and now realistic dream. “There is a fair bit of pressure, and then people writing stuff about you – good, bad, whatever – so that’s when you lean on people you’re close with and talk to them,” Hicks said. “If you’re struggling, or you want to talk about something, that’s when your friends and family are so important. You just have to focus on yourself and listen to your coaches and people who really know you.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

Step off the plane in Cairns and the air hits warm and wet, carrying frangipani and salt. Ten minutes later you’re on the Esplanade at Crystalbrook Riley, five-star and facing the Coral Sea, with seven nights ahead and no real reason to rush them. The reef and the rainforest are a short walk from the lobby for whenever you’re ready. Find your Zen at Crystalbrook Riley. Still water The lagoon sits at the resort’s centre, a sand beach down one side, cabanas the other, a lap lane for those inclined. Because the water is guests-only, it never gets crowded. The poolside menu is Calypso Club’s, carried down to your cabana: Moreton Bay bugs with burnt lime, a Calypso’s Treasure of Havana Club, coconut and kaffir lime. The afternoon is small choices, shaded cabana or open sand, deep end or the shallow edge where the beach slides in. One wild day



Sooner or later, the reef and the rainforest get their day. Your package includes one tour, your pick of four, with the rest bookable on top. The reef day sails on Evolution, a 35-metre superyacht, to two of the outer reefs, Norman, Saxon or Hastings depending on conditions, for five hours in the water and a barbecue lunch of fish, steak and prawns. At Saxon, white-tip reef sharks rest on the sand below the snorkellers and turtles rise for air. Prefer land? A four-wheel drive follows the Bloomfield Track into the Daintree, with a crocodile cruise on the river and a swim at Emmagen Creek. The wildlife option climbs to the Atherton Tablelands for platypus at dusk and a torchlit search for Lumholtz’s tree kangaroos. The fourth rides the Skyrail gondolas over World Heritage rainforest to Kuranda and takes the 1891 railway back down through the Barron Gorge. 



On the days you’re anchored, Eleme Day Spa is on site and a 24-hour gym for anyone with energy to burn. The resort bikes cover the Esplanade boardwalk, past the galleries and night markets, and the reef boats leave from the wharf a short walk south. It is all within reach, and easy to ignore. On the last evening the lagoon empties out and goes gold with the sky, and the only hard part of the week is leaving it. World.content:
NationalQueenslandChildcare Community rallies to stop closure of long-standing Brisbane daycare centre Catherine Strohfeldt November 15, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. A community in Brisbane’s south is fighting to stop the closure of a local childcare and kindergarten centre they say has been a community pillar for decades. Western Brisbane local Angelina Tila said she continued to send her children to the YMCA Acacia Ridge Early Learning Centre despite moving away from the suburb years ago. “For my family, this centre has never simply been a childcare facility … our relationship with the centre spans decades,” she said. Angelina Tila and Luke McMahon are among several dozen parents fighting the closure of the YMCA Acacia Ridge Early Learning Centre. Catherine Strohfeldt Parents and staff members at the early learning centre were notified in mid-October Y Queensland (formerly YMCA Queensland) would shutter from December 18, ending more than 40 years of operation at the community organisation’s oldest – and now last standing – childcare centre in the state.



Fellow parent Luke McMahon said the closure meant he was scrambling ahead of Christmas to find a new centre for his daughter. Related Article Exclusive

Schools These schools might have saved the state $456 million: report “It’s not just that, it’s that … it took her about five months before she started feeling comfortable at the centre,” he said. Another parent who expected to keep her son enrolled at the Acacia Ridge Early Learning Centre for kindergarten next year said she was now struggling to find placements at other centres with fewer than three months’ notice. The families have launched several petitions with the Brisbane City Council and online, attracting several hundred signatures.



A Y Queensland spokesperson said the not-for-profit organisation had found it “increasingly challenging” to keep the early learning facility afloat. “The decision to close Acacia Ridge Early Learning Centre was not made lightly,” the spokesperson said. The YMCA Acacia Ridge Early Learning Centre has a scheduled close for December 18. Catherine Strohfeldt “Despite our best efforts, we’ve reached a point where continuing to operate the centre is no longer viable.” The early education facility sits on several blocks leased to Y Queensland until 2050, with the plot also housing sports and recreation fields, a community centre, a special assistance school.



Tila said part of the centre’s appeal was it connection to the community, including the educators’ commitment to children in their care, and the diverse cultural background of the centre’s community. “My children are the only ones who have Fijian heritage in the centre, so [one educator] said to me, ‘how can we celebrate Fiji Day, can we do this?’ – they include everyone,” Tila said. Families were also concerned the early learning centre was subject to conditions laid out in its Brisbane City Council lease more than 50 years ago that would require council approval to change the use of the land to anything but a child care facility. McMahon said he hoped Y Queensland could transfer its lease to another childcare provider, which had occurred for the organisation’s Birtinya centre – which closed down earlier in the year.



The council said decisions concerning the lease fell to Y Queensland. Related Article Early learning Multiple early learning centres to close after failed bid to find buyers The not-for-profit organisation declined to comment on the lease conditions, and could not reveal plans for the site, although a spokesperson said Y Queensland would maintain its presence in the suburb though its other community facilities. Y Queensland said it had checked for vacancies with nearby childcare centres, and emailed families a list of six options in late October. World.title: Two Americans, two journeys, but how many roads?
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Two shepherds met recently. One wore white, the other black. They both carried their faith with them to the meeting; the one in white conspicuously so, the other beneath the hood. Their meeting made news worldwide, for one was Pope Leo and the other was Bob Dylan, songwriter legend and Nobel laureate. Shepherds both, but with different flocks, and with different meanings to the description.

Pope Leo tends a global flock of more than a billion followers of the Catholic Church. Dylan’s flock cannot be quantified, and nor would he consider himself as tending it, but in many of his followers there is an unbreakable thread of devotion. His music has tested that strand over the course of a career of almost 70 years. But to paraphrase the man himself, he’s an artist, he don’t look back. One of those followers, as it happens, in a sort of divine coincidence, is the Pope, also from the American Midwest, the former from Chicago, the latter from Duluth.

Pope Leo and Bob Dylan meet at the Vatican. LaPresse via AP

Pope Leo quoted Dylan’s lyric in the preface to a book entitled Disarmed and Disarming: Peace Is a Gift, published by the Vatican Publishing House. The words weren’t from one of Dylan’s universally known songs such as Blowin’ in the Wind, but from an ultra-obscure one from 1963 that was never released. The song was Go Away You Bomb, the lyric the Pope quoted, “I hate you cause yer man-made and man-owned, an’ man-handled.” Some may say, it was easy to see why it never saw the light of day.

At the recent meeting in the Apostolic Palace in Rome, the Pope gave Dylan a rosary, while Dylan gave the Pope a copy of his book Chronicles: Volume One.

World.title: New study shows what does and doesn't work for ADHD kids
World.content:
A new study says giving kids with ADHD extra time for tasks and more frequent breaks while in class may not affect their behaviour.

Researchers from Florida International University got more than 200 primary school children at summer camps in the US to switch between taking and not taking medication and different classroom environments.

The study, published in the Jama Pediatrics medical journal found medication improved the kids' rule-following and test results but the adaptations in the classroom, including extended time for tasks, frequent breaks, using a standing desk and having a low distraction space, didn't affect their behaviour or achievement.

University of Auckland development neuropsychology expert Professor Karen Waldie said the study came as no surprise to those who work with children with ADHD and do research in the area.

"Procrastination and time blindness are one of the key symptoms of ADHD. The main reason for the benefits of medication and behavioural therapy comes down to the brain chemical dopamine and the reward system of the brain.

"Stimulant medication such as Ritalin works to increase dopamine in the prefrontal cortex and this helps those with ADHD focus on the task at hand: right now."

Waldie said the study found that medication and behaviour therapy improved academic productivity and rule-following behaviour in the classroom, but accommodations such as extended time on tasks had no effect.

"Another thing that works in a similar way as stimulant meds is a hard deadline and quick consequences of actions - so basically people with ADHD work very well under pressure, which gives them a dopamine reward hit, and do less well when there is time available to perform a task like a test or when there is a distant or inconsequential reward."

Consultant clinical psychologist and honorary senior lecturer at University of Auckland's Te Ara Hāro Centre for Infant, Child and Adolescent Mental Health, Dr Melanie Woodfield, said the study is an important signal from a carefully designed experiment, but needs testing in the real world.

"Positive behaviour supports, medication, or both, are known to improve academic performance and decrease challenging behaviour for many children with ADHD."

Woodfield said the study leaned towards strict control, excluding children with low IQ or autism alongside ADHD, and taking place in a specialist American summer camp treatment classroom, where staff even counted the ratio of teacher praise to commands, to ensure it was 3:1.

"That's quite far removed from a messy, complex, real world classroom with fewer resources, stretched teachers, and children with higher needs. The authors themselves recommend the study now needs to be repeated in real- world classrooms, where they expect the effects would be weaker.

"Ideally, we should also acknowledge that some accommodations do work for some children, some of the time," Woodfield said.

"However, this research suggests that a blanket, Oprah-style giveaway 'You get extra time! And you get extra time' may not return reliable dividends, compared to behavioural approaches and/or medication."

Clinical psychologist Giselle Bahr said there's been no specific research about what happens when children with ADHD are offered structured classroom changes, and while the study showed they did not make a difference to behaviour in this instance, it was food for thought.

"It's like, of course it would make sense to give a child more time if they're struggling, but it looks like it's not as simple as that," she said.

"What we already know is that behavioural strategies help children and they don't have any adverse effects, there's no risks associated with them. We already know that methylphenidate changes children's behaviour in the short term, but over the long term it leads to worse outcomes."

Bahr said the study had not been done in a normal classroom setting, but at a summer camp during one-hour class periods, and the adjustments were randomised.

"The rest of the hours of the day they were doing fun activities and the classes were small. They only had 15 to 18 students in them and there were two adults in each of those classrooms. It's not an exact match with how a classroom generally run, so we have to be careful about what we extrapolate from that.

"It doesn't look like they matched a child's kind of need for what's going to help them learn better in a classroom, they just kind of trailed these adaptations."

She said the researchers, Fabiano and Pelham, had authored papers about children and ADHD for decades and said behavioural interventions remained an important, low-risk strategy for supporting children with ADHD.

"Some of their previous work looked at the best order for interventions. They found that starting with behavioural strategies was more effective than starting with medication. Also, that ADHD medication made things worse for children in the long term, even if it produced improvements in the short-term."

Bahr said ADHD medication came with serious risks, including reduced growth, a risk of psychotic symptoms, and cardiovascular problems.

World.title: Cyber protection of critical infrastructure is 'priority work' but taking at least a year
World.content:
Government officials are working on policies to strengthen cyber protection of critical infrastructure more than seven months after consultations closed.

"This remains priority work," they told RNZ this week.

They are working through submissions to refine policy options, after the February-April public consultation.

"Our intention is to provide advice to ministers early in the next term of government."

Friday's Microsoft Outlook outage has sparked fresh questions about New Zealand's vulnerability to global technology glitches and whether government was doing enough.

"From a cyber security perspective, the government needs to be much more engaged," said frequent critic Don Christie of Catalyst IT.

Other countries move

In early 2026, the officials laid out two new proposed categories of infrastructure that could be subject to mandatory minimum requirements to enhance cyber security and resilience.

Official documents said critical national infrastructure was "increasingly vulnerable to cyber attack".

"Current regulatory settings are not designed to drive a consistent uplift in cyber security across the critical infrastructure system".

It was acknowledged New Zealand's approach was not keeping pace with other countries.

This week, Australia flagged changes to criminal law to crack down on future breaches by artificial intelligence companies, after a frontier artificial intelligence agent hacked government systems for sensitive information in OpenAI tests.

The European Union has mandated stringent cyber security measures for operators of critical infrastructure since 2024.

The EU has also moved to boost the ways consumers and businesses determine which products are cybersecure, with more measures coming in two months ago.

'Priority work'

The government's 'Enhancing the cyber security of critical infrastructure' work revolves around a public consultation that ran from February to April.

"Submissions have since been worked through to refine policy options," the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet said.

It said the 2026 submissions from the public would be shared in due course. However, the website carries submissions from three years ago.

"Our intention is that submissions would be published on the DPMC website around the same time in 2027."

Big new threats in months

Since the consultation in early 2026, the threats globally and here have escalated rapidly, and morphed greatly, with the advent of frontier AI models that have launched unauthorised, autonomous swarm attacks on government and commercial targets in testing.

In June, Five Eyes cyber agencies warned that frontier models would fundamentally alter offensive and defensive capabilities.

"The timeline is not years, it is months."

In New Zealand, the National Cyber Security Centre said that, by early 2027, "malicious actors may have access to advanced AI capabilities currently available only through leading frontier AI models".

Attacks could occur with little warning and organisations should prepare now, it said in September.

Early 2027 co-incides with when some policy on enhancing cyber security for critical infrastructure might emerge.

Concrete achievements

The proposals have envisaged "a minimum level of cyber risk management by all critical infrastructure entities" and effective management of cyber threats affecting national security.

In addition, a category of critical infrastructure of national significance (CINS) could have additional obligations beyond the minimum requirements.

As of early 2026, the documents said, "Cyber risks are generally not well understood or collectively managed to a consistent level across New Zealand's critical infrastructure system".

The critical infrastructure work was signed off by Christopher Luxon as national security and intelligence minister. It is part of a cyber security strategy 2026-2030 the government put out in February.

RNZ asked officials what concrete achievements there had been.
